Bump-and-revalue sensitivities with Monte Carlo: common random numbers / overview
atoms.text:
# Bump-and-revalue sensitivities with Monte Carlo: common random numbers

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this when a sensitivity is computed by repricing a simulated value with a parameter moved up and down.

atoms.title: Bump-and-revalue sensitivities with Monte Carlo: common random numbers / Common random numbers
atoms.text:
## Common random numbers

- Draw every random number once (for example a fixed array `Z` of shape (paths, steps), generated from the stated seed before any pricing) and reuse the same array for the base, up and down valuations. Only the parameter changes between them.
- A pricing function that draws fresh numbers on each call (calling a generator inside the function, or advancing one global generator) gives the up and down prices independent noise. The difference quotient then carries noise of order $\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{SE}_{\mathrm{price}}/h$, which for a small bump $h$ is far larger than the sensitivity itself.
- Recompute every quantity that depends on the bumped parameter inside the revaluation (simulated paths, drift or mean-reversion terms, seasonal levels, discounting); keep everything else, including the random draws, identical.
- Two layouts of the random numbers (array shape, draw order, one scalar draw per step versus one array) give different paths, so prices from two layouts agree only within sampling error, never digit for digit. Do not assert that a revalued base price equals an earlier figure exactly: price the base, up and down with one function and one array, and let that base replace the earlier figure.

atoms.title: Bump-and-revalue sensitivities with Monte Carlo: common random numbers / Difference quotient and its error
atoms.text:
## Difference quotient and its error

Central difference: $(V(p+h) - V(p-h)) / (2h)$ with the bump and denominator exactly as the task states them. For a relative bump of $x\%$ the parameter moves by $h = (x/100)\,p$. Compute the quotient path by path from the paired payoffs, $d_i = (\text{payoff}_i(p+h) - \text{payoff}_i(p-h)) / (2h)$; the sensitivity is the mean of $d_i$ and its standard error is `np.std(d, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(N)`.

When an output field records a bump size → write it in the unit its definition or the stated input gives: a relative change as a fraction (0.01 for one percent) where the input is a fraction, percentage points where the field is defined in percent, an absolute parameter increment where the bump is absolute → check that the written value, applied through the stated formula, reproduces the parameter change used in the calculation.

atoms.title: Bump-and-revalue sensitivities with Monte Carlo: common random numbers / Check
atoms.text:
## Check

Rerun the sensitivity with a second seed (same number of paths): with common random numbers the two values agree within a few standard errors; with independent draws they can differ in sign. Halving $h$ should change a smooth sensitivity only slightly.

atoms.title: CIR short-rate transitions and discount bonds / overview
atoms.text:
# CIR short-rate transitions and discount bonds

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this reference for a nonnegative square-root rate process, exact discrete transition likelihood and affine zero-coupon valuation. Historical estimation and pricing use different probability measures unless a modeling assumption explicitly equates them. A fitted historical rate process is not automatically a calibrated market discount curve.

Map notation, calendar-time increments, rate scale and probability measure to the stated model. If definitions conflict, distinguish the supplied convention from the mathematical model rather than silently mixing them. All formulas below use consistent time units and decimal rates; they do not support negative observations without an explicit model extension.

atoms.title: CIR short-rate transitions and discount bonds / 1. Process and moments
atoms.text:
## 1. Process and moments

Here r is the short rate; $\kappa  > 0$ is reversion speed, $\theta  > 0$ the long-run rate, $\sigma  > 0$ the square-root diffusion coefficient, and W standard Brownian motion under the chosen measure.

CIR dynamics:

$$
\mathrm{d}r = \kappa \cdot (\theta -r)\cdot \mathrm{d}t + \sigma \cdot \sqrt{r}\cdot \mathrm{d}W
$$

For annual time, $\kappa$ has inverse-year units. Rescaling a rate $r_{\mathrm{new}} = a\cdot r$ changes $\theta$ to $a\theta$ and $\sigma$ to $\sqrt{a}\cdot \sigma$, while $\kappa$ is unchanged. Rescaling percentages is not the same as changing the clock.

Conditional mean over a positive interval h, given current rate r:

$$
\operatorname{mean}_{h} = \theta  + (r-\theta )\cdot \exp (-\kappa \cdot h)
$$

Conditional variance over the same interval:

$$
\mathrm{var}_{h} = r\cdot \sigma ^{2}\cdot \exp (-\kappa \cdot h)\cdot (1-\exp (-\kappa \cdot h))/\kappa  + \theta \cdot \sigma ^{2}\cdot (1-\exp (-\kappa \cdot h))^{2}/(2\cdot \kappa )
$$

These follow from the first two moment equations. They provide a scale and time-decay check independent of a density parameterization.

Feller ratio for the zero boundary:

$$
\mathrm{Feller}_{\mathrm{ratio}} = 2\cdot \kappa \cdot \theta /\sigma ^{2}
$$

For r initially positive, ratio >= 1 makes zero inaccessible. A smaller positive ratio permits hitting zero but does not make the exact process negative; the ordinary Euler approximation may nevertheless go negative. Failure of this condition does not invalidate the positive-parameter transition law.

atoms.title: CIR short-rate transitions and discount bonds / 2. Exact transition and likelihood
atoms.text:
## 2. Exact transition and likelihood

For current rate $r \ge  0$ and interval $h > 0$, define a positive scale $s_{h}$, degrees of freedom $\nu$, and noncentrality $\lambda _{h}$ [1,2]. The noncentrality is a dimensionless parameter, not a standard deviation.

Transition scale:

$$
s_{h} = \sigma ^{2}\cdot (1-\exp (-\kappa \cdot h))/(4\cdot \kappa )
$$

Degrees of freedom:

$$
\nu  = 4\cdot \kappa \cdot \theta /\sigma ^{2}
$$

Noncentrality, including mean-reversion decay of the initial state:

$$
\lambda _{h} = \exp (-\kappa \cdot h)\cdot r/s_{h}
$$

Conditional next rate as a scaled noncentral $\chi$-square random variable:

$$
\begin{gathered}
r_{\mathrm{next}} = s_{h} \cdot  Y \\
Y \sim \text{noncentral }\chi^2(\nu,\lambda_h)
\end{gathered}
$$

If $f_{\mathrm{ncx2}}$ is the density of Y, changing variables gives the rate density. The Jacobian is parameter-dependent and belongs in estimation.

Conditional log density for a positive observed rate x:

$$
\ln p(x \vert  r,h) = \ln f_{\mathrm{ncx2}}(x/s_{h}; \nu ,\lambda _{h}) - \log (s_{h})
$$

Conditional log likelihood of successive observed rates $r_{i}$ at times $t_{i}$:

$$
\mathrm{LL} = \sum _{i=1}^{n} \ln p(r_{i} \vert  r_{i-1}, t_{i}-t_{i-1})
$$

Time increments refer to consecutive retained observations. Equal business-day steps and elapsed calendar fractions are different models of the observation clock. A missing observation does not itself create an additional observed transition. Direct evaluation of a small density can underflow; its log-density is the appropriate numerical quantity. Exact or rounded zeros need an explicit observation/boundary treatment: assigning a tiny positive replacement changes the likelihood.

The noncentral $\chi$-square mean and variance imply the moment checks:

$$
\operatorname{E}[r_{\mathrm{next}}] = s_{h}\cdot (\nu +\lambda _{h})
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}[r_{\mathrm{next}}] = 2\cdot s_{h}^{2}\cdot (\nu +2\cdot \lambda _{h})
$$

As h tends to zero, the conditional mean tends to r and variance tends to zero. At $r=0$ the noncentrality vanishes, leaving a scaled central $\chi$-square law.

atoms.title: CIR short-rate transitions and discount bonds / Transition-parameterization consistency
atoms.text:
## Transition-parameterization consistency

Some density expressions use $c_h=1/(2s_h)$ rather than the scale $s_h$. With the transition definitions above, the equivalent density is:

$$
p(x\mid r,h)=2c_h\,f_{\mathrm{ncx2}}\left(2c_hx;\nu,2c_he^{-\kappa h}r\right)
$$

The initial state in noncentrality decays by $e^{-\kappa h}$, and the density includes its transformation Jacobian. A scale taken from one convention and a noncentrality from another need not describe CIR. An independent short-interval check is:

$$
\mathrm{E}[r_{t+h}\mid r_t=r]=r+\kappa(\theta-r)h+O(h^2),\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(r_{t+h}\mid r_t=r)=\sigma^2rh+O(h^2)
$$

At $r=0$ the leading variance term is zero and the next order matters. These checks distinguish a formula's stochastic meaning without selecting an unspecified calibration convention. If two supplied transition formulas disagree, keep their parameterizations separate and identify the conflict; the standard process does not make contradictory formulas equal.

atoms.title: CIR short-rate transitions and discount bonds / 3. Pricing measure and affine bond
atoms.text:
## 3. Pricing measure and affine bond

For bond pricing, $\kappa$ and $\theta$ in this section are risk-neutral parameters. Historical likelihood usually estimates physical-measure parameters. Equating the two sets is an additional assumption, not a consequence of maximum likelihood. The original CIR paper includes a risk-premium adjustment; it is absorbed into the risk-neutral coefficients here [1].

A claim paying one unit after remaining maturity $\tau$ has risk-neutral value:

$$
\operatorname{P}(r,\tau ) = \operatorname{E}_{Q}[\exp (-\int _{0}^{\tau} r_{s} \mathrm{d}s) \vert  r_{0}=r]
$$

Affine representation:

$$
\operatorname{P}(r,\tau ) = \exp (a(\tau ) - B(\tau )\cdot r)
$$

For $\sigma  > 0$, the following scaled-exponential form avoids exponentials growing with maturity.

Auxiliary decay speed:

$$
\gamma  = \sqrt{\kappa ^{2}+2\cdot \sigma ^{2}}
$$

Decaying exponential and denominator:

$$
\operatorname{E}_{\tau} = \exp (-\gamma \cdot \tau )
$$

$$
H_{\tau} = (\gamma +\kappa )\cdot (1-\operatorname{E}_{\tau}) + 2\cdot \gamma \cdot \operatorname{E}_{\tau}
$$

Rate loading in the affine price:

$$
B(\tau ) = 2\cdot (1-\operatorname{E}_{\tau})/H_{\tau}
$$

Logarithm of the affine prefactor, $a(\tau)=\ln A(\tau)$:

$$
a(\tau ) = (2\cdot \kappa \cdot \theta /\sigma ^{2})\cdot (\ln (2\cdot \gamma /H_{\tau}) + (\kappa -\gamma )\cdot \tau /2)
$$

For very small $\tau$, accurate evaluation of $1-\exp (-\gamma \cdot \tau )$ matters. At $\tau =0, B=0, a=0$ and $\operatorname{P}=1$.

The Riccati equations provide an independent characterization; primes mean derivatives in remaining maturity:

$$
B' = 1-\kappa \cdot B-0.5\cdot \sigma ^{2}\cdot B^{2}
$$

$$
(a)' = -\kappa \cdot \theta \cdot B
$$

Their initial conditions are $B(0)=0$ and $a(0)=0$. The negative quadratic term belongs in B', not its positive version.

For $\sigma =0$ the path is deterministic and division by $\sigma^{2}$ is unnecessary. The integrated short rate is:

$$
I(\tau ) = \theta \cdot \tau  + (r-\theta )\cdot (1-\exp (-\kappa \cdot \tau ))/\kappa
$$

Deterministic-limit bond price:

$$
\operatorname{P}(r,\tau ) = \exp (-I(\tau ))
$$

atoms.title: CIR short-rate transitions and discount bonds / 4. Yield, forward and scope checks
atoms.text:
## 4. Yield, forward and scope checks

Continuous zero yield for $\tau  > 0$:

$$
y(\tau ) = -\ln (\operatorname{P}(r,\tau ))/\tau
$$

The exponent $-\ln (\operatorname{P})$ equals $\tau y$, not the annualized yield. An observed par or coupon-equivalent yield is not inherently a zero yield.

Continuous average forward over $a < b$:

$$
f_{\mathrm{avg}}(a,b) = (\ln (\operatorname{P}(r,a))-\ln (\operatorname{P}(r,b)))/(b-a)
$$

Instantaneous forward at remaining maturity $\tau$:

$$
f_{\mathrm{inst}}(\tau ) = -(a)'(\tau ) + B'(\tau )\cdot r
$$

A finite interval average is not the derivative at either endpoint. With nonnegative paths, $0<\operatorname{P}\le 1$ and P is nonincreasing in maturity; nonnegative B makes price nonincreasing in the current short rate. At vanishing maturity y and $f_{\mathrm{inst}}$ approach r. These bounds are model properties, not statements about all real-world yield curves.

atoms.title: CIR short-rate transitions and discount bonds / References
atoms.text:
## References

[1] Cox, Ingersoll and Ross (1985), A Theory of the Term Structure of Interest Rates, Econometrica 53, 385–407, equations (18)–(19) and (23). [Original article scan](https://roycheng.cn/files/papers/interestRate/paper_Cox%26Ingersoll%26Ross_1985.pdf). Notation here uses risk-neutral coefficients directly for valuation.

[2] Malham and Wiese, Chi-square simulation of the CIR process and the Heston model, section on CIR simulation: scaled noncentral $\chi$-square transition. [Author manuscript](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0802.4411).

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / overview
atoms.text: # Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / Check first: wrapped mass, renormalization and the Monte Carlo cross-check
atoms.text:
## Check first: wrapped mass, renormalization and the Monte Carlo cross-check

These add to the grid-span section below.

- For the FFT, 1 - g.sum() is not a tail check: the circular transform keeps total mass at one by folding the mass beyond (n - 1) h back onto the small amounts. Measure the wrap instead: rerun with twice as many grid points at the same h and compare the probabilities on the original grid; their largest difference (and the change in VaR and ES) is the wrapped mass. Double until VaR and ES stop changing at the reported precision.
- Do not divide g by g.sum() to hide missing mass. On a Panjer grid that is too short this rescales every probability upward and lowers VaR and ES; the fix is a longer grid. Renormalize only when the text asks for it, and report how much mass was missing.
- When a Monte Carlo estimate of the same ES or VaR is available, compare: a gap of more than about three Monte Carlo standard errors, with the grid result lower, points at a short grid (or at the severity discretization) before it points at noise.

Worked check of the FFT method against simulation:

1. Aggregate probability mass on a grid of step $h$: the real part of the inverse FFT of $\exp(\lambda(\hat{f} - 1))$, where $\hat{f}$ is the FFT of the discretized severity.
2. TVaR at level $p$ on the grid: with $G$ the cumulative mass and $k$ the first grid index where $G_k \ge p$, $\mathrm{TVaR}_p = \left(\sum_{j > k} g_j x_j + (G_k - p)\, x_k\right)/(1-p)$, where $x_j = jh$.
3. Discretize the severity by rounding to the grid (the mass of $[(j - \tfrac12)h, (j + \tfrac12)h)$ goes to $jh$, the first cell starting at 0).
4. Double the number of grid points until the TVaR changes by less than a relative $10^{-6}$.
5. Simulate the frequency (Poisson) and the severities and sum them per scenario; the FFT TVaR must agree with the simulated tail mean within about three standard errors plus one grid step.

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / Monte Carlo check: one random stream for counts and severities
atoms.text:
## Monte Carlo check: one random stream for counts and severities

Create the generator once, `rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)`, and draw the claim counts and then all severities from that same object. A sampler that builds a new generator inside, such as `def sev(size): return np.random.default_rng(seed).gamma(k, theta, size)`, restarts the stream on every call: each simulated year gets the first N numbers of one fixed sequence, the severities no longer vary between years, and the simulated quantiles come out well below the FFT ones for every severity law. Vectorised form with the task's seed and draw order:

Simulation of the aggregate loss: draw the counts $N_i$ from a Poisson law, draw all $\sum_i N_i$ severities at once from the task's severity law (gamma, lognormal or Pareto), and add each severity to its scenario's total (for example `numpy.add.at` with the scenario index repeated $N_i$ times).

If the task fixes another draw order (all severities of one simulation before the next count), follow it. Check: the simulated VaR and ES agree with the FFT values within sampling error at every level; a gap in the same direction for all severity laws points to the random stream, not the discretisation.

Severity samplers differ by library. `rng.pareto(a, size)` (also `np.random.pareto`) draws the Lomax (Pareto II) law on
[0, inf); a Pareto law with shape a and minimum x_m is `x_m * (1 + rng.pareto(a, size))`, the same law as
`scipy.stats.pareto(b=a, scale=x_m)`. `rng.lognormal(mean, sigma, size)` takes the mean and standard deviation of log X,
the same law as `scipy.stats.lognorm(s=sigma, scale=np.exp(mean))`. Before aggregating, compare each sampler's sample
mean with its exact mean (Pareto a x_m / (a - 1) for a > 1, lognormal exp(mean + sigma^2 / 2)):

A Pareto law with shape $a$ and minimum $x_m$ is $x_m(1 + Y)$ with $Y$ from `Generator.pareto(a)` (a Lomax draw); its mean is $a x_m/(a-1)$ for $a > 1$ and its minimum is $x_m$.

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / Before the FFT / Panjer run: grid span and tail checks
atoms.text:
## Before the FFT / Panjer run: grid span and tail checks

The grid covers 0 to n h. A span that is too short cuts the tail: Panjer loses mass and FFT wraps it to the left, and both understate VaR and TVaR. A requirement such as "n h covers a high percentile of S" is a minimum. Set the span from the distribution itself, then confirm it:

Grid span: run a pilot simulation with the same frequency and severity, set the starting step to $h = 1.5 \times Q_{0.9999}(\text{pilot})/n_{\mathrm{grid}}$ (heavy or skewed severities need the pilot, not a mean-plus-$z$-standard-deviations rule), compute the aggregate mass on the grid (FFT or Panjer), and print the tail mass left out ($1 - \sum g$) and the error of the grid mean against the exact mean. Enlarge $h$ or the grid and rerun until VaR and TVaR stop changing at the reported precision.

The grid's amounts are k h; f_j and g_k are probabilities and are never multiplied by h (section "Discretizing the severity").

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / Model and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Model and assumptions
- Claim count N; severities $X_{i} \ge  0$ iid with cdf F, independent of N. $S = 0$ when $N = 0$, so S has an atom at 0 of mass $\operatorname{P}(N = 0)$(keep it).
- Exact numerical methods need an arithmetic severity on the grid `0, h, 2h, ...` (span h, money units). Panjer needs N in the
  (a, b, 0) class (Poisson, negative binomial incl. geometric, binomial); FFT needs only the pgf $\operatorname{P}_{N}(z) = \operatorname{E}[z^{N}]$.

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| lam | Poisson mean | claims per period |
| $r, \beta$ | negative binomial: $\operatorname{P}(N=k) = C(k+r-1, k) (1+\beta )^{-r} (\beta /(1+\beta ))^{k}$, mean $r\beta$, variance $r\beta(1+\beta)$ | none |
| $m, q$ | binomial: m trials, probability q | none |
| $h, n$ | grid span (money) and number of grid points; amounts are $s_{k} = k h$, k = 0..n-1 | money, count |
| $f_{j}, g_{k}$ | $\operatorname{P}(\mathrm{discretized} X = j h), \operatorname{P}(S = k h)$ | probabilities |
Negative binomial in success-probability form (scipy $\mathrm{nbinom}(n=r, p)$): $p = 1/(1+\beta )$, mean $r (1-p)/p$.

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / Moments (exact, no discretization)
atoms.text:
## Moments (exact, no discretization)

$$
\operatorname{E}[S] = \operatorname{E}[N] \operatorname{E}[X]
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}[S] = \operatorname{E}[N] \operatorname{Var}[X] + \operatorname{Var}[N] \operatorname{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Poisson case:

$$
\operatorname{Var}[S] = \mathrm{lam} \operatorname{E}[X^{2}]
$$

Third central moment, denoted $\mathrm{k3}$:

$$
\operatorname{E}[(S - \operatorname{E} S)^{3}] = \operatorname{E}[N] \mathrm{k3}(X) + 3 \operatorname{Var}[N] \operatorname{E}[X] \operatorname{Var}[X] + \mathrm{k3}(N) \operatorname{E}[X]^{3}
$$

For $\mathrm{k3}(N)$, Poisson gives $\mathrm{lam}$, negative binomial gives $r \beta  (1+\beta )(1+2 \beta )$, and binomial gives $m q (1-q)(1-2q)$.

$$
\mathrm{Skewness} = \mathrm{k3}(S) / \operatorname{Var}[S]^{1.5}
$$

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / Discretizing the severity (all f_j are probabilities: never multiply them by h)
atoms.text:
## Discretizing the severity (all f_j are probabilities: never multiply them by h)
- Rounding (= "mass dispersal"; actuar calls it "rounding", its examples "midpoint"): mass of $[jh - h/2, jh + h/2)$ goes to jh:
  $f_{0} = F(h/2)$, $f_{j} = F(jh + h/2) - F(jh - h/2)$. Mean of S is off by O(h^2); VaR is accurate to about h.
- Round down ("forward difference", actuar "upper"): $f_{j} = F((j+1)h) - F(jh)$ ($f_{0}$ includes any mass at 0). S is stochastically smaller:
  E[S] drops by about E[N] h/2 and its cdf lies ABOVE the true cdf (VaR, TVaR lower bounds). Round up ("backward", actuar "lower"):
  $f_{0} = F(0)$, $f_{j} = F(jh) - F((j-1)h)$, the matching upper bounds.
- Local moment matching (Gerber 1982; actuar "unbiased"), with $L(x) = \operatorname{E}[\min (X, x)]$:
  $f_{0} = 1 - L(h)/h$, $f_{j} = (2 L(jh) - L((j-1)h) - L((j+1)h)) / h$; E[discretized $X] = \operatorname{E}[X$] exactly.
- Midpoint pitfall: the mass of a bin $[jh, (j+1)h)$ belongs to its midpoint $(j + 1/2) h$, which is NOT on the grid. Reading it as amount jh is
  the round-down method; keeping amounts at (j + 1/2)h breaks the recursion (a sum of k claims sits at $(i + k/2) h$). Always put mass on multiples of h from 0.
- $\operatorname{pdf}(jh) \cdot  h$ is only a Riemann approximation (does not sum to 1, fails when the density is infinite at 0); prefer cdf differences.
- Mass beyond the last point `(n-1)h` is either dropped or added to the last point: check it is negligible, and say which.

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / Panjer recursion for the (a, b, 0) class: P(N=k) = (a + b/k) P(N=k-1), k >= 1
atoms.text:
## Panjer recursion for the (a, b, 0) class: P(N=k) = (a + b/k) P(N=k-1), k >= 1
| $N$ | $a$ | $b$ | $\operatorname{P}(N=0)$ | $\operatorname{P}_{N}$(z) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Poisson(lam) | 0 | lam | $\exp ( -\mathrm{lam} )$ | $\exp (\mathrm{lam} (z - 1))$ |
| negative binomial $(r,\beta)$ | $\beta/(1+\beta)$ | $(r-1)\beta/(1+\beta)$ | $(1+\beta)^{-r}$ | $(1-\beta(z-1))^{-r}$ |
| binomial(m, q) | -q/(1-q) | (m+1) q/(1-q) | (1-q)^m | (1 + q (z - 1))^m |

$$
g_{0} = \operatorname{P}_{N}(f_{0})
$$

This is NOT $\operatorname{P}(N=0)$ unless $f_{0} = 0$.

$$
g_{k} = [1 / (1 - a f_{0})] \cdot  \sum _{j=1}^{k} (a + b j / k) f_{j} g_{k-j}
$$

For $k = 1, 2, \ldots , n-1$. Poisson case:

$$
g_{k} = (\mathrm{lam}/k) \sum _{j} j f_{j} g_{k-j}
$$

- O(n^2) operations; exact on the truncated grid (no wrap-around), only mass beyond (n-1)h is missing.
- Underflow: if $\operatorname{P}_N(f_0)$ underflows to 0 (large $\mathrm{lam}(1-f_0)$), every $g_{k}$ is 0. Run Panjer with lam / 2^k (neg. binomial: r / 2^k)
  so the start value is representable, then replace g by g * g (self-convolution, truncated to the grid) k times in a row; each step doubles lam (or r). Or use the FFT.

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / FFT method
atoms.text:
## FFT method
Pad $f$ with zeros to length $n$ (a power of 2 is fastest).

$$
\phi  = \mathrm{DFT}(f)
$$

Complex transform:

$$
\psi _{k} = \operatorname{P}_{N}(\phi _{k})
$$

$$
g = \mathrm{Re}(\mathrm{IDFT}(\psi ))
$$

- With numpy: $g = \mathrm{real}(\mathrm{ifft}(\operatorname{P}_{N}(\mathrm{fft}(f))))$. The circular DFT puts any mass of S beyond (n-1)h back at index `k mod n` (aliasing),
  inflating the LEFT part of g (including $g_{0}$). Choose n h so that $\operatorname{P}(S > n h)$ is negligible (check against E[S], Var[S]; heavy tails need
  much more room than mean + a few sd); compare with a run at 2n.
- Exponential tilting (Grubel & Hermesmeier 1999): use $f_{j} \exp (-\theta  j)$, apply the same steps, then multiply $g_{k}$ by $\exp (\theta  k)$.
  Wrapped mass is damped by $\exp (-\theta  n)$ but round-off is amplified by $\exp (\theta  k)$: pick $\theta$ n so that both $\exp (-\theta  n)$ and
  $\exp (\theta  n) \cdot  1e-16$ are below the tolerance (roughly 10 to 20 in double precision; too large blows up the right tail).
- $O(n \log  n)$. Works for any N with a pgf (also mixtures); Panjer and FFT give the same g up to round-off when the grid is long enough.

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / VaR and TVaR from the discrete distribution
atoms.text:
## VaR and TVaR from the discrete distribution

$$
G_{k} = \sum _{i\le k} g_{i}
$$

Use the smallest index $k$ such that $G_{k} \ge  p$ (allow a tiny floating-point tolerance):

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{p} = s_{k}
$$

Coherent TVaR (Acerbi–Tasche):

$$
\mathrm{TVaR}_{p} = \operatorname{VaR}_{p} + (1/(1-p)) \sum _{k} \max (s_{k} - \operatorname{VaR}_{p}, 0) g_{k}
$$

- Variants a task may define instead: $\operatorname{E}[S \vert  S > \operatorname{VaR}_{p}]$ (sum over $s_{k} > \operatorname{VaR}_{p}$ divided by $1-G(\operatorname{VaR}_p)$) or $\operatorname{E}[S \vert  S \ge  \operatorname{VaR}_{p}]$; on a grid they
  differ from the coherent value by O(h). Interpolate between grid points only if the task says so. Report amounts k h, not indices.

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / Common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common mistakes
- Multiplying by h twice: $f_{j}$ and $g_{k}$ are already probabilities; amounts are `k h` ($\operatorname{E}[S] = \sum _{k} k h g_{k}$). Do not scale lam, r, $\beta$ by h.
- Grid too short: Panjer silently loses tail mass ($\sum  g < 1$) and understates TVaR even when the missing mass is tiny; FFT wraps it
  to the left tail. Check $1 - \sum  g$ and $\operatorname{E}[S] - \sum  s_{k} g_{k}$ against the exact moments.
- Grid span: the representable range is n h. When n is fixed, the span is set by h. A requirement such as "n h covers a high percentile of S" is a minimum: estimate that percentile from the discrete distribution itself (a pilot FFT with a generous span) or from a simulation, not from mean + z * sd, which badly understates lognormal or Pareto tails. Then increase h (or n, when it is free) until VaR and TVaR at every requested level stop changing within the reporting precision, and the discrete mean $\sum s_{k} g_{k}$ agrees with the exact $\operatorname{E}[S]$. TVaR at level p divides the tail sum by $1-p$, so a relative shortfall of the mean of order $10^{-3}$ can become several percent in TVaR at 0.995.
- Hiding a short grid: moving the severity mass beyond the grid into the last bin, or renormalizing $f$ or $g$ to sum to 1, makes $1 - \sum g$ look clean while the tail is still cut off.
- Using $\operatorname{P}(N=0)$ as $g_{0}$ when $f_{0} > 0$; mixing up negative-binomial parametrizations ($\beta$ vs $p = 1/(1+\beta )$); severity and h in different units.
- When a Monte Carlo check disagrees by more than its own sampling error at the high levels → check in turn the grid span against the simulated high quantile and the tail mass left beyond n·h, the severity discretization, the parameters and the risk-measure definition → enlarge the span and confirm that VaR and ES no longer move before reporting.
- When choosing the grid span for heavy or skewed severities → take the starting high quantile from a pilot simulation, not from mean + z·sd, then run the mean, tail-mass and span checks of this entry and enlarge the span until VaR and ES stop moving:

The pilot's 99.99% quantile times 1.5, divided by the number of grid points, is only a starting step; refine it as above.

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- Requires N independent of iid X. Panjer covers only (a, b, 0); zero-modified (a, b, 1) counts need a different start (Sundt & Jewell 1981),
  FFT just uses the right pgf. Discretization error shrinks as h falls (O(h) for VaR, O(h^2) for moments with rounding).
  Monte Carlo needs large samples for far-tail VaR / TVaR, especially for heavy-tailed (lognormal) severities.

atoms.title: Aggregate loss $S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$: severity discretization, Panjer recursion, FFT, VaR / TVaR / Sources
Conditional volatility: GARCH forecasts and dynamic correlations / overview
atoms.text:
# Conditional volatility: GARCH forecasts and dynamic correlations

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

This note defines changing return variances and covariances for risk forecasts. It distinguishes fitted variance, future variance and long-run variance; it does not define trading signals or regulatory capital rules.

**Fitting GARCH with arch:** use the two-case recipe at the top of the garch_fitting entry: percent returns converted back where the task leaves units open, a reparameterized native-unit MLE where the task fixes native units. Do not silence warnings, and check that the estimates moved away from arch's starting values.

atoms.title: Conditional volatility: GARCH forecasts and dynamic correlations / Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## Shared Foundations

Map notation by economic meaning and units. Explicit task conventions determine return scaling, mean model, initialization, forecast horizon and likelihood normalization. Identify conflicting conventions rather than silently changing them.

Here t indexes observations, $r_{t}$ is a return, $m_{t}$ its conditional mean, and $F_{t}$ the information available through t. Innovations have zero conditional mean. All covariance quantities use the same observation frequency.

atoms.title: Conditional volatility: GARCH forecasts and dynamic correlations / Univariate conditional variance
atoms.text:
## Univariate conditional variance

The innovation removes the specified mean, which may be zero.

$$
\epsilon _{t} = r_{t} - m_{t}
$$

GARCH(1,1) specifies variance known before observing $r_{t}$. Here $\omega  > 0, \alpha  \ge  0$ and $\beta  \ge  0; z_{t}$ has conditional mean zero and variance one.

$$
\begin{gathered}
h_{t} = \omega  + \alpha \cdot \epsilon _{t-1}^{2} + \beta \cdot h_{t-1} \\
\epsilon _{t} = \sqrt{h_{t}}\cdot z_{t}
\end{gathered}
$$

Gaussian conditional negative log likelihood, for a fixed initialization and included sample of N observations, is:

$$
\mathrm{NLL} = (1/2)\cdot \sum _{t} [\ln (2\cdot \pi ) + \ln (h_{t}) + \epsilon _{t}^{2}/h_{t}]
$$

With non-Gaussian innovations this is a Gaussian quasi-likelihood, not their exact likelihood. Removing constants does not change an optimizer but changes the reported objective. Initialization and sample inclusion also matter.

The finite unconditional variance, when $\alpha  + \beta  < 1$ and the model assumptions hold, is:

$$
\bar{h} = \omega /(1-\alpha -\beta )
$$

This finite-second-moment condition is not a necessary condition for every form of strict stationarity. At $\alpha  + \beta  = 1$ the formula above is unavailable.

atoms.title: Conditional volatility: GARCH forecasts and dynamic correlations / Scale and horizon
atoms.text:
## Scale and horizon

Multiplying returns and their mean by a positive factor c changes dimensional parameters as follows; $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are unchanged.

$$
\begin{gathered}
\epsilon _{\mathrm{scaled}} = c\cdot \epsilon \\
h_{\mathrm{scaled}} = c^{2}\cdot h \\
\omega _{\mathrm{scaled}} = c^{2}\cdot \omega
\end{gathered}
$$

Thus percent-return variance is converted to decimal-return variance by dividing by $100^2$; standard deviation is divided by 100. Under the same transformed initialization the Gaussian NLL changes by $N\cdot \ln (c)$. Numerical fitting tolerances need not be invariant to scaling.

The next-observation variance forecast includes the latest observed innovation; it is not the final in-sample $h_{t}$.

$$
h_{t+1\vert t} = \omega  + \alpha \cdot \epsilon _{t}^{2} + \beta \cdot h_{t}
$$

For $k \ge  2$, conditional expectations give the multi-step forecast:

$$
h_{t+k\vert t} = \omega  + (\alpha +\beta )\cdot h_{t+k-1\vert t}
$$

For $\alpha  + \beta  < 1$ its equivalent closed form is:

$$
h_{t+k\vert t} = \bar{h} + (\alpha +\beta )^{k-1}\cdot (h_{t+1\vert t}-\bar{h})
$$

With martingale-difference innovations and finite second moments, the variance of the cumulative innovation over H observations is:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\sum _{k=1}^{H} \epsilon _{t+k} \vert  F_{t}) = \sum _{k=1}^{H} h_{t+k\vert t}
$$

It equals H times the one-step forecast only under an additional flat-variance assumption. Annualizing a daily standard deviation by $\sqrt{A}$, where A is observations per year, is a reporting convention; it does not replace the horizon recursion. A nontrivial mean model can add forecast uncertainty to cumulative returns.

atoms.title: Conditional volatility: GARCH forecasts and dynamic correlations / Dynamic conditional correlation
atoms.text:
## Dynamic conditional correlation

Use DCC for a vector of innovations with separate univariate conditional variances. Marginal standardization removes scale, not cross-sectional dependence. $D_{t}$ is diagonal with positive standard deviations.

$$
\begin{gathered}
D_{t} = \operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{h_{1,t}}, \ldots , \sqrt{h_{n,t}}) \\
z_{t} = D_{t}^{-1}\cdot \epsilon _{t}
\end{gathered}
$$

The scalar DCC recursion uses nonnegative a,b with $a+b<1$, a positive-definite target $\bar{Q}$, and positive-definite initial Q. A zero-mean standardized second-moment target and a demeaned sample covariance are distinct finite-sample conventions.

$$
Q_{t} = (1-a-b)\cdot \bar{Q} + a\cdot z_{t-1}\cdot z_{t-1}' + b\cdot Q_{t-1}
$$

The correlation normalization makes each diagonal entry one. $Q_{t}$ itself is not generally a correlation matrix.

$$
R_{i,j,t} = Q_{i,j,t}/\sqrt{Q_{i,i,t}\cdot Q_{j,j,t}}
$$

The conditional covariance restores each asset's scale.

$$
H_{t} = D_{t}\cdot R_{t}\cdot D_{t}
$$

The correlation part of the Gaussian log likelihood, after fixing the univariate fits, is:

$$
\mathrm{logL}_{\mathrm{corr}} = -(1/2)\cdot \sum _{t} [\ln (\det (R_{t})) + z_{t}'\cdot R_{t}^{-1}\cdot z_{t} - z_{t}'\cdot z_{t}]
$$

Omitting the last term leaves the same correlation estimates but a different reported log likelihood. The full multivariate likelihood also includes marginal variance and Gaussian normalization terms.

atoms.title: Conditional volatility: GARCH forecasts and dynamic correlations / Checks and Scope
atoms.text:
## Checks and Scope

Positive-definite Q and positive diagonal h imply positive-definite H; R must be symmetric with unit diagonal. For portfolio weights w, conditional variance is w'*H*w, not a weighted average of marginal variances. With $a=b=0$, the correlation is the normalization of $\bar{Q}$.

Empirical standardized residual rows can still be correlated. Resampling complete rows preserves their empirical contemporaneous dependence; multiplying those already correlated rows by another correlation factor generally changes it. Whitening and subsequent recoloring is a different construction. Serial block resampling and independent resampling also represent different dependence assumptions.

Forecast origin, variance estimation window and parameter estimation window are separate concepts. A lagged position does not remove future information from full-sample fitted parameters. A one-step risk estimate is not automatically a risk-neutral option volatility or a regulatory capital formula.

atoms.title: Conditional volatility: GARCH forecasts and dynamic correlations / Constrained likelihood fitting and numerical diagnostics
atoms.text:
## Constrained likelihood fitting and numerical diagnostics

Separate the economic parameter domain from the optimizer's coordinate system. Box bounds on two persistence parameters do not enforce a bound on their sum. One strictly interior parameterization, applicable to either a nonnegative GARCH pair or a scalar DCC pair with sum below one, is:

$$
p_1=\frac{e^{u_1}}{1+e^{u_1}+e^{u_2}},\qquad
p_2=\frac{e^{u_2}}{1+e^{u_1}+e^{u_2}}.
$$

Evaluate the denominator with log-sum-exp. In exact real arithmetic, finite coordinates give strictly positive parameters and positive slack; floating-point exponentials can underflow or round the sum to one. After mapping, explicitly verify finite values, positive intercept/variances and the requested strict persistence inequality. Reject an infeasible objective evaluation or use documented bounded coordinates; silently clipping the result changes the parameterization. exact zero coefficients or unit persistence are boundary cases outside this interior map. Do not force a stationary interior model when another domain is explicitly requested. For a positive variance intercept, a positive fixed reference variance $h_{\mathrm{ref}}$ allows $\omega=h_{\mathrm{ref}}e^v$; changing parameter coordinates is different from rescaling the observed returns. Preserve the specified input units, likelihood initialization, sample and allowed optimization method.

Finite-difference gradients are sensitive to coordinate scale. With a fixed mean and a parameter-independent seed $h_0$, useful analytic derivatives follow the same recursion as the variance:

$$
\partial_\omega h_t=1+\beta\partial_\omega h_{t-1},\qquad
\partial_\alpha h_t=\epsilon_{t-1}^2+\beta\partial_\alpha h_{t-1},\qquad
\partial_\beta h_t=h_{t-1}+\beta\partial_\beta h_{t-1}.
$$

Their initial values are zero only under that fixed-seed assumption. A seed defined by long-run variance, or a fitted mean affecting innovations, needs the corresponding derivatives too. For the Gaussian NLL with fixed innovations, the gradient is:

$$
\partial_\theta\mathrm{NLL}
=\frac12\sum_t\left(\frac1{h_t}-\frac{\epsilon_t^2}{h_t^2}\right)\partial_\theta h_t.
$$

For a positive-definite DCC correlation matrix $R_t=L_tL_t'$ with lower triangular Cholesky factor $L_t$, solve $L_t y_t=z_t$. Then:

$$
\log\det R_t=2\sum_i\log(L_{t,ii}),\qquad
z_t'R_t^{-1}z_t=y_t'y_t.
$$

A linear solve avoids forming the inverse. Cholesky failure can reveal infeasible parameters or numerical loss of definiteness; an arbitrary diagonal adjustment changes the fitted objective. Nearly singular feasible matrices also need numerical scrutiny.

A fitted model needs finite likelihood, feasible parameters, positive filtered variances and a documented termination reason. Compare the objective at the returned parameters and the start, the gradient where meaningful, and small feasible perturbations. Zero optimizer iterations can indicate a genuine optimum or a scale/stopping problem; it is not by itself proof of either. Multiple admissible starts can expose local optima when allowed, but do not establish a global optimum. Rescaling returns, clipping parameters and changing initialization are different changes and must not be substituted silently for diagnosis.

Sources: [arch estimation results](https://arch.readthedocs.io/en/stable/univariate/generated/arch.univariate.base.ARCHModelResult.html) exposes convergence, optimization result and scale; [arch model settings](https://arch.readthedocs.io/en/stable/univariate/introduction.html) describes mean and rescaling choices. The derivative and Cholesky identities follow from the variance recursion and matrix factorization.

atoms.title: Conditional volatility: GARCH forecasts and dynamic correlations / References
atoms.text:
## References

[arch documentation: forecasting](https://arch.readthedocs.io/en/latest/univariate/forecasting.html), conditional GARCH forecast recursions. Scale, cumulative-variance and likelihood-shift identities above follow directly from the stated model.

[Engle, Dynamic Conditional Correlation (2002), author manuscript](https://archive.nyu.edu/bitstream/2451/26482/2/02-38.pdf), Sections III–IV, correlation recursion and likelihood decomposition. Definiteness and scale checks are direct matrix identities.

atoms.title: Bivariate copula fitting by pseudo-maximum likelihood: Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank / overview
atoms.text:
# Bivariate copula fitting by pseudo-maximum likelihood: Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

Before forming pairs, fix two things the outputs depend on: the order of the instruments and the pair label.

Order of instruments (it decides which instrument is first in each pair, and the row order):
- the order the task lists them in (a list in the text, or the column order of a wide input table as supplied): the
  default when the task lists them and says nothing about sorting; do not sort them then. A table the code builds
  itself (pivot, unstack, groupby) has sorted columns, and that order is not the task's order: take the names from
  the task's list and reindex the built table to it;
- the order of first appearance in a long table: when the instruments are only found in the data;
- alphabetical: when the task says "sorted" or "alphabetical", or its example labels are alphabetical;
- an order defined by a value (market cap, sector): when the task names it.

Pair label (key or column value):
- the task's example label or stated separator wins ("AAA-BBB", "AAA_BBB", "AAA/BBB");
- a JSON list ["AAA", "BBB"] or two columns (asset_1, asset_2) when the task asks for an unambiguous encoding or two
  fields; avoid joining with a character that can occur inside a ticker (a hyphen in "BRK-B");
- without either, "FIRST-SECOND" with the earlier instrument first; state the order used.

Pairs: take the asset names in the chosen order (first appearance in the data, or sorted when the task sorts), form all pairs $(a, b)$ with $a$ before $b$ in that order, label them with the task's separator, and print the first few to compare with the task's list before fitting. There are $n(n-1)/2$ pairs.

atoms.title: Bivariate copula fitting by pseudo-maximum likelihood: Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank / Setting and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Setting and assumptions
- n i.i.d. pairs ($x_{i}$, $y_{i}$) with continuous margins (for returns: often i.i.d. residuals after a volatility filter, if the task says so).
  $H(x, y) = C(F(x), G(y))$; the copula C carries all dependence. Margins are NOT modelled (canonical / pseudo-ML, Genest, Ghoudi & Rivest 1995).
- Pseudo-observations: $u_{i} = R_{i} / (n + 1)$, $v_{i} = S_{i} / (n + 1)$, $R_{i} = \operatorname{rank}$ of $x_{i}$ among $x_{1}$..$x_{n}$ (1 = smallest), $S_{i}$ likewise for y; ties get average ranks.
  Ranks are unchanged by strictly increasing transforms of a series (e.g. standardizing), but prices and returns are different series: rank the series the task names.
- Estimate: $\hat{\theta} = \mathrm{argmax} l(\theta )$, $l(\theta ) = \sum _{i} \log  c(u_{i}, v_{i}; \theta )$ (c = copula density).
- Variant IFM ("inference functions for margins"): fit parametric margins first and use $u_{i} = \hat{F}(x_{i})$. Use it only if the task says so.

atoms.title: Bivariate copula fitting by pseudo-maximum likelihood: Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | domain |
|---|---|---|
| $u, v$ | pseudo-observations | strictly inside (0, 1) |
| $\rho$ | Gaussian / t copula correlation parameter (not Pearson of raw data) | (-1, 1) |
| $\nu$ | t copula degrees of freedom | $\nu  > 0$(many tasks/libraries restrict to $\nu  > 2$ and cap large $\nu$) |
| $\theta$ (Clayton) | Clayton parameter; $\theta  \to  0$ is independence | $\theta  > 0$ |
| $\theta$ (Gumbel) | Gumbel parameter; $\theta  = 1$ is independence | $\theta  \ge  1$ |
| $\theta$ (Frank) | Frank parameter; $\theta  \to  0$ independence, $\theta  < 0$ negative dependence | $\mathrm{real}, \theta  \ne  0$ |
| $\hat{\tau}$ | sample Kendall's $\tau$ of (x, y) (equals that of (u, v)) | [-1, 1] |

atoms.title: Bivariate copula fitting by pseudo-maximum likelihood: Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank / Log-densities (natural logs; Phi^-1 standard normal quantile; t_nu^-1 standard Student-t quantile w
atoms.text:
## Log-densities (natural logs; Phi^-1 standard normal quantile; t_nu^-1 standard Student-t quantile with nu df)
- Gaussian, $x = \Phi ^{-1}(u)$, $y = \Phi ^{-1}(v)$: $\log  c = -0.5 \ln (1 - \rho ^{2}) - [\rho ^{2} (x^{2} + y^{2}) - 2 \rho  x y] / [2 (1 - \rho ^{2})]$.
- Student-t, $x = t_{\nu}^{-1}(u)$, $y = t_{\nu}^{-1}(v)$ (same $\nu$ as the copula):
  $\log  c = \mathrm{lnGamma}((\nu +2)/2) + \mathrm{lnGamma}(\nu /2) - 2 \mathrm{lnGamma}((\nu +1)/2) - 0.5 \ln (1 - \rho ^{2})$
  $- ((\nu +2)/2) \ln (1 + (x^{2} - 2 \rho  x y + y^{2}) / (\nu  (1 - \rho ^{2}))) + ((\nu +1)/2) [\ln (1 + x^{2}/\nu ) + \ln (1 + y^{2}/\nu )]$.
- Clayton, $C = (u^{-\theta}  + v^{-\theta}  - 1)^{-1/\theta}$:
  $\log  c = \ln (1 + \theta ) - (1 + \theta )(\ln  u + \ln  v) - (2 + 1/\theta ) L$, $L = \ln (u^{-\theta}  + v^{-\theta}  - 1)$.
  Stable L: $a = -\theta  \ln  u$, $b = -\theta  \ln  v$, $m = \max (a, b)$, $l = \min (a, b)$: $L = m + \mathrm{log1p}(\exp (l - m) \cdot  (-\mathrm{expm1}(-l)))$.
- Gumbel, $s = -\ln  u$, $t = -\ln  v$, $S = s^{\theta} + t^{\theta}$, $A = S^{1/\theta}$, $C = \exp (-A)$:
  $\log  c = -A + s + t + (\theta  - 1)(\ln  s + \ln  t) + (1/\theta  - 2) \ln  S + \ln (A + \theta  - 1)$;
  stable $\ln  S = \theta  \ln  \max (s, t) + \mathrm{log1p}((\min (s, t)/\max (s, t))^{\theta})$.
- Frank, $C = -(1/\theta ) \ln [1 + (e^{-\theta  u} - 1)(e^{-\theta  v} - 1) / (e^{-\theta} - 1)]$,
  $c = \theta  (1 - e^{-\theta}) e^{-\theta  (u+v)} / D^{2}$, $D = (1 - e^{-\theta}) - (1 - e^{-\theta  u})(1 - e^{-\theta  v})$.
  Stable for $\theta  > 0$: $D = e^{-\theta  u}(1 - e^{-\theta  v}) + e^{-\theta  v}(1 - e^{-\theta  (1-v)})$ (two non-negative terms):
  $\log  c = \ln  \theta  + \ln (1 - e^{-\theta}) - \theta  (u + v) - 2 \ln  D$, $\ln  D$ by log-sum-exp, $1 - e^{-z}$ as `-expm1(-z)`.
  For $\theta  < 0$ use $c(u, v; \theta ) = c(u, 1 - v; -\theta )$ (avoids overflow of e^(-$\theta$)).

atoms.title: Bivariate copula fitting by pseudo-maximum likelihood: Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank / Negative dependence with Clayton / Gumbel (they only reach tau >= 0)
atoms.text:
## Negative dependence with Clayton / Gumbel (they only reach tau >= 0)
- Rotation: fit the base copula to transformed pseudo-observations. 90 deg: density $c(1 - u, v)$; 270 deg: $c(u, 1 - v)$
  (both give $\tau$ = -$\tau _{\mathrm{base}}$); 180 deg (survival): $c(1 - u, 1 - v)$ (same sign of $\tau$, tail moved to the other corner).
  Which of the two is called "90" vs "270" differs between libraries: follow the task's definition and state the transform.
- Restriction: keep the base domain; for $\hat{\tau} < 0$ the maximum sits on the boundary (Clayton $\theta  \to  0$, Gumbel $\theta  = 1$,
  i.e. independence, log-likelihood near 0). Report it as such; do not let $\theta$ leave the domain.
- Clayton's extension to $\theta$ in [-1, 0) has support only where $u^{-\theta}  + v^{-\theta}  - 1 > 0$; points outside give $\log  c = -\infty$. Avoid in pseudo-ML unless the task requires it.
- Gaussian, t and Frank cover both signs directly; no rotation needed.

atoms.title: Bivariate copula fitting by pseudo-maximum likelihood: Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank / Starting values: Kendall's tau inversion (also an estimator in its own right, "method of moments")
atoms.text:
## Starting values: Kendall's tau inversion (also an estimator in its own right, "method of moments")
- Gaussian and t: $\rho  = \sin (\pi  \hat{\tau} / 2)$. Clayton: $\theta  = 2 \hat{\tau} / (1 - \hat{\tau})$. Gumbel: $\theta  = 1 / (1 - \hat{\tau})$.
- Frank: solve $1 - 4/\theta  + 4 D_{1}(\theta )/\theta  = \hat{\tau}$ by root finding (monotone; $\operatorname{sign}(\theta ) = \operatorname{sign}(\hat{\tau})$),
  $D_{1}(x) = (1/x) \int _{0}^{x} t / (e^{t} - 1) \mathrm{d}t$.
- t: $\nu$ has no $\tau$ relation; start from a profile likelihood over a $\nu$ grid. A common two-step variant fixes $\rho$ by $\tau$ inversion and maximizes over $\nu$ only.
- If the task says "estimate by inversion of Kendall's $\tau$", report these values, not the MLE.

atoms.title: Bivariate copula fitting by pseudo-maximum likelihood: Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank / Information criteria
atoms.text:
## Information criteria
$\mathrm{AIC} = 2k - 2 \hat{l}$, $\mathrm{BIC} = k \ln (n) - 2 \hat{l}$, n = number of pairs, $\hat{l}$ = maximized copula log-likelihood. Lower is better.
$k = 1$ for Gaussian, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank (rotated or not: rotation is a discrete choice, not a parameter); k = 2 for t ($\rho$, $\nu$);
independence $k = 0, l = 0$. Marginal parameters are not counted under pseudo-ML. Some tasks report AIC/n or -AIC; follow the task.

atoms.title: Bivariate copula fitting by pseudo-maximum likelihood: Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank / Numerical practice and common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Numerical practice and common mistakes
- Write each log-density as a per-observation array `logc` (constants broadcast to every row) and take `loglik = logc.sum()` once; a constant added once instead of n times shifts the likelihood and can reverse the model ranking. The t copula nests the Gaussian: at very large $\nu$ with the same $\rho$ the two log-likelihoods agree, so a fitted t log-likelihood far below the Gaussian one is a bug.
Check: the Student t copula log-likelihood with a very large number of degrees of freedom (for example $10^6$) equals the Gaussian copula log-likelihood at the same correlation, to a relative $10^{-3}$.
- Optimize on unconstrained variables: $\rho  = \tanh (z)$, Clayton $\theta  = e^{z}$, Gumbel $\theta  = 1 + e^{z}$, $\nu  = \nu _{\mathrm{min}} + e^{z}$;
  for Frank avoid $\theta  = 0$ exactly (formula 0/0; density is 1 there). $\nu$: likelihood is flat for large $\nu$ (t tends to Gaussian); report if at the cap.
- Raw data instead of pseudo-observations: $\Phi^{-1}(x)$ is nan outside (0, 1); with data inside (0, 1) the fit is silently wrong.
- $\operatorname{rank} / n$ instead of $\operatorname{rank} / (n + 1)$: the largest point gets $u = 1$; Gaussian / t / Gumbel log-likelihoods become nan or inf,
  while Clayton and Frank stay finite but biased (no error is raised, so the mistake is silent there).
- Parameter outside the domain ($\rho  = \pm 1$, Clayton $\theta  \le  0$, Gumbel $\theta  < 1$) gives nan/-inf or meaningless numbers;
  enforce the domain in the parametrization instead of relying on the formula to fail.
- t copula: the quantiles use the copula $\nu$, not a marginal df; counting $k = 1$ for t is wrong.
- Naive overflow: u^-$\theta$ (large Clayton $\theta$), e^(-$\theta$) (Frank $\theta  < 0), s^{\theta} ($large Gumbel $\theta$). Use the stable forms above.
- Tail dependence (helps choose a family): Clayton lower $2^{-1/\theta}$, upper 0; Gumbel upper $2 - 2^{1/\theta}$, lower 0;
  t both tails $2 t_{\nu +1}(-\sqrt{(\nu +1)(1-\rho )/(1+\rho )})$; Gaussian and Frank 0. Survival rotation swaps lower and upper.

atoms.title: Bivariate copula fitting by pseudo-maximum likelihood: Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- Pseudo-ML is consistent and asymptotically normal but its standard errors are not the inverse Hessian of l (rank effect); use the task's method or a bootstrap.
- Assumes i.i.d. pairs and continuous margins; heavy ties (discrete data, stale prices) break the rank argument.
- AIC/BIC compare families with the same pseudo-observations only; a fitted family can still fail a goodness-of-fit test.

atoms.title: Bivariate copula fitting by pseudo-maximum likelihood: Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank / Sources
Sampling bivariate copulas (Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank) and their Kendall's tau / Spearman's rho / overview
atoms.text:
# Sampling bivariate copulas (Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank) and their Kendall's tau / Spearman's rho

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

atoms.title: Sampling bivariate copulas (Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank) and their Kendall's tau / Spearman's rho / Setting
atoms.text:
## Setting
- Output: pairs (U, V) with uniform(0, 1) margins and copula C. Data with margins F, G: $X = F^{-1}(U)$, $Y = G^{-1}(V)$.
- Notation: Z1, Z2 i.i.d. N(0, 1); E1, E2 i.i.d. Exp(1) (mean 1); W uniform(0, 1); all independent; one fresh set per pair.
  $\Phi$ = standard normal CDF; $t_{\nu}$ = Student-t CDF with $\nu$ df.
- Parameter domains as in the fitting entry: $\rho$ in (-1, 1), $\nu$ > 0, Clayton $\theta  > 0$, Gumbel $\theta  \ge  1$, Frank $\theta  \ne  0$.

atoms.title: Sampling bivariate copulas (Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank) and their Kendall's tau / Spearman's rho / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $\rho$ | Gaussian / t copula correlation parameter | none |
| $\nu$ | t copula degrees of freedom | none |
| $\theta$ | Clayton / Gumbel / Frank parameter | none |
| $n$ | number of simulated pairs | count |

atoms.title: Sampling bivariate copulas (Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank) and their Kendall's tau / Spearman's rho / Samplers
atoms.text:
## Samplers
- Gaussian: $Y = \rho  \mathrm{Z1} + \sqrt{1 - \rho ^{2}} \mathrm{Z2}$; $U = \Phi (\mathrm{Z1})$, $V = \Phi (Y)$ (Cholesky of [[1, $\rho$], [$\rho$, 1]]).
- Student-t: Z1, Y as above and ONE $Q \sim \chi^2(\nu)$ per pair: $U = t_{\nu}(\mathrm{Z1} / \sqrt{Q/\nu})$, $V = t_{\nu}(Y / \sqrt{Q/\nu})$.
  A separate $\chi$-square per margin is a different copula (at $\rho  = 0$ it is independence, no tail dependence).
- Archimedean via Marshall-Olkin (frailty): $C(u, v) = \psi (\psi ^{-1}(u) + \psi ^{-1}(v))$ with $\psi$ the Laplace transform of a positive frailty M.
  Draw M, then $U = \psi (\mathrm{E1} / M)$, $V = \psi (\mathrm{E2} / M)$ (same M for both coordinates).
  - Clayton ($\theta  > 0$): $\psi (s) = (1 + s)^{-1/\theta}$, $M \sim \Gamma (\mathrm{shape} = 1/\theta , \mathrm{scale} = 1)$ (mean $1/\theta$, NOT shape $\theta$):

$$
`U = (1 + \mathrm{E1}/M)^{-1/\theta}`.
$$

  - Gumbel ($\theta  \ge  1$): $\psi (s) = \exp (-s^{1/\theta})$, M positive stable with $\alpha  = 1/\theta$, $\operatorname{E}[\exp (-s M)] = \exp (-s^{\alpha})$.
Kanter / Chambers–Mallows–Stuck:

$$
\Theta  \sim \mathrm{uniform}(0, \pi )
$$

$$
E \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1)
$$

$$
M = [\sin (\alpha  \Theta ) / \sin (\Theta )^{1/\alpha}] \cdot  [\sin ((1 - \alpha ) \Theta ) / E]^{(1 - \alpha )/\alpha}
$$

Written out, with the exponent $1/\alpha$ on $\sin(\Theta)$ (not $\alpha$):

$$
M = \frac{\sin(\alpha \Theta)}{(\sin \Theta)^{1/\alpha}} \left( \frac{\sin((1-\alpha)\Theta)}{E} \right)^{(1-\alpha)/\alpha}
$$

Check the frailty before using it: $\operatorname{E}[\exp(-M)]$ should be close to $\exp(-1) \approx 0.3679$ (the Laplace transform at $s = 1$), and each sampled margin U should have mean about 0.5 and an empirical CDF close to uniform. A wrong exponent fails both (for $\theta = 2$: about 0.48 and a margin mean about 0.40), so a failed check means the sampler is wrong, not that a tail statistic needs a different threshold.

$\theta  = 1$ gives $M = 1$ (independence). In Nolan's $S(\alpha , \beta , \gamma , \delta ; 1)$ notation this is

$$
S(\alpha , 1, (\cos (\pi  \alpha  / 2))^{1/\alpha}, 0; 1)
$$

A generic stable generator must use exactly this scale, not $\gamma  = 1$. Then

$$
U = \exp (-(\mathrm{E1}/M)^{1/\theta})
$$

  - Frank ($\theta  > 0$): $\psi (s) = -(1/\theta ) \ln (1 - (1 - e^{-\theta}) e^{-s})$, M logarithmic-series on {1, 2, ...} with

$$
`p = 1 - e^{-\theta}`, `\operatorname{P}(M = k) = p^{k} / (k \theta )`; `U = \psi (\mathrm{E1} / M)`.
$$

- Conditional inversion (draw $U = \mathrm{W1}$, solve $\mathrm{dC}/\mathrm{d}u (u, v) = \mathrm{W2}$ for v; works for any $\theta$ in the domain):
  - Frank: $V = -(1/\theta ) \ln (1 + \mathrm{W2} (e^{-\theta} - 1) / (\mathrm{W2} + (1 - \mathrm{W2}) e^{-\theta  U}))$. Also the simplest route for $\theta  < 0$
    (or sample Frank(|$\theta$|) and return (U, 1 - V)).
  - Clayton: $V = [U^{-\theta} (\mathrm{W2}^{-\theta /(1+\theta )} - 1) + 1]^{-1/\theta}$.
- Rotations / survival: transform the sample: 90 deg $(1 - U, V)$, 270 deg $(U, 1 - V)$, 180 deg $(1 - U, 1 - V)$ (match the task's convention).

atoms.title: Sampling bivariate copulas (Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank) and their Kendall's tau / Spearman's rho / Theoretical Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho
atoms.text:
## Theoretical Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho
| family | $\tau$ | $\rho _{S}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Gaussian | $(2/\pi ) \arcsin (\rho )$ | $(6/\pi ) \arcsin (\rho /2)$ |
| Student-t | $(2/\pi ) \arcsin (\rho )$ (does not depend on $\nu$) | no closed form; NOT the Gaussian formula for finite $\nu$ |
| Clayton | $\theta  / (\theta  + 2)$ | no closed form (numerical) |
| Gumbel | $1 - 1/\theta$ | no closed form (numerical) |
| Frank | $1 - (4/\theta )(1 - D_{1}(\theta ))$ | $1 - (12/\theta )(D_{1}(\theta ) - D_{2}(\theta ))$ |

- Debye function $D_{k}(x) = (k / x^{k}) \int _{0}^{x} t^{k} / (e^{t} - 1) \mathrm{d}t$ (integrand -> 1 at $t = 0$ for $k = 1, \to  0$ for $k \ge  2$);
  use the same integral for $x < 0$(or $D_{k}(-x) = D_{k}(x) + k x / (k + 1)$); Frank $\tau$ and $\rho _{S}$ are odd in $\theta$.
- Numerical $\rho _{S}$: $\rho _{S} = 12 \int _{0}^{1} \int _{0}^{1} [C(u, v) - u v] \mathrm{d}u \mathrm{d}v$. For t (or Gaussian) integrate in score space:
  $\rho _{S} = 12 \operatorname{E}[(t_{\nu}(X) - 1/2)(t_{\nu}(Y) - 1/2)]$ under the bivariate t density with correlation $\rho$ and $\nu$ df.
- Numerical $\tau$: $\tau  = 4 \operatorname{E}[C(U, V)] - 1 = 4 \int  \int  C(u, v) c(u, v) \mathrm{d}u \mathrm{d}v - 1$; Archimedean $\tau  = 1 + 4 \int _{0}^{1} \phi (t)/\phi '(t) \mathrm{d}t$, $\phi  = \psi ^{-1}$.
- Sample statistics: Kendall $\tau$ ($\tau_a=\tau_b$ with continuous data), Spearman = Pearson correlation of the ranks.

atoms.title: Sampling bivariate copulas (Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank) and their Kendall's tau / Spearman's rho / Self-checks (do them before using a sampler or density)
atoms.text:
## Self-checks (do them before using a sampler or density)
- Sampling: margins uniform (KS test); empirical $\tau$ and $\rho _{S}$ within a few standard errors of the table for several parameters
  (std. error about $1/\sqrt{n}$ scale; replicate to estimate it); empirical C(a, b) = share of pairs with $U \le  a, V \le  b$ vs the closed-form C.
- Density: integrates to 1 over the unit square (integrate in normal-score space to tame corner singularities) and equals the
  mixed finite difference $[C(u+h, v+h) - C(u+h, v-h) - C(u-h, v+h) + C(u-h, v-h)] / (4 h^{2})$ of the CDF.
- Frailty: $\operatorname{mean}(\exp(-sM))$ matches $\psi(s)$ for a few s.

atoms.title: Sampling bivariate copulas (Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank) and their Kendall's tau / Spearman's rho / Common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common mistakes
- Clayton frailty with shape $\theta$ (or scale $\theta$) instead of shape $1/\theta$, scale 1: wrong $\tau$.
- Gumbel frailty from a stable generator with unit scale or $\beta  \ne  1$, or $\alpha  = \theta$ instead of $1/\theta$.
- Drawing a new frailty (or $\chi$-square) per coordinate: destroys the dependence.
- Using $\exp (-\operatorname{E}/M)$ instead of $\psi (\operatorname{E}/M)$, or uniforms instead of Exp(1) without the `-ln W` transform.
- Reporting Pearson correlation of (U, V) as Kendall's $\tau$; using $(6/\pi ) \arcsin (\rho /2)$ for the t copula.
- Frank frailty with $\theta  < 0$(p would exceed 1): use conditional inversion instead.

atoms.title: Sampling bivariate copulas (Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank) and their Kendall's tau / Spearman's rho / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- Marshall-Olkin needs a completely monotone generator: valid for Clayton $\theta  > 0$, Gumbel $\theta  \ge  1$, Frank $\theta  > 0$ only.
- Very large $\theta$: Frank frailty M becomes heavy-tailed (mean $p / ((1 - p) \theta )$, about $e^\theta/\theta$) and Gumbel M extreme;
  conditional inversion and log-space evaluation stay stable.
- Pseudo-random results depend on the generator and seed; tasks with a fixed seed usually also fix the sampling order and method.

atoms.text:
# Credit portfolio: one-factor Gaussian copula / Vasicek ASRF, Basel IRB, Euler risk contributions

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

**Before writing the stressed default probability (VaR, granularity adjustment, any formula with a quantile of the factor):** the number fed to the normal quantile is either the confidence level q (for example 0.999) or the tail probability 1 - q (0.001), and which one depends on the sign in front of the factor term:

| Formula as written | Quantile to use | Stressed factor |
|---|---|---|
| `Phi((Phi^-1(PD) + sqrt(rho) * Phi^-1(x)) / sqrt(1 - rho))` (high factor is bad) | x = q | `Phi^-1(q)`, a large positive number |
| `Phi((Phi^-1(PD) - sqrt(rho) * z) / sqrt(1 - rho))` with z the factor (low factor is bad) | z = `Phi^-1(1 - q)` | a large negative number |

A task or paper that writes the factor quantile with a symbol such as alpha may mean either; read the sign in its formula and check the result rather than the symbol name. The same quantile goes into every formula that evaluates the worst-case factor (conditional PD, its derivatives in a granularity adjustment, the conditional variance).

Stressed (conditional) default probability at confidence level $q$, in the form where a high factor value is bad: $p(q) = \Phi\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}) + \sqrt{\rho}\,\Phi^{-1}(q)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)$. Check: it exceeds the PD and rises with $q$.

atoms.title: Credit portfolio: one-factor Gaussian copula / Vasicek ASRF, Basel IRB, Euler risk contributions / Model and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Model and assumptions
- Obligor i has latent asset return $A_{i} = \sqrt{\rho _{i}} Z + \sqrt{1 - \rho _{i}} \mathrm{eps}_{i}$, with Z (systematic factor) and $\mathrm{eps}_{i}$ i.i.d. N(0, 1).
  Default over the horizon iff $A_{i} < c_{i} = \Phi ^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}_{i})$. Here LOW Z is the bad state. $\rho _{i}$ is the ASSET correlation, not the default correlation.
- Conditional on $Z = z$, defaults are independent with

$$
p_{i}(z) = \Phi ( (\Phi ^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}_{i}) - \sqrt{\rho _{i}} z) / \sqrt{1 - \rho _{i}} )
$$

  Some texts write $+ \sqrt{\rho} z$ with HIGH z bad (Z replaced by -Z); then the stressed factor is $z = \Phi ^{-1}(q)$ instead of $\Phi^{-1}(1-q)$. Same numbers.
- Loss $L = \sum _{i} \mathrm{EAD}_{i} \cdot  \mathrm{LGD}_{i} \cdot  1\{\mathrm{default}_{i}\}$; EAD, LGD deterministic unless the task says otherwise. Horizon is usually one year.
- ASRF (asymptotic single risk factor): infinitely many small exposures, so $L \to  \operatorname{E}[L \vert  Z] = \sum _{i} \mathrm{EAD}_{i} \mathrm{LGD}_{i} p_{i}(Z)$, a monotone function of Z.

atoms.title: Credit portfolio: one-factor Gaussian copula / Vasicek ASRF, Basel IRB, Euler risk contributions / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{PD}_{i}$ | unconditional default probability over the horizon (1% is 0.01) | none |
| $\rho _{i} (R)$ | asset correlation parameter: $\operatorname{Corr}(A_i,Z)=\sqrt{\rho_i}$ and $\operatorname{Corr}(A_i,A_j)=\sqrt{\rho_i\rho_j}$ for distinct names, $0 < \rho  < 1$ | none |
| $\mathrm{EAD}_{i}, \mathrm{LGD}_{i}$ | exposure at default; loss given default as a fraction of EAD | currency, none |
| $q$ | confidence level (99.9% is 0.999) | none |
| $M$ | effective maturity for the Basel maturity adjustment | years |

atoms.title: Credit portfolio: one-factor Gaussian copula / Vasicek ASRF, Basel IRB, Euler risk contributions / Vasicek large homogeneous pool (same PD, rho; default fraction L in [0, 1])
atoms.text:
## Vasicek large homogeneous pool (same PD, rho; default fraction L in [0, 1])

$$
\operatorname{P}(L \le  x) = \Phi ( (\sqrt{1 - \rho} \Phi ^{-1}(x) - \Phi ^{-1}(\mathrm{PD})) / \sqrt{\rho} )
$$

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{q}(L) = \Phi ( (\Phi ^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}) + \sqrt{\rho} \cdot  \Phi ^{-1}(q)) / \sqrt{1 - \rho} )
$$

$q$ is the confidence level. A positive normal quantile by itself does not imply that the loss quantile exceeds the mean. Compare the displayed quantile with PD under the specified parameters. The stressed factor in the low-factor-is-bad convention is $\Phi^{-1}(1-q)$.

$$
\operatorname{E}[L] = \mathrm{PD}
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}[L] = \mathrm{Phi2}(c, c; \rho ) - \mathrm{PD}^{2}
$$

Default correlation:

$$
(\mathrm{Phi2}(c, c; \rho ) - \mathrm{PD}^{2}) / (\mathrm{PD} (1 - \mathrm{PD}))
$$

$$
\operatorname{ES}_{q}(L) = \mathrm{Phi2}( \Phi ^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}), \Phi ^{-1}(1 - q); \sqrt{\rho} ) / (1 - q)
$$

$\mathrm{Phi2}(a, b; r)$ is the bivariate normal CDF with correlation $r$. Loss in currency: multiply by $\mathrm{EAD}_{\mathrm{total}}$ * LGD. Heterogeneous ASRF: $\operatorname{VaR}_{q} = \sum _{i} \mathrm{EAD}_{i} \mathrm{LGD}_{i} \Phi ( (\Phi ^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}_{i}) + \sqrt{\rho _{i}} \cdot  \Phi ^{-1}(q)) / \sqrt{1 - \rho _{i}} )$ (same q, same sign), $\operatorname{ES}_{q} = \sum _{i} \mathrm{EAD}_{i} \mathrm{LGD}_{i} \mathrm{Phi2}(c_{i}, \Phi ^{-1}(1 - q); \sqrt{\rho _{i}}) / (1 - q)$.
Finite homogeneous pool of n names: $\operatorname{P}(D = k) = \int  C(n, k) p(z)^{k} (1 - p(z))^{n - k} \phi (z) \mathrm{d}z$ (quadrature over z).

atoms.title: Credit portfolio: one-factor Gaussian copula / Vasicek ASRF, Basel IRB, Euler risk contributions / Basel II IRB (BCBS 2005 explanatory note; ASRF at q = 0.999, regulatory constants below)
atoms.text:
## Basel II IRB (BCBS 2005 explanatory note; ASRF at q = 0.999, regulatory constants below)
Capital per unit EAD, UL only:

$$
K = [ \mathrm{LGD} \cdot  \Phi ( (\Phi ^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}) + \sqrt{R} \Phi ^{-1}(0.999)) / \sqrt{1 - R} ) - \mathrm{PD} \cdot  \mathrm{LGD} ] \cdot  \mathrm{MA}
$$

Corporate/bank/sovereign maturity adjustment ($\mathrm{MA} = 1$ at $M = 1$):

$$
\mathrm{MA} = (1 + (M - 2.5) b) / (1 - 1.5 b)
$$

$$
b = (0.11852 - 0.05478 \ln (\mathrm{PD}))^{2}
$$

$$
\mathrm{RWA} = 12.5 \cdot  K \cdot  \mathrm{EAD}
$$

Corporate correlation:

$$
R = 0.12 w + 0.24 (1 - w)
$$

$$
w = (1 - \exp (-50 \mathrm{PD})) / (1 - \exp (-50))
$$

For SMEs, subtract $0.04 (1 - (S - 5)/45)$, where $S$ is sales in EUR mn clipped to $[5, 50]$. Retail uses no MA: residential mortgage $R = 0.15$, qualifying revolving $R = 0.04$; other retail uses the corporate expression with 0.03, 0.16 and 35 in place of 0.12, 0.24 and 50. Variant without MA: set $\mathrm{MA} = 1$. The Basel II Annex 5 illustrative risk weights are reproduced with $\mathrm{RWA} = 12.5 K \mathrm{EAD}$ and no extra scaling factor; PD floors or scaling only if the task states them.

atoms.title: Credit portfolio: one-factor Gaussian copula / Vasicek ASRF, Basel IRB, Euler risk contributions / Monte Carlo of correlated defaults
atoms.text:
## Monte Carlo of correlated defaults
Per scenario s: draw $Z_{s}$, $\mathrm{eps}_{i,s}\sim N(0,1)$; $D_{i,s} = 1\{ \sqrt{\rho _{i}} Z_{s} + \sqrt{1 - \rho _{i}} \mathrm{eps}_{i,s} < \Phi ^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}_{i}) \}$; $L_{i,s} = \mathrm{EAD}_{i} \mathrm{LGD}_{i} D_{i,s}$, $L_{s} = \sum _{i} L_{i,s}$.
Homogeneous shortcut: draw $Z_{s}$, then $D_{s} \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n, p(Z_{s}))$. Keep the per-obligor losses if contributions are needed.
- $\operatorname{VaR}_{q}$ = empirical q-quantile of $L_{s}$ (state the convention: order statistic `L_(ceil(N q))` ascending, or interpolated).
- Integrated-quantile ES uses exactly upper-tail mass $1-q$, including fractional mass at the cutoff; a largest-k average or a conditional tail mean is a separate convention. Follow an explicit task definition and label it accordingly.
- $\mathrm{EL} = \sum _{i} \mathrm{EAD}_{i} \mathrm{LGD}_{i} \mathrm{PD}_{i}$. Economic capital (unexpected loss) = $\operatorname{VaR}_q-\mathrm{EL}$ (or $\operatorname{ES}_q-\mathrm{EL}$). Some texts call sd(L) "unexpected loss"; follow the task.

atoms.title: Credit portfolio: one-factor Gaussian copula / Vasicek ASRF, Basel IRB, Euler risk contributions / Several correlated systematic factors (for example sector factors)
atoms.text:
## Several correlated systematic factors (for example sector factors)
When each obligor loads on one of k systematic factors with correlation matrix R (k x k), `C = np.linalg.cholesky(R)` is
lower triangular with `C @ C.T = R`. With one row of independent standard normals per scenario, `Z` of shape
(n_scenarios, k), the correlated factors are `F = Z @ C.T` (each row is C z). `Z @ C` has covariance `C.T @ C`, which is
not R; check the sample correlation and unit variances of F before using it. Obligor i in factor s(i) then has
$A_{i} = \sqrt{\rho _{i}} F_{s(i)} + \sqrt{1 - \rho _{i}} \mathrm{eps}_{i}$. In a Student-t copula one mixing draw
$W \sim \chi^2_{\nu}/\nu$ per scenario divides both parts of every obligor in that scenario, and the default threshold is
$t_{\nu}^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}_{i})$.

An (n_scenarios, n_obligors) float64 array takes 8 bytes per cell (0.8 GB for 1e5 x 1e3), and one vectorised step
often holds several such arrays. Simulate in consecutive scenario batches and keep the per-scenario portfolio loss plus
only the per-obligor quantities needed later. Drawing the small arrays for all scenarios first and then the large
idiosyncratic array batch by batch from the same generator reproduces the unbatched stream when the unbatched code drew
them in that order (arrays fill row by row); otherwise results differ by Monte Carlo noise only.

Reduce what is stored, not its precision: keep losses and running sums in float64. float32 keeps about seven significant digits (its spacing near 1e8 is 8), so a portfolio total passed through float32 can differ between two output files by several units. Batching keeps the draws only if each batch takes the next rows of the same arrays: a loop that draws a factor and then names for every batch, after a whole run that drew all factors first, gives different numbers; check batched against unbatched on a small case before the full run.

Multi-factor simulation of portfolio losses:

1. Correlated sector factors: standard normals times the transpose of the Cholesky factor $C$ of the factor correlation matrix; check that their sample correlation is close to $CC^{\top}$.
2. In batches of scenarios (to bound memory), draw idiosyncratic normals per obligor and form the asset value $A = \sqrt{\rho}\, F_{\mathrm{sector}} + \sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon$.
3. An obligor defaults when $A$ is below its threshold $\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{PD})$; the scenario loss is the sum of the loss given default of the defaulted obligors.

atoms.title: Credit portfolio: one-factor Gaussian copula / Vasicek ASRF, Basel IRB, Euler risk contributions / Risk contributions (Euler allocation; risk measure homogeneous of degree 1 in exposures w_i)
atoms.text:
## Risk contributions (Euler allocation; risk measure homogeneous of degree 1 in exposures w_i)

$$
\mathrm{RC}_{i} = w_{i} \cdot  \mathrm{d}R/\mathrm{d}w_{i}
$$

$$
\sum _{i} \mathrm{RC}_{i} = R(L)
$$

For a continuous loss distribution with no atom at its quantile and suitable differentiability, ES components are tail conditional means. For losses with atoms, select only the needed probability at the boundary.

Let $v=\inf\{x:F_L(x)\ge q\}$ and $a=1-q$. The fraction of the boundary atom included in the upper tail is:

$$
\eta=\frac{a-\Pr(L>v)}{\Pr(L=v)}
$$

This definition applies when the denominator is positive; otherwise the boundary term vanishes. The component allocation, using the same boundary fraction for every component, is:

$$
\mathrm{RC}_i^{\mathrm{ES}}=\frac{\mathrm{E}[L_i\mathbf{1}_{L>v}]+\eta\,\mathrm{E}[L_i\mathbf{1}_{L=v}]}{a}
$$

The allocations sum to integrated-quantile ES because scenario losses sum across components. In an equally weighted sample, allocate fractional mass at the cutoff rather than taking every tied scenario. Averaging all losses above or equal to VaR is a different quantity when excess probability enters through ties. Tail mass below one scenario gives the largest scenario loss; component selection at a tie need not be unique, although total ES is.

For a continuous distribution, under regularity, VaR Euler contributions can be expressed by conditional component losses at the quantile. A finite discrete portfolio need not have a differentiable VaR. A window average is a smoothing approximation; rescaling it to match total VaR is a normalization, not proof of correct marginal allocation.

When the total risk measure is estimated by Monte Carlo, compute the contributions from the same simulated scenarios (tail conditional means), so that they add up to the simulated total; check that their sum divided by the total is 1 within simulation noise. The ASRF formulas below are for the analytic one-factor model and do not add up to a simulated portfolio total.

ASRF allocations:

$$
\mathrm{RC}_{i}^{\operatorname{VaR}} = \mathrm{EAD}_{i} \mathrm{LGD}_{i} p_{i}(\Phi ^{-1}(1 - q))
$$

$$
\mathrm{RC}_{i}^{\operatorname{ES}} = \mathrm{EAD}_{i} \mathrm{LGD}_{i} \mathrm{Phi2}(c_{i}, \Phi ^{-1}(1 - q); \sqrt{\rho _{i}}) / (1 - q)
$$

Marginal ES of obligor i = dES$/\mathrm{dEAD}_{i} = \mathrm{RC}_{i}^{\operatorname{ES}} / \mathrm{EAD}_{i}$. Capital contributions net of EL: $\mathrm{RC}_{i}$ - $\mathrm{EAD}_{i}$ $\mathrm{LGD}_{i}$ $\mathrm{PD}_{i}$.

atoms.title: Credit portfolio: one-factor Gaussian copula / Vasicek ASRF, Basel IRB, Euler risk contributions / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- ASRF/Basel ignore name concentration (fix: MC) and sector concentration (single factor). Gaussian copula has no tail dependence.
- Common mistakes: using $+ \sqrt{\rho} \Phi ^{-1}(1 - q)$ (for $\mathrm{PD}<0.5$ and $q>0.5$, gives a value below EL); using default correlation as $\rho$; forgetting $- \mathrm{PD}\cdot \mathrm{LGD}$ in Basel K; applying MA to retail.
- MC tail estimates at q near 1 need many scenarios (only N (1 - q) tail points); report the seed and N. VaR is not subadditive; ES is.

Choose one loss convention and confidence level for each calculation. Use that same convention for total loss, components, units and diagnostics; a sign conversion changes all of them together.
