Day-count fractions, accrual dates and settlement calendars / overview
atoms.text:
# Day-count fractions, accrual dates and settlement calendars

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use explicit contract conventions. A year fraction, a business-day adjustment and a cashflow's payment entitlement are separate definitions. Currency names alone do not select a calendar or day-count variant. Dates below are ordered start $a\le b$ and end $b$; the discussion concerns date-only accrual, not intraday timestamps. When both endpoints carry a time of day, the ACT/365 numerator is the elapsed time in days, `total_seconds()/86400`, not the whole-day count `.days`.

**Before computing accruals or discount factors in two currencies:** each currency's leg, deposit rate and curve uses that currency's own day-count basis (the trade or quote conventions name it, for example ACT/360 for one currency and ACT/365F for another). One shared year fraction for both legs is a common error that the totals do not reveal. Write one year-fraction function per currency and check that the two give different values for the same dates whenever the bases differ:

Example: from 15 January to 15 February (31 days) the year fraction is $31/360 = 0.0861$ under ACT/360 and $31/365 = 0.0849$ under ACT/365F. If two legs with different bases get the same fraction, one leg used the other currency's basis.

atoms.title: Day-count fractions, accrual dates and settlement calendars / Actual day counts
atoms.text:
## Actual day counts

Let $D(a,b)$ be the integer calendar-day difference. Actual/360 and Actual/365 Fixed use:

$$
\tau_{360}(a,b)=\frac{D(a,b)}{360},\qquad
\tau_{365F}(a,b)=\frac{D(a,b)}{365}.
$$

Leap days belong in the numerator; Actual/365 Fixed does not replace its denominator by 366. Actual/Actual is another family requiring its own definition. Counting business days is not a substitute for actual calendar-day accrual. The ordinary date difference excludes the start and includes the end; reversing the inclusion convention without changing a count can obscure endpoint errors.

atoms.title: Day-count fractions, accrual dates and settlement calendars / A specified 30/360 US convention
atoms.text:
## A specified 30/360 US convention

For year, month and day components $(Y_i,M_i,D_i)$, replace the day components by $D_i^*$ using the stated variant. The accrual is:

$$
\tau_{30/360}=\frac{360(Y_2-Y_1)+30(M_2-M_1)+D_2^*-D_1^*}{360}.
$$

For the `Thirty360::USA` implementation cited below, apply these adjustments in order: if the start is February's last day, set its day to 30 and also set the end day to 30 when it too is February's last day; next change an end day of 31 to 30 when the adjusted start day is at least 30; finally change a start day of 31 to 30. Both common and leap-year February endpoints need this test.

This is not a license to use one formula for every label containing 30/360. Bond Basis omits February rules; European 30E/360 clips each 31 independently. Other variants can depend on the termination date. Use the declared variant and applicable market specification rather than silently exchanging them.

As synthetic arithmetic checks, January 31 to February 28 in a non-leap year has a 28/360 US fraction under that variant; February 28 to March 31 has 30/360. A year beginning and ending at February month-end can have actual-day count different from its 30/360 numerator.

atoms.title: Day-count fractions, accrual dates and settlement calendars / Business-day calendars and date rolls
atoms.text:
## Business-day calendars and date rolls

A calendar decides whether a date is open, including its holiday set and weekend definition. Following moves a closed date to the next open date. Modified Following instead uses the preceding open date if Following would cross the original calendar month. This is different from adding a fixed number of calendar days.

Where settlement requires both markets to be open, the joint business-day indicator is:

$$
I_{\mathrm{joint}}(d)=I_1(d)I_2(d).
$$

The joint holiday set is therefore the union, not the intersection. Some products use other joint-calendar rules; the contract governs. Adding a positive business-day lag counts eligible following business days without counting the start. A zero lag still needs a declared adjustment convention if the start is closed.

Calendar-month advancement precedes any specified business-day roll. Month-end preservation, clamping a nonexistent day and holiday adjustment are distinct rules. Advancing from the original schedule anchor and repeatedly advancing the previous adjusted date can produce different schedules. Under ordinary calendar clamping, a synthetic leap-year January 31 plus one month is February 29; another month from that clamped date is March 29, whereas two months from the original anchor reaches March 31. An explicit end-of-month schedule is a different rule.

atoms.title: Day-count fractions, accrual dates and settlement calendars / Accrual versus payment
atoms.text:
## Accrual versus payment

For fixed notional $N$, annual simple coupon rate $r$ and contractual accrual $\tau$, the coupon is:

$$
C=Nr\tau.
$$

For a coupon period with stated full coupon $C$, an elapsed/full-period fraction convention gives accrued interest:

$$
\mathrm{AI}=C\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{elapsed}}}{\tau_{\mathrm{full}}}.
$$

This equals $Nr\tau_{\mathrm{elapsed}}$ only when the coupon and full-period accrual were defined compatibly. A delayed payment date does not automatically lengthen the interest accrual period. Discounting time can use a different day-count basis from coupon accrual. Stub coupons, ex-coupon entitlement and settlement ownership require their contractual rules.

atoms.title: Day-count fractions, accrual dates and settlement calendars / Sources and limits
atoms.text:
## Sources and limits

[QuantLib Thirty360 implementation](https://github.com/lballabio/QuantLib/blob/master/ql/time/daycounters/thirty360.cpp) and [variant definitions](https://github.com/lballabio/QuantLib/blob/master/ql/time/daycounters/thirty360.hpp) identify the day adjustments above. [Calendar adjustment implementation](https://github.com/lballabio/QuantLib/blob/master/ql/time/calendar.cpp) and [joint calendar rules](https://github.com/lballabio/QuantLib/blob/master/ql/time/calendars/jointcalendar.hpp) distinguish date rolling and calendar combinations. Formula scaling, synthetic examples and the joint-indicator identity follow by date arithmetic and the stated definitions; no live holiday calendar or transaction-specific settlement date is supplied here.

atoms.title: Dependent resampling and conditional risk coverage / overview
atoms.text:
# Dependent resampling and conditional risk coverage

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use block resampling when preserving serial dependence matters. Explicit task definitions determine residual normalization, block length, refitting, risk horizon and quantile convention. Resampling is not a substitute for a correctly specified conditional variance model.

atoms.title: Dependent resampling and conditional risk coverage / Stationary bootstrap
atoms.text:
## Stationary bootstrap

Let the historical series have $n$ ordered rows. A stationary-bootstrap path starts with a uniformly sampled row. For subsequent rows, continue to the next circular index with probability $1-p$, otherwise choose another uniform starting row. The mean block length is $b=1/p$, with $b\ge1$.

The resulting block length has geometric probability:

$$
\Pr(K=k)=p(1-p)^{k-1},\qquad k=1,2,\ldots
$$

For a multivariate series, a common row index preserves within-row dependence. Sampling each column independently destroys that dependence. Taking circular successors preserves time ordering inside blocks; sorting sampled rows does not preserve the bootstrap law.

atoms.title: Dependent resampling and conditional risk coverage / Standardized-residual simulation
atoms.text:
## Standardized-residual simulation

For conditional covariance $H_t=A_tA_t'$ with nonsingular $A_t$, whitened shocks have identity conditional covariance under the model:

$$
z_t=A_t^{-1}(r_t-m_t)
$$

Drawing historical vectors standardized only by marginal volatilities retains cross-sectional correlation. Applying a fresh correlation factor to those already correlated vectors generally counts correlation again. Whitening/recoloring and complete-row filtered historical simulation are distinct choices. Centering and scaling historical residuals are finite-sample conventions, not automatic model identities.

atoms.title: Dependent resampling and conditional risk coverage / Sampling uncertainty
atoms.text:
## Sampling uncertainty

For scalar bootstrap estimates $\widehat\theta^{*(1)},\ldots,\widehat\theta^{*(M)}$, the bootstrap standard error is their sample standard deviation, not that standard deviation divided by $\sqrt M$:

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_{\mathrm{boot}}=
\sqrt{\frac1{M-1}\sum_{j=1}^M(\widehat\theta^{*(j)}-\overline\theta^*)^2}
$$

The latter division describes Monte Carlo error in a bootstrap mean. Refit parameters in each replicate when the target includes parameter-estimation uncertainty; holding them fixed addresses a conditional target. A percentile interval uses empirical quantiles of the bootstrap estimates, not quantiles of their individual standard errors.

atoms.title: Dependent resampling and conditional risk coverage / Risk coverage
atoms.text:
## Risk coverage

For loss $L_t$ and a forecast made with information through the preceding observation, define the violation indicator by the chosen strict/non-strict convention. Under a continuous correctly calibrated conditional quantile, its conditional probability is:

$$
I_t=\mathbf{1}\{L_t>\operatorname{VaR}_{q,t}\},\qquad
\operatorname{E}[I_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=1-q
$$

Correct average coverage alone does not imply independent violations. Overlapping multi-period losses can create dependence even with reasonable forecasts. With atoms, an unrandomized quantile can have violation probability below $1-q$, so exact equality is not automatic. Clipping zero transition counts changes likelihood-ratio backtests; evaluate limiting terms such as $0\log0=0$ instead.

atoms.title: Dependent resampling and conditional risk coverage / References
atoms.text:
## References

[arch: StationaryBootstrap](https://bashtage.github.io/arch/bootstrap/generated/arch.bootstrap.StationaryBootstrap.html), geometric block construction following Politis and Romano (1994). The whitening, variance and conditional-expectation distinctions are direct consequences of the definitions above.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / overview
atoms.text:
# Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type

This reference explains how to identify a payoff, select its Black–Scholes pricing formula, and check the result. It covers European terminal payoffs and continuously monitored single barriers with constant model parameters. Read Shared Foundations first, then the sections needed for the contract. Follow the contract specification when it differs from this reference; do not force a contract outside these assumptions into these formulas. American exercise and stochastic volatility require other methods.

Follow the task’s prescribed steps. Use the referenced sections for definitions and formulas; the section order is not an execution plan.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## Shared Foundations

Map the task’s symbols and units to the definitions here before the first calculation. Recheck the mapping when the contract, model, or input definitions change; there is no need to repeat an unchanged mapping in every response.

Before choosing a formula, identify what is paid, when it is paid, and which event causes payment. Also identify exercise style, any barrier monitoring schedule, rebate rules, and input/output units. If a necessary convention is unspecified, state the assumption used.

European describes exercise timing; digital describes the payoff; barrier describes a path condition. These features can occur in the same contract.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $S$ | Current underlying price |
| $K$ | Strike |
| $H$ | Barrier level |
| $Q$ | Fixed cash payment, distinct from the risk-neutral measure $\mathbb Q$ |
| $R$ | Rebate amount |
| $r$ | Continuously compounded risk-free rate |
| $q$ | Continuous dividend yield |
| $\sigma$ | Annualized volatility in decimal units |
| $T$ | Remaining maturity in years |
| N, $\phi$ | Standard normal CDF and density |
| $S_{T}$ | Underlying price at maturity |
| $\Pi$ | Payoff function, written $\Pi$ in formulas |
| $V$ | Present value of a payoff |
| $C, \operatorname{P}$ | Ordinary European call and put prices, unless a subscript specifies another contract |

Notation: $\mathbf1_A$ equals 1 when event A occurs and 0 otherwise; $z^+=\max(z,0)$; ln is the natural logarithm. All probabilities and expectations in this reference use the risk-neutral measure $\mathbb Q$, including expressions where the superscript is omitted.

For FX, the foreign interest rate plays the role of q. Rates and volatility use annual units here, so T must be in years. The discount factor $\exp (-rT)$ applies to a payment at maturity. The formulas below assume positive spot, strike, volatility, and maturity. At zero maturity evaluate the payoff; at zero volatility use the deterministic terminal price and path.

The model describes proportional price changes. Under the risk-neutral measure,
**Risk-neutral stock dynamics**

$$
dS_t=(r-q)S_tdt+\sigma S_tdW_t^{\mathbb Q}.
$$

Applying Itô's lemma converts the price process into the log-price process:
**Risk-neutral log-price dynamics**

$$
d\ln S_t=(r-q-\sigma^2/2)dt+\sigma dW_t^{\mathbb Q}.
$$

Define log drift $\nu=r-q-\sigma^2/2$. Then
**Terminal stock distribution**

$$
S_T=S\exp(\nu T+\sigma\sqrt T Z),\quad Z\sim N(0,1).
$$

If an input already describes log drift, do not subtract the Itô correction again.

For a payoff $\Pi(S_T)$ paid at maturity, calculate its risk-neutral expectation and discount it:
**Discounted expected payoff**

$$
V=e^{-rT}\mathbb E^{\mathbb Q}[\Pi(S_T)].
$$

**Black–Scholes exercise thresholds**

$$
d_2=\frac{\ln(S/K)+(r-q-\sigma^2/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T},\qquad d_1=d_2+\sigma\sqrt T.
$$

The event $S_{T} > K$ is equivalent to $Z > -\mathrm{d2}$. Normal symmetry therefore gives probability N(d2). For an asset payment, the expectation also contains $S_{T}$. The following identity, valid for real a and z, evaluates that weighted normal integral:
**Normal-density exponential tilting identity**

$$
e^{az}\phi(z)=e^{a^2/2}\phi(z-a)
$$

**Truncated terminal asset expectation**

$$
\mathbb E[S_T\mathbf1_{S_T>K}]=Se^{(r-q)T}N(d_1).
$$

### Transfer across notation and parameter values

For example, a dividend yield named D can replace q here only if it denotes the same continuous annual yield; a cash dividend amount cannot.

Renaming symbols consistently does not change the mathematics or numerical result. The definitions, relationships, and derivations transfer to another task when the payoff, model assumptions, payment timing, and monitoring convention match. Changing parameter values usually changes the result. Re-evaluate branch conditions such as the ordering of strike and barrier for each new input; do not carry over a previously selected branch or Boolean conclusion.

Notation invariance is different from parameter invariance. A relationship can remain valid across admissible parameter values without the price being constant. Some transformations imply a predictable change rather than equality: multiplying a fixed cash payoff Q by a positive factor multiplies its price by that factor, with the other inputs unchanged. For a vanilla cash digital, jointly scaling positive S and K by the same factor leaves its price unchanged when Q, r, q, $\sigma$, and T are fixed, because S/K is unchanged. That test is not a test of sensitivity to spot alone.

Use these as transformation checks only after deriving what must remain equal and what must scale. If a new task changes the payoff, stochastic process, exercise rights, or observation schedule, re-establish applicability before reusing a formula.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / European Vanilla Options
atoms.text:
## European Vanilla Options

**Ordinary European payoff.** A call pays $(S_T-K)^+$; a put pays $(K-S_T)^+$, both at maturity. These are payoffs, not profits after deducting the premium.

**Ordinary European pricing.** Decompose the call payoff as
**Call payoff decomposition**

$$
(S_T-K)^+=S_T\mathbf1_{S_T>K}-K\mathbf1_{S_T>K}.
$$

Using the shared probability and asset moment gives
**European call price**

$$
C=Se^{-qT}N(d_1)-Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)
$$

**European put price**

$$
P=Ke^{-rT}N(-d_2)-Se^{-qT}N(-d_1).
$$

Apply contract quantity separately if the requested value is for a position.

**Ordinary European checks.** Compare contracts with the same spot, strike, maturity, rates, and volatility:
**European put-call parity**

$$
C-P=Se^{-qT}-Ke^{-rT}.
$$

**European call price bounds**

$$
\max(Se^{-qT}-Ke^{-rT},0)\le C\le Se^{-qT}
$$

**European put price bounds**

$$
\max(Ke^{-rT}-Se^{-qT},0)\le P\le Ke^{-rT}.
$$

Do not apply these European formulas as an American early-exercise solution.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / Cash or Nothing Digital Options
atoms.text:
## Cash or Nothing Digital Options

**Cash-or-nothing payoff.** A call pays $Q\mathbf1_{S_T>K}$; a put pays $Q\mathbf1_{S_T<K}$. Identify the cash amount rather than assuming $Q = 1$. Under the nondegenerate continuous terminal distribution, equality at the strike has zero probability.

**Cash digital pricing.** Multiply the fixed cash payment by its payment probability, then discount:
**Cash digital call price**

$$
C_{cash}=Qe^{-rT}N(d_2)
$$

**Cash digital put price**

$$
P_{cash}=Qe^{-rT}N(-d_2).
$$

Use d2 for the terminal probability. An ordinary option formula would price a different payoff.

**Cash digital checks.** Use the same parameters and cash amount for the call and put. For positive Q,
**Cash digital complement and bounds**

$$
C_{cash}+P_{cash}=Qe^{-rT},\qquad 0\le C_{cash},P_{cash}\le Qe^{-rT}.
$$

Holding all other inputs fixed,
**Cash-call sensitivity to spot**

$$
\frac{\partial C_{cash}}{\partial S}=\frac{Qe^{-rT}\phi(d_2)}{S\sigma\sqrt T}>0,\quad
$$

**Cash-call sensitivity to strike**

$$
\frac{\partial C_{cash}}{\partial K}=-\frac{Qe^{-rT}\phi(d_2)}{K\sigma\sqrt T}<0.
$$

To check spot sensitivity, change spot alone and retain the original strike. Holding moneyness fixed changes another input. Allow floating-point tolerance in saturated tails. These signs cannot be assumed for barrier digitals.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / Asset or Nothing Digital Options
atoms.text:
## Asset or Nothing Digital Options

**Asset-or-nothing payoff.** A call pays $S_T\mathbf1_{S_T>K}$; a put pays $S_T\mathbf1_{S_T<K}$. There is no strike payment in these contracts. The delivered asset value is the terminal value, not the initial spot.

**Asset digital pricing.** Discount the asset-weighted expectation to obtain
**Asset digital call price**

$$
C_{asset}=Se^{-qT}N(d_1)
$$

**Asset digital put price**

$$
P_{asset}=Se^{-qT}N(-d_1).
$$

The use of d1 follows from weighting the terminal distribution by $S_{T}$; it is not the same calculation as a fixed-cash payment probability.

**Asset digital checks.** With matching parameters, call and put events cover all terminal outcomes, so
**Asset digital complement**

$$
C_{asset}+P_{asset}=Se^{-qT}.
$$

**Payoff decomposition and price checks.** Decomposition means expressing one payoff as a linear combination of other payoffs. For European contracts with the same underlying, strike K and maturity T,
**Call payoff decomposition**

$$
(S_T-K)^+=S_T\mathbf1_{S_T>K}-K\mathbf1_{S_T>K}
$$

**Put payoff decomposition**

$$
(K-S_T)^+=K\mathbf1_{S_T<K}-S_T\mathbf1_{S_T<K}.
$$

The asset digital supplies the asset leg; K units of a unit-payment cash digital supply the strike leg. Discounted expectation is linear, so their prices satisfy
**Call price from digital legs**

$$
C=C_{asset}-K C_{cash}^{(1)}
$$

**Put price from digital legs**

$$
P=K P_{cash}^{(1)}-P_{asset}.
$$

Use matching spot, strike, maturity, rates, volatility, payment time and currency for all legs. Here C and P are ordinary European option prices; the superscript (1) means a cash payment of one currency unit. If the cash digital instead pays $Q > 0$, divide its price by Q. For $Q = 0$, obtain a unit-payment digital separately rather than dividing by zero.

Check the prices already computed by the implementation, separately for calls and puts at every parameter set:

**Compute both decomposition residuals using the priced legs**

With $Q > 0$ the cash amount of the cash-or-nothing legs and matching inputs for all legs:

1. Unit cash call and put: $c = C_{\mathrm{cash}} / Q$ and $p = P_{\mathrm{cash}} / Q$.
2. Call replica: $C_{\mathrm{rep}} = C_{\mathrm{asset}} - K c$.
3. Put replica: $P_{\mathrm{rep}} = K p - P_{\mathrm{asset}}$.
4. Residuals: $C_{\mathrm{vanilla}} - C_{\mathrm{rep}}$ and $P_{\mathrm{vanilla}} - P_{\mathrm{rep}}$.

Compare each residual with a suitable absolute-plus-relative numerical tolerance; for simulation, account for the sampling error of the difference, including covariance when estimates share paths. Do not replace the computed vanilla prices with the replicas merely to make this check pass. If vanilla prices were constructed from these same digital legs, zero residuals hold by construction and provide no independent pricing validation.

Put-call parity checks a different relation: $C - \operatorname{P} = S \exp (-qT) - K \exp (-rT)$. It does not check the asset/cash decomposition of either option. A passing parity residual cannot substitute for the two decomposition residuals. These identities concern matched European terminal payoffs; do not combine plain and barrier legs or different exercise styles.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / Gap Options
atoms.text:
## Gap Options

**Gap payoff.** A call pays $(S_T-K_{pay})\mathbf1_{S_T>K_{trigger}}$; a gap put pays $(K_{pay}-S_T)\mathbf1_{S_T<K_{trigger}}$. The trigger strike selects the event; the payment strike determines the cash leg. Identify these roles from definitions, since K1/K2 conventions vary.

**Gap pricing.** Substitute $K_{\mathrm{trigger}}$ for K in both d1 and d2; use $K_{\mathrm{pay}}$ only in the cash-payment terms below. Linearity of expectation gives
**Gap call price**

$$
C_{gap}=Se^{-qT}N(d_1^{trigger})-K_{pay}e^{-rT}N(d_2^{trigger})
$$

**Gap put price**

$$
P_{gap}=K_{pay}e^{-rT}N(-d_2^{trigger})-Se^{-qT}N(-d_1^{trigger}).
$$

**Gap checks.** When the trigger and payment strikes coincide, the gap formulas reduce to ordinary European formulas. For a matched gap call and put,
**Gap put-call parity**

$$
C_{gap}-P_{gap}=Se^{-qT}-K_{pay}e^{-rT}.
$$

The specified gap payoff can be negative on some outcomes. Adding a positive-part operator or clipping changes the contract.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / Vanilla Barrier Options
atoms.text:
## Vanilla Barrier Options

**Barrier condition.** Let $\tau_H$ be the first time the continuously monitored price reaches or crosses H during the contract. Use $\tau_H=\infty$ if no touch occurs. For a lower barrier, a touch means $S_{t} \le  H$; for an upper barrier, it means $S_{t} \ge  H$. A knock-out pays $\Pi(S_T)\mathbf1_{\tau_H>T}$; a knock-in pays $\Pi(S_T)\mathbf1_{\tau_H\le T}$. Identify upper or lower barrier, monitoring schedule, and rebate terms. A terminal condition alone does not determine whether the path previously touched the barrier.

For an ordinary barrier call or put, first apply the assumptions and knock-in/out rules in [Shared Barrier Mathematics](#shared-barrier-mathematics), then use its interval and surviving moments:
**Knock-out call from surviving moments**

$$
C_{KO}=e^{-rT}(J_1-KJ_0)
$$

**Knock-out put from surviving moments**

$$
P_{KO}=e^{-rT}(KJ_0-J_1).
$$

These combine surviving asset and cash legs. They price an ordinary payoff, not a fixed-cash digital payoff.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / Digital Barrier Options
atoms.text:
## Digital Barrier Options

**Digital barrier payoff.** A cash digital knock-out call pays $Q\mathbf1_{S_T>K}\mathbf1_{\tau_H>T}$. An asset digital knock-out call replaces Q by $S_{T}$. For a put, replace the terminal event $S_{T} > K$ with $S_{T} < K$. For a knock-in, replace the survival event $\tau _{H} > T$ with $\tau _{H} \le  T$. Keep the terminal trigger as well as the path condition; activation alone does not guarantee payment.

For a digital barrier payoff, first apply the assumptions and knock-in/out rules in [Shared Barrier Mathematics](#shared-barrier-mathematics), then use its interval and surviving moments:
**Cash digital knock-out value**

$$
V_{cash,KO}=Qe^{-rT}J_0
$$

**Asset digital knock-out value**

$$
V_{asset,KO}=e^{-rT}J_1.
$$

As an explicit branch, consider a down-and-out cash call with $S > H$ and $K \ge  H$. Define $z_{\mathrm{ref}}$ as the standardized reflected log-price threshold below. Then the price is
**Down-and-out cash-call branch and reflected threshold**

$$
Qe^{-rT}\left[N(d_2)-(H/S)^{2\nu/\sigma^2}N(z_{ref})\right],\quad
z_{ref}=\frac{\ln(H^2/(SK))+\nu T}{\sigma\sqrt T}.
$$

If $K < H$, surviving above H already guarantees finishing above K; use the interval beginning at $\ln  H$ instead. Choose branches from events, not labels alone.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / Shared Barrier Mathematics
atoms.text:
## Shared Barrier Mathematics

This section calculates two building blocks: J0 is the joint probability of surviving and ending in a selected interval; J1 is the expected terminal asset value multiplied by the indicator of that same joint event. Neither quantity is divided by survival probability. Use them in the ordinary or digital barrier pricing section. Here, survival means the barrier has not been touched during monitoring. The formulas assume continuous monitoring, constant parameters, no rebate, and an initially unbreached barrier. For discretely monitored barriers, see [Discrete Monitoring and the BGK Approximation](#discrete-monitoring-and-the-bgk-approximation); the continuous formulas here are not exact discrete-monitoring formulas. The barrier H must be positive. An initially unbreached lower barrier requires $S > H$; an initially unbreached upper barrier requires $S < H$.

In the following identity, $V_{\mathrm{vanilla}}$ means the price of the same terminal payoff with the barrier condition removed. For a digital barrier, this is a vanilla digital, not an ordinary call or put. Knock-in and knock-out events partition paths, so with matching payoff, payment time, and monitoring, and no rebates,
**Knock-in value from in-out parity**

$$
V_{KI}=V_{vanilla}-V_{KO}.
$$

For nonnegative payoffs, both prices lie between zero and the matching vanilla price. A knock-out approaches vanilla as its barrier becomes sufficiently remote. Determine barrier status before using these formulas. If monitoring has already begun, check the monitored history as well as the current spot: a past touch remains effective even if spot has returned to the safe side. During active continuous monitoring, $S \le  H$ touches a lower barrier and $S \ge  H$ touches an upper barrier. Once touched, a no-rebate knock-out has value zero and a knock-in becomes the matching contract without a barrier. If a knock-out rebate remains payable, value only that outstanding payment according to its specified payment time; do not include a rebate that has already been paid. Rebate terms modify simple parity. Do not hide a material negative value or branch error by clipping.

Define $x = \ln  S, h = \ln  H, k = \ln  K, s = \sigma  \sqrt{T}, s^{2} = \sigma ^{2} T$, and $\nu  = r - q - \sigma ^{2}/2$. The variable y below denotes a possible terminal log-price. With no barrier restriction, its density conditional on initial log-price x is
**Unrestricted terminal log-price density**

$$
p_{free}(y\mid x)=\phi((y-x-\nu T)/s)/s.
$$

Reflect the initial log-price to 2h-x and define
**Reflection weight**

$$
w=\exp(2\nu(h-x)/\sigma^2).
$$

The safe side is $y > h$ for a lower barrier and $y < h$ for an upper barrier. On that side, the density for paths that survive is
**Surviving terminal log-price density**

$$
p_{survive}(y)=p_{free}(y\mid x)-wp_{free}(y\mid 2h-x).
$$

The subtraction removes paths that touch the barrier. Both density terms solve the drift–diffusion equation, and the weighted difference equals zero at the barrier. The reflected initial point lies outside the safe domain. Integrating $p_{\mathrm{survive}}$ over the safe domain gives survival probability; it is not a density conditional on survival and need not integrate to one.

Set $\mathrm{a0} = x + \nu  T$ and $\mathrm{a1} = 2h - x + \nu  T$: these are the terminal means of the original and reflected log-price processes. In F0 and F1, a is a generic log-price mean, while l and u are lower and upper terminal log-price limits. **Probability mass of a lognormal interval**

$$
F_0(a;l,u)=N((u-a)/s)-N((l-a)/s)
$$

**Asset moment of a lognormal interval**

$$
F_1(a;l,u)=e^{a+s^2/2}[N((u-a-s^2)/s)-N((l-a-s^2)/s)].
$$

F0 integrates the normal density over (l,u). F1 integrates $\exp (y)$ times that density, so it measures terminal asset value over the same interval. Completing the square gives the expression for F1. Subtract the reflected contributions to obtain
**Surviving probability moment**

$$
J_0=F_0(a_0;l,u)-wF_0(a_1;l,u),\quad
$$

**Surviving asset moment**

$$
J_1=F_1(a_0;l,u)-wF_1(a_1;l,u).
$$

| Knock-out | Allowed terminal log-price interval (l,u) |
|---|---|
| Down call | $(\max(h,k),\infty)$ |
| Down put | $(h,k)$ if $k > h$; otherwise empty |
| Up call | $(k,h)$ if $k < h$; otherwise empty |
| Up put | (-infinity,$\min ( h,k )$) |

Select the row using barrier direction and call/put type. The interval is the intersection of the safe side and the terminal payoff event; its endpoints are log-prices, not prices. Evaluate F0 and F1 at a0 and a1, form J0 and J1, and then apply the payoff-specific pricing formula. J0 and J1 are not discounted; apply $\exp (-rT)$ once in that pricing formula.

An empty interval contributes zero. Use $N(-\infty )=0$ and $N(\infty )=1$. For gap barriers, select the interval with the trigger strike and combine moments with the payment strike. Evaluate extreme normal tails and differences carefully to avoid cancellation or overflow.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / Rebates and Independent Verification
atoms.text:
## Rebates and Independent Verification

**Rebate payment timing.** R is the rebate amount. The expressions below give the rebate component only; add it to the contract's no-rebate payoff value as appropriate. A knock-out rebate paid at touching time has value
**Touch-time rebate value**

$$
R\mathbb E[e^{-r\tau_H}\mathbf1_{\tau_H\le T}].
$$

If paid at maturity instead, its value is
**Rebate paid at expiry after a hit**

$$
Re^{-rT}\mathbb Q(\tau_H\le T).
$$

A maturity-paid knock-in rebate for nonactivation has value
**Rebate paid at expiry if never hit**

$$
Re^{-rT}\mathbb Q(\tau_H>T).
$$

Payment timing determines the discounting; do not substitute one rebate convention for another. The following subsection supplies the continuous-monitoring computation.

### Computing continuous-monitoring rebates

Use the definitions and assumptions in [Shared Foundations](#shared-foundations), together with the initial barrier-status rules in [Shared Barrier Mathematics](#shared-barrier-mathematics). The formulas here apply to a positive, initially unbreached barrier, constant parameters, continuous monitoring, and positive volatility and maturity. Define the positive log-distance and drift toward the barrier by
**Barrier distance and drift toward the barrier**

$$
a=|\ln(H/S)|,\qquad
\theta=\begin{cases}\nu,&H>S\quad\text{(upper barrier)},\\-\nu,&H<S\quad\text{(lower barrier)}.\end{cases}
$$

Here a is the first-passage distance, local to this section; it is not a log-price mean used in F0 or F1. Reflecting the process for a lower barrier converts both cases to hitting the positive level a. Its first-passage density is
**First-passage-time density**

$$
f_\tau(t)=\frac{a}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi t^3}}
\exp\left[-\frac{(a-\theta t)^2}{2\sigma^2t}\right],\quad t>0.
$$

Thus the at-touch rebate value can be evaluated by quadrature:
**Touch-time rebate as a discounted density integral**

$$
V_{rebate,hit}=R\int_0^T e^{-rt}f_\tau(t)\,dt.
$$

For a closed form, define $\kappa=\sqrt{\theta^2+2r\sigma^2}$, provided its radicand is nonnegative. Expanding the density exponent gives
**Exponent rearrangement for the rebate integral**

$$
-rt-\frac{(a-\theta t)^2}{2\sigma^2t}
=\frac{a\theta}{\sigma^2}-\frac{a^2}{2\sigma^2t}
-\frac{\kappa^2t}{2\sigma^2}.
$$

Integrating, or differentiating the expression below with respect to T, yields
**Closed-form touch-time rebate**

$$
V_{rebate,hit}=R\left[
 e^{a(\theta-\kappa)/\sigma^2}N\left(\frac{\kappa T-a}{\sigma\sqrt T}\right)
+e^{a(\theta+\kappa)/\sigma^2}N\left(\frac{-\kappa T-a}{\sigma\sqrt T}\right)
\right].
$$

This already includes discounting to the random hit time: do not multiply it by $\exp (-rT)$. If negative rates make the radicand negative, use the real-valued integral instead of this square-root form. For extreme parameters, evaluate exponential-times-normal-tail products in log space.

The undiscounted probability of a touch by T is
**Barrier-hit probability by expiry**

$$
p_T=N\left(\frac{\theta T-a}{\sigma\sqrt T}\right)
+e^{2a\theta/\sigma^2}N\left(\frac{-\theta T-a}{\sigma\sqrt T}\right).
$$

Therefore a knock-out rebate paid at maturity is $Re^{-rT}p_T$, and a knock-in nonactivation rebate paid at maturity is $Re^{-rT}(1-p_T)$. These formulas concern the rebate component only. At $r = 0$, the at-touch value reduces to R $p_{T}$. For $R \ge  0$ and $r \ge  0$, it lies between $Re^{-rT}p_T$ and $Rp_T$.

The at-touch expression is equivalent to the Rubinstein–Reiner F component implemented in [QuantLib's analytic barrier engine](https://github.com/lballabio/QuantLib/blob/master/ql/pricingengines/barrier/analyticbarrierengine.cpp); the positive-distance notation above makes the lower/upper drift mapping explicit.

This check uses a different calculation path from the closed-form moments, but shares their Black–Scholes assumptions. First read [Shared Barrier Mathematics](#shared-barrier-mathematics) for x, h, w, and $p_{\mathrm{free}}$. Simulate terminal prices from Shared Foundations. For each terminal sample, calculate the probability of a barrier touch conditional on that endpoint. When both endpoints are on the safe side, this probability is
**Conditional bridge hit probability**

$$
p_{hit}=\frac{wp_{free}(\ln S_T\mid 2h-x)}{p_{free}(\ln S_T\mid x)}
=\exp\left[-\frac{2\ln(S/H)\ln(S_T/H)}{\sigma^2T}\right].
$$

If either endpoint touches or crosses the barrier, set $p_{\mathrm{hit}} = 1$ instead of using the exponential formula. For every sample, evaluate the terminal payoff $\Pi(S_T)$, multiply it by $1-p_{\mathrm{hit}}$ for a knock-out or $p_{\mathrm{hit}}$ for a knock-in, and discount. Averaging these values estimates, with no rebates,
**Bridge-weighted knock-out value**

$$
V_{KO}=e^{-rT}\mathbb E[\Pi(S_T)(1-p_{hit})],\quad
$$

**Bridge-weighted knock-in value**

$$
V_{KI}=e^{-rT}\mathbb E[\Pi(S_T)p_{hit}].
$$

Estimate sampling error from the discounted weighted payoffs. For independent samples, standard error is their sample standard deviation divided by $\sqrt{\text{sample count}}$. Checking the barrier only at the specified monitoring dates, without bridge probabilities, prices a discretely monitored contract. By contrast, sampling only a terminal price and weighting its payoff by the bridge survival probability above accounts for continuous monitoring under this model. When simulation already checks the actual discrete monitoring dates, do not add Brownian-bridge crossings between them. The BGK approximation below instead maps a continuous closed form to a discretely monitored contract.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / Consistency checks
atoms.text:
## Consistency checks

Contract terms determine parameter meanings. Price, variance, probability and position value are different quantities. For a sensitivity check, perturb only the intended input and keep the others fixed.

When a check fails, inspect its design, contract interpretation, parameter mapping, branch selection, and numerical stability. An identity satisfied by construction can detect inconsistency but cannot independently certify its components.

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / Discrete Monitoring and the BGK Approximation
atoms.text:
## Discrete Monitoring and the BGK Approximation

Use the definitions and assumptions in [Shared Foundations](#shared-foundations). For equally spaced observations with interval $\Delta t$ measured in years, consistent with annualized volatility, the Broadie–Glasserman–Kou approximation uses the continuous-barrier formula with
**Discrete-monitoring correction for an upper barrier**

$$
H_{adj}=H\exp(+\beta\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t})\quad\text{for an upper barrier}
$$

**Discrete-monitoring correction for a lower barrier and its constant**

$$
H_{adj}=H\exp(-\beta\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t})\quad\text{for a lower barrier},
\qquad \beta=-\frac{\zeta(1/2)}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\approx0.5826.
$$

Here $\zeta$ is the Riemann $\zeta$ function. The shift moves the barrier away from spot. Apply it only when using a continuous formula to approximate discrete monitoring; do not shift the barrier in a simulation that already checks the actual observation dates. This is an asymptotic approximation, not an exact identity. Accuracy can deteriorate near the barrier or with coarse monitoring. Irregular observation schedules require separate treatment. Follow a specified algorithm rather than silently substituting this approximation.

Source: [Broadie, Glasserman and Kou (1997), A Continuity Correction for Discrete Barrier Options](https://business.columbia.edu/sites/default/files-efs/pubfiles/1845/bgk_mf.pdf).

atoms.title: Black–Scholes Reference by Contract Type / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources

Foundational references: Black and Scholes (1973), *The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities*; Merton (1973), *Theory of Rational Option Pricing*. Implementation cross-reference: [QuantLib analytic binary barrier engine](https://github.com/lballabio/QuantLib/blob/master/ql/pricingengines/barrier/analyticbinarybarrierengine.cpp). Use model and contract assumptions to determine applicability; availability of a library does not establish that its defaults match a contract.

atoms.title: Discrete delta hedging and cash-account accounting / overview
atoms.text:
# Discrete delta hedging and cash-account accounting

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this reference to track a discrete $\delta$ hedge through trades, financing, dividends and settlement, and reconcile its cash flows and P&L.

Map task quantities to these definitions by meaning and units, not by letter, before the first calculation; recheck when inputs or conventions change.

Explicit task definitions and contract conventions take precedence. If they conflict or are incomplete, identify the ambiguity and state the convention used.

atoms.title: Discrete delta hedging and cash-account accounting / 1. Shared foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared foundations
**Portfolio positions and marked wealth**

Symbols are local. Let $n_{\mathrm{opt}}$ be the signed number of option units (negative for a short position), $V_{t}$ the value per unit, $\Delta _{t}$ its spot derivative, $h_{t}$ the stock units held, and $B_{t}$ cash (negative means borrowing). Include any contract multiplier in $n_{\mathrm{opt}}$ exactly once. Portfolio wealth is $W_{t}=n_{\mathrm{opt}}\cdot V_{t}+h_{t}\cdot S_{t}+B_{t}$. Time is in years. Explicitly distinguish a realized stock path from pricing-model assumptions.

atoms.title: Discrete delta hedging and cash-account accounting / 2. Initialization and rebalancing
atoms.text:
## 2. Initialization and rebalancing
A Delta-neutral stock target is $h_{\mathrm{target}}=-n_{\mathrm{opt}}\cdot \Delta _{t}$.

**Opening cash balance**

For an initially zero-wealth book with stock position $h_{0}$, set $B_{0}=-n_{\mathrm{opt}}\cdot V_{0}-h_{0}\cdot S_{0}-\mathrm{TC}_{0}$, so wealth after opening costs is -$\mathrm{TC}_{0}$. If an initial cash endowment exists, add it separately. Selling an option receives cash; buying the hedge consumes cash.

**Cash change and self-financing at rebalancing**

At a rebalance trade $\mathrm{d}h=h_{\mathrm{new}}-h_{\mathrm{old}}$, cash changes by $-\mathrm{d}h\,S_{\mathrm{trade}}-\mathrm{TC}(\mathrm{d}h,S_{\mathrm{trade}})$. Use the actual specified fill price; proportional costs are nonnegative and typically depend on $|\mathrm{d}h|$, not signed $\mathrm{d}h$. At a common mark and fill price, without costs or market movement, $hS+B$ must be unchanged by the trade. If fill differs from the mark, the wealth change also includes $\mathrm{d}h(S_{\mathrm{mark}}-S_{\mathrm{trade}})$. This is the self-financing check.

atoms.title: Discrete delta hedging and cash-account accounting / 3. Cash accrual and dividends
atoms.text:
## 3. Cash accrual and dividends
Choose the event order from the contract and data timestamps.
**Financing between events**

Between events, with a single financing rate, $B_{\mathrm{before}}=B_{\mathrm{previous}}\cdot \exp (r_{\mathrm{cash}}\cdot \mathrm{d}t)$. If borrowing and lending rates differ, choose the rate from the cash sign over that interval; split at intervening cash events. Do not earn financing twice by also adding an overlapping daily interest term.

Dividend entitlement is determined by the shares held across the ex-dividend event. If the model treats ex-date and payment date as the same, a cash dividend $D_{\mathrm{cash}}$ adds $h_{\mathrm{entitled}}D_{\mathrm{cash}}$ to cash on that date; a short stock position owes it. If payment is later, record a receivable or payable at ex-date and move it into cash on payment date, using the entitled shares even if the hedge has since changed. Include the value of this receivable/payable in interim wealth; do not count it again after payment. Accrue cash interest only after cash is received or paid.

Under the same-date deterministic dividend convention, the theoretical ex-dividend spot falls by $D_{\mathrm{cash}}$, offset by dividend cash. With delayed payment the idealized drop corresponds to the value of the dividend entitlement; real price moves need not equal this theoretical drop. Observed ex-dividend prices already contain the event: do not subtract it a second time. Continuous dividend yield belongs to a continuous-income model and must not duplicate separately booked cash dividends.

atoms.title: Discrete delta hedging and cash-account accounting / 4. Closing and interpreting P&L
atoms.text:
## 4. Closing and interpreting P&L
Settle the option and stock under the stated contract.
For cash settlement at expiry and stock liquidation at $S_{T}$:
**Terminal wealth after settlement and stock liquidation**

$$
W_{\mathrm{final}}=B_{\mathrm{before}}+n_{\mathrm{opt}}\cdot g(S_{T})+h_{\mathrm{before}}\cdot S_{T}-\mathrm{TC}_{\mathrm{close}}.
$$

Subtract the appropriate initial capital or financed benchmark if the requested P&L definition requires it. Physical settlement, exercise fees and residual positions need their own cash flows. Mark-to-market wealth includes the option liability before settlement; do not subtract it again afterward.

Changing implied volatility changes V and $\Delta$, not cash directly. A revaluation of the option is not a cash receipt. Discrete hedging, transaction costs, model mismatch and volatility changes can all generate nonzero hedge P&L. Do not require a zero terminal error as a universal test.

atoms.title: Discrete delta hedging and cash-account accounting / 5. Checks and related knowledge
atoms.text:
## 5. Checks and related knowledge
Retain an event ledger: previous positions, financing, dividends, trades, costs, settlement and closing wealth. Reconcile each cash update with the trade ledger. Selling h shares adds h·S to cash and buying subtracts it; after the closing sale the stock position is zero. Use one update for every trade, the closing sale included: with $\mathrm{d}h=h_{\mathrm{new}}-h_{\mathrm{old}}$ (so $\mathrm{d}h=-h$ at the close), cash changes by $-\mathrm{d}h\,S-\mathrm{TC}$. Writing the close as `cash += dh * S` with a negative dh subtracts the sale proceeds. A hedged P&L of several times the option premium is a hint to recheck signs, not proof; the decisive checks are cash conservation through the ledger, a zero stock position after the close, and every fee recomputed from its trade's direction. Check the zero-trade case, a dividend event with fixed shares, long/short sign reversal only with zero transaction costs, symmetric financing and sign-symmetric trading/settlement rules, and zero-cost rebalancing conservation. For a Black-Scholes hedge use the analytic Greeks entry; discrete-dividend pricing is not generally obtained exactly by replacing S with S-PV(dividends). Follow an explicitly requested approximation and label it.

atoms.title: Discrete delta hedging and cash-account accounting / 6. References
atoms.text:
## 6. References
Black and Scholes (1973), dynamic replication framework. The cash equations here are direct bookkeeping identities; financing, event order and cost conventions are contract inputs, not universal market conventions.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / overview
atoms.text:
# European option finite-difference PDE

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this reference to assemble and check a finite-difference solver for European vanilla prices and Greeks, including specified cash-dividend events.

Before choosing the time step: backward Euler (eta = 1) has first-order error in dtau, so the discounting of the strike
alone is off by about r^2 T dtau / 2 relative to K exp(-rT), largest at long maturities; Crank-Nicolson (eta = 1/2) is
second order. Use Crank-Nicolson with a Rannacher start (two backward-Euler half steps) unless the task names the
scheme; with backward Euler, refine dtau until the check passes. Check every row of the output, not only a few:

For every $(S, K, T)$ row of the output table: the parity residual $C - P - (S e^{-qT} - K e^{-rT})$, and the difference between $C$ and the closed-form Black-Scholes call on the same inputs, must both stay within the accuracy the task states (otherwise about $10^{-4}$ of the price scale), at all maturities.

Map task quantities to these definitions by meaning and units, not by letter, before the first calculation; recheck when inputs or conventions change.

Explicit task definitions and contract conventions take precedence. If they conflict or are incomplete, identify the ambiguity and state the convention used.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / 1. Shared foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared foundations
Symbols are local. Use S for spot, K for strike, $\sigma$ for annualized decimal volatility, r for the rate, q for continuous yield, and $\tau =T_{\mathrm{expiry}}-t$ for remaining time in years. European payoff is $g(S); V(S,0)=g(S)$. This entry assumes constant coefficients and payment at expiry. For closed-form comparisons use Black-Scholes under identical inputs. For American exercise, impose the early-exercise constraint using an LCP solver or another justified American method; a plain European linear solve alone is insufficient. Require $K>0$ and $\sigma \ge 0$; the grid formulas describe the diffusion case $\sigma >0$. Zero volatility is a first-order transport limit and needs suitable deterministic or monotone handling.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / 2. Space operator and time stepping
atoms.text:
## 2. Space operator and time stepping
In remaining time:
**European pricing PDE in remaining time**

$$
V_{\tau} = L V = \sigma ^{2}\cdot S^{2}\cdot V_{\mathrm{SS}}/2 + (r-q)\cdot S\cdot V_{S} - r\cdot V.
$$

On a uniform spot grid $S_{i}=i\cdot h$, interior row i has
**Lower-diagonal operator coefficient**

$$
\mathrm{lower}_{i} = \sigma ^{2}\cdot S_{i}^{2}/(2\cdot h^{2}) - (r-q)\cdot S_{i}/(2\cdot h)
$$

**Main-diagonal operator coefficient**

$$
\operatorname{diag}_{i} = -\sigma ^{2}\cdot S_{i}^{2}/h^{2}-r
$$

**Upper-diagonal operator coefficient**

$$
\mathrm{upper}_{i} = \sigma ^{2}\cdot S_{i}^{2}/(2\cdot h^{2}) + (r-q)\cdot S_{i}/(2\cdot h).
$$

**Apply the assembled spatial operator**

Thus $(LV)_i=\mathrm{lower}_i V_{i-1}+\operatorname{diag}_i V_i+\mathrm{upper}_i V_{i+1}$. The coefficient belongs to row i, not to the neighboring value's index.

For a step dtau and theta-method weight $\eta$:
**One theta-method time step with boundary contributions**

$$
(I-\eta \cdot \mathrm{dtau}\cdot L_{\mathrm{II}})\cdot V_{\mathrm{new}} = (I+(1-\eta )\cdot \mathrm{dtau}\cdot L_{\mathrm{II}})\cdot V_{\mathrm{old}} + \mathrm{dtau}\cdot ((1-\eta )\cdot b_{\mathrm{old}}+\eta \cdot b_{\mathrm{new}}).
$$

$L_{\mathrm{II}}$ contains interior-to-interior coefficients. The first component of b is $\mathrm{lower}_1V_0$ and the last is $\mathrm{upper}_{M-1}V_M$; other components are zero (add both terms if only one interior node exists). Weight old and new boundary contributions by $(1-\eta)$ and $\eta$ respectively; for backward Euler the old contribution is zero. $\eta =1$ gives backward Euler; $\eta =1/2$ gives Crank-Nicolson. Solve the tridiagonal system rather than explicitly inverting it. Nonsmooth payoffs can cause CN oscillations: two backward-Euler half steps for the first full step are a common Rannacher startup; document the schedule. Central differencing can lose monotonicity when drift dominates diffusion; refine or use a justified monotone discretization.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / 3. Boundaries and Greeks
atoms.text:
## 3. Boundaries and Greeks
Boundaries use remaining time $\tau$.
**Call boundary values**

$$
\;\text{Call}\;: V(0,\tau )=0; V(S_{\mathrm{max}},\tau ) \approx  S_{\mathrm{max}}\cdot \exp (-q\cdot \tau )-K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot \tau ).
$$

**Put boundary values**

$$
\;\text{Put}\;: V(0,\tau )=K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot \tau ); V(S_{\mathrm{max}},\tau ) \approx  0.
$$

The large-spot approximations require a sufficiently distant boundary; enlarge $S_{\mathrm{max}}$ to test truncation error. Negative rates are allowed and can make the put's left boundary exceed K.

**$\Delta$ and $\Gamma$ on the stock grid**

At interior nodes $\Delta\approx(V_{i+1}-V_{i-1})/(2h)$, $\Gamma\approx(V_{i+1}-2V_i+V_{i-1})/h^2$. Calendar $\Theta =-V_{\tau}$, and may be computed from the PDE operator or a time difference with the correct sign. Using the same operator for Theta and the PDE residual makes that residual a consistency check, not independent validation.

Vega/Rho from bumped PDE solves require identical domains, grids and interpolation conventions. If reporting values off-grid, state the interpolation; differentiating a piecewise-linear interpolant twice does not give a useful Gamma.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / 4. Events and convergence
atoms.text:
## 4. Events and convergence
Between discrete dividend events use the PDE above; do not also include those same dividends in q. For a deterministic cash dividend $D_{\mathrm{cash}}$, assumed ex-dividend and paid at calendar time $t_{d}$, the backward event map is $V_{\mathrm{before}}(S)=V_{\mathrm{after}}(\max (S-D_{\mathrm{cash}},0))$ under this specified stock-jump convention. Interpolate from the post-event grid; do not reverse the sign. This convention needs explicit treatment near zero and is not the continuous-yield model. Align time steps with events; do not smooth a discrete dividend across time.

Refine space and time separately and enlarge the domain. Compare prices AND Greeks with an independent closed form when applicable. Test puts, calls, nonzero q, non-ATM inputs, and expiry kinks. A residual near zero alone does not establish accuracy. Calendar t and remaining $\tau$ are different coordinates; their relation is $\tau =T_{\mathrm{expiry}}-t$.

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / Efficient linear time stepping
atoms.text:
## Efficient linear time stepping

A one-dimensional nearest-neighbor spatial stencil gives a tridiagonal interior system. Store three diagonals and form the right-hand side using adjacent vector slices, including the appropriate boundary terms. Dense construction and dense factorization discard this structure.

For row coefficients $a_i,d_i,c_i$, SciPy's three-row band storage places the upper entry $c_i$ in column $i+1$, the diagonal $d_i$ in column $i$, and the lower entry $a_i$ in column $i-1$. The two unused corners are zero. A small-system comparison to a dense solve tests this packing.

When the operator, grid, step length and scheme weight are unchanged, the left matrix can be factored once and used for multiple right-hand sides. A new coefficient regime or a different step length may require new factors. Repeated calls to `solve_banded` do not promise cached factors. Thomas elimination needs safe pivots; it does not justify ignoring a near-zero pivot. These are linear European solves, not an obstacle solver.

Source: [SciPy solve_banded](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.solve_banded.html).

atoms.title: European option finite-difference PDE / 5. References
atoms.text:
## 5. References
Crank and Nicolson (1947), A practical method for numerical evaluation of solutions of partial differential equations of the heat-conduction type. Black and Scholes (1973). The operator above follows directly by central differencing the stated PDE.

atoms.title: Event-study conventions: event time, market model, CAR/CAAR, cross-event tests / overview
atoms.text:
# Event-study conventions: event time, market model, CAR/CAAR, cross-event tests

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Read the topics relevant to the task; a task usually needs several of them.

atoms.title: Event-study conventions: event time, market model, CAR/CAAR, cross-event tests / Topic 1: Event time as a row position
atoms.text:
## Topic 1: Event time as a row position

**Purpose:** Locate event day 0 and every window on the data's trading-day index.

**When to use:** Any study of returns or rate changes around dated events.

**Constraints:**

1. Day 0 is a row of the merged return index, not a calendar date plus $k$ days; every other offset is a row offset.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Resolve "the event date, or the next trading day" against the date column: the position of the first row dated on or after the event date (`DatetimeIndex.searchsorted(date, side="left")`).

Step 2: Estimation window rows $\text{pos}+e_{lo},\dots,\text{pos}+e_{hi}$ and event window rows $\text{pos}+w_{lo},\dots,\text{pos}+w_{hi}$, with the relative days the task sets.

Step 3: Apply the task's validity rule to events whose windows run past the data's ends.

Step 4: A change across event days (of a level, a rate, or a spread between two series) is one series read at two row offsets: convert that series to the reporting unit once (for example percent to basis points), then take the difference of the two rows.

**Double check:**

1. The estimation window ends before the event window starts; the row found in Step 1 is dated on or after the event date.
2. A change in Step 4 equals the change of the raw series times the unit factor; subtracting a raw-unit value from a converted series mixes units.

atoms.title: Event-study conventions: event time, market model, CAR/CAAR, cross-event tests / Topic 2: Pre-event features
atoms.text:
## Topic 2: Pre-event features

**Purpose:** Pick the rows that features defined "before the event" use.

**When to use:** The panel includes values, changes or statistics measured before each event.

**Constraints:**

1. Rows are positions on the filtered valid-row index of the underlying daily series (the yield, price or return table), not on the table of events: "the $w$ valid dates before the event" are $w$ daily rows, however many earlier events fall in them.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Find the event's position pos on the filtered valid-row index (`Index.get_loc`).

Step 2: Read each feature from the rows its definition names:

| Definition says | Rows |
|---|---|
| the value $k$ valid rows before the event | pos $-k$ (the day before is pos $-1$) |
| a change from $k$ rows before to $m$ rows before ($k>m$) | $x_{\text{pos}-m}-x_{\text{pos}-k}$ |
| a statistic over the $w$ rows immediately before | rows pos $-w$ to pos $-1$; the value it standardises comes from its own stated row |
| a regression of $y_j$ on $y_{j-1}$ for $j=a,\dots,b$ | pairs built on the full series, then rows $a$ to $b$ kept: $b-a+1$ pairs |

Step 3: A trailing statistic of a pre-event quantity (for example a z-score of the level on the day before): take the value from its stated row (pos $-1$) and the window from its stated rows (pos $-w$ to pos $-1$); reading a rolling column at the event row instead standardises the event-day value against a window shifted by one.

Step 4: A lagged regression over a stated range: build the lag on the full series (`shift(1)`), then keep rows $a$ to $b$ of both; slicing first and lagging inside the slice loses the pair at $j=a$.

**Double check:**

1. For the first event, print the dates of the rows each feature uses (its value row, its window ends, the two rows of each change) next to the event date, and compare every one with its definition; the number of regression pairs is $b-a+1$.

atoms.title: Event-study conventions: event time, market model, CAR/CAAR, cross-event tests / Topic 3: Market model, abnormal returns, CAR and CAAR
atoms.text:
## Topic 3: Market model, abnormal returns, CAR and CAAR

**Purpose:** Estimate normal returns and accumulate abnormal returns.

**When to use:** Abnormal returns relative to a market model.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: On the estimation window, fit the security return on a constant plus the market return (ordinary least squares, for example `np.linalg.lstsq` on a design that includes a column of ones, or `statsmodels` OLS after `add_constant`): intercept $\alpha$, slope $\beta$, residuals $e$.

Step 2: Abnormal returns on the event window: $AR_t=R_t-(\alpha+\beta R_{m,t})$.

Step 3: Stack the valid events' abnormal returns as an $N\times M$ matrix: $CAR_i$ is a row sum and the column mean is the average abnormal return of day $t$, $AAR(t)$. A per-day series named $CAAR(t)$ is one of two things, decided by the task's definition: the column mean itself, when the task defines $CAAR(t)$ as the day-$t$ average over events and then sums it over windows; or the running sum $\sum_{s \le t} AAR(s)$, when the task defines it as cumulated from the window start. Check: the sum of the reported daily values over a window equals the reported window total; with a running sum, the value on the last day equals that total instead.

**Double check:**

1. The residuals sum to zero and are orthogonal to the market return (to about $10^{-10}$); the sum of the column means equals the mean of the row sums.

atoms.title: Event-study conventions: event time, market model, CAR/CAAR, cross-event tests / Topic 4: Standardized tests and cross-correlation
atoms.text:
## Topic 4: Standardized tests and cross-correlation

**Purpose:** Test abnormal returns across events with standardized statistics.

**When to use:** Patell, BMP or Kolari-Pynnonen tests.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Per event, $s_i^2=\sum e^2/(L_i-2)$, with $L_i$ estimation days.

Step 2: Prediction-error correction on each event day:

$$C_{it}=1+\frac1{L_i}+\frac{(R_{m,t}-\bar R_m)^2}{\sum(R_m-\bar R_m)^2}$$

(sums over the estimation window).

Step 3: Standardized abnormal returns $SAR_{it}=AR_{it}/(s_i\sqrt{C_{it}})$ and the window value $CSAR_i=\sum_tSAR_{it}/\sqrt M$.

Step 4: BMP statistic: $t_{BMP}=\sqrt N\cdot\text{mean}/\text{sd}$ over events, using the cross-sectional sample standard deviation (`ddof=1`).

Step 5: Average cross-correlation $\bar\rho$: the mean pairwise Pearson correlation of estimation residuals matched on the calendar dates both series share (index each residual series by its dates and intersect; never align by row number).

Step 6: Dependence adjustment, by the reading the task names: (i) $t_{BMP}/\sqrt{1+(N-1)\bar\rho}$; (ii) Kolari-Pynnonen, $t_{BMP}\sqrt{(1-\bar\rho)/(1+(N-1)\bar\rho)}$, whose extra $\sqrt{1-\bar\rho}$ undoes the shrinkage that correlation causes in the BMP cross-sectional variance.

atoms.title: Event-study conventions: event time, market model, CAR/CAAR, cross-event tests / Topic 5: Rank test across events
atoms.text:
## Topic 5: Rank test across events

**Purpose:** A nonparametric test of abnormal returns.

**When to use:** The task asks for a rank (Corrado-type) test.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Per event, pool the estimation residuals with the window abnormal returns, rank them jointly with midranks for ties (`scipy.stats.rankdata`, default `"average"`), and set $U=\text{rank}/(T_i+1)$, $d=U-\tfrac12$.

Step 2: Reading A, portfolio time-series standard deviation (Corrado 1989): $D_t$ is the mean over events of $d$ on pooled day $t$; $S=\sqrt{\text{mean of }D_t^2}$ over all pooled days; day statistic $D_t/S$; window statistic $\sum_tD_t/(\sqrt M\,S)$. Needs one pooled-day grid (equal $T_i$).

Step 3: Reading B, per-event standardization aggregated across events: $sd_i=\sqrt{\text{mean}(d_i^2)}$ over that event's own days, $\theta_{it}=d_{it}/sd_i$; day statistic $\sqrt N\cdot\text{mean}_i\theta_{it}$; window statistic $\sum_t(\text{day statistic})/\sqrt M$.

**Limitations and cautions:**

1. Both readings share the numerator; only the denominator differs, so state which one is used.

**Double check:**

1. Without ties, the mean of $d^2$ over $T$ pooled days equals $(T-1)/(12(T+1))$.

atoms.title: Event-study conventions: event time, market model, CAR/CAAR, cross-event tests / Topic 6: Sign-flip and permutation p-values
atoms.text:
## Topic 6: Sign-flip and permutation p-values

**Purpose:** Exact or randomization p-values for a regression coefficient.

**When to use:** The task asks for a sign-flip or permutation test.

**Constraints:**

1. The draw that reproduces the observed sample (all signs $+1$, the identity permutation) counts as a hit.
2. Compare with a roundoff margin: a draw is a hit when $\lvert b^*\rvert\ge\lvert b_{obs}\rvert(1-10^{-12})$; an exact $\ge$ can drop the identity draw by floating-point noise and change the p-value by one draw.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Keep the design fixed across draws and precompute its pseudo-inverse (`np.linalg.pinv`).

Step 2: Build all sign vectors (the first sign fixed at $+1$ when the statistic is symmetric; `itertools.product`) as a matrix, form every resampled response as fitted values plus signed residuals, and get all coefficients at once by one matrix product with the pseudo-inverse.

Step 3: Mark hits with the roundoff margin, as a vector over all draws:

$$\text{hit}_d=\Big(\lvert b^*_d\rvert\ \ge\ \lvert b_{obs}\rvert\,(1-10^{-12})\Big)$$

Never compare $\lvert b^*_d\rvert\ge\lvert b_{obs}\rvert$ exactly: the identity draw reproduces $b_{obs}$ only up to floating-point noise, so an exact comparison can miss it and moves the p-value by one draw.

Step 4: p-value: the share of draws that are hits (the mean of the hit vector).

**Double check:**

1. Assert that the identity draw (all signs $+1$) is a hit before reporting the p-value; if it is not, the comparison has no margin: apply Step 3.

atoms.title: Event-study conventions: event time, market model, CAR/CAAR, cross-event tests / Topic 7: Full panel versus regression subset
atoms.text:
## Topic 7: Full panel versus regression subset

**Purpose:** Report summary fields from the rows their definitions name.

**When to use:** The panel is summarized and some regressions use a subset of it.

**Constraints:**

1. A summary field without a subset qualifier, reported beside an unqualified count, ranges over the same rows as that count; a count and a first or last date reported side by side come from the same frame.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Keep the full panel and each regression sample under different names.

Step 2: Take every summary field from the frame its definition names.

Step 3: When several regressions run on the same sample, each takes its own left-hand column from its own equation; a left-hand variable left over from the previous fit silently regresses the wrong series. Print each fit's left- and right-hand columns.

Step 4: When the task says to round the panel and use the rounded values as inputs, read the written panel back and regress on that, after checking that every numeric column is a float (a cell such as `[0.3133]` is a one-element array written as text, and rounding skipped it). If the panel changes after a regression ran, rerun the regressions.

**Double check:**

1. The reported count equals the number of rows in the frame its definition names, and the first and last dates come from the same frame.

atoms.title: Event-study conventions: event time, market model, CAR/CAAR, cross-event tests / Topic 8: Task wording to API arguments
atoms.text:
## Topic 8: Task wording to API arguments

**Purpose:** Choose the arguments that silently change results.

**When to use:** Before calling any of the functions below.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Choose by the task's wording:

| Call | Choice and wording |
|---|---|
| `DatetimeIndex.searchsorted(v, side=...)` | `"left"`: first row dated on or after $v$ ("on or after", "the event date or the next trading day"); `"right"`: first row dated after $v$ ("strictly after"); `searchsorted(v, side="right") - 1`: last row dated on or before $v$ ("on or before", "as of") |
| `pd.merge_asof(..., direction=..., allow_exact_matches=...)` | `"backward"` (default): last key at or before $v$ ("most recent as of"); `"forward"`: first key at or after $v$ ("next available"); `allow_exact_matches=False` makes either strict; both frames sorted on the key |
| `Series.shift(k)` | $k>0$ takes the value $k$ rows earlier ("previous", "lagged"); after filtering to valid rows, $k$ counts valid rows ("valid dates, not calendar days": filter first, then shift) |
| `Series.rolling(w, min_periods=...)` | the window ends at and includes the current row; "the $w$ rows before the event" is `shift(1).rolling(w)`; `min_periods=1` uses all available rows if fewer |
| standard deviation | `np.std` defaults to `ddof=0`, pandas `.std` to `ddof=1`; a "sample" standard deviation means `ddof=1` |
| `np.linalg.lstsq`, `sm.OLS` | add no intercept; `sm.add_constant` with the default `has_constant="skip"` adds nothing when a constant column exists, `"add"` always adds one |
| `OLS(...).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": L})` | Bartlett weights $1-l/(L+1)$; `use_correction=False` (default) leaves the sandwich unscaled, `True` multiplies it by $n/(n-k)$; `"nonrobust"` is $s^2(X'X)^{-1}$ with $s^2=SSE/(n-k)$ |
| `scipy.stats.rankdata(a, method=...)` | `"average"` (default) gives midranks to ties; `"min"` and `"ordinal"` rank ties differently |
| `scipy.stats.ttest_1samp(a, 0, alternative=...)` | uses `ddof=1`; two-sided p is $2\,t.\mathrm{sf}(\lvert t\rvert,n-1)$; `"greater"` gives $t.\mathrm{sf}(t,n-1)$ |
| `DataFrame.corr()` vs `np.corrcoef` | `corr` drops missing values pairwise; `corrcoef` returns NaN if any value is missing, so align on common dates first |

atoms.title: Event study (method): market model, abnormal returns and CAAR, Patell, BMP and Kolari-Pynnonen tests / overview
atoms.text:
# Event study (method): market model, abnormal returns and CAAR, Patell, BMP and Kolari-Pynnonen tests

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

atoms.title: Event study (method): market model, abnormal returns and CAAR, Patell, BMP and Kolari-Pynnonen tests / Setting and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Setting and assumptions
- N events (firms) i = 1..N. Event time: day 0 = event date, counted in trading days of the data (not calendar days).
  Estimation window $\operatorname{E}_{i}$: L1 days before the event window ($t = \mathrm{T0}+1\ldots \mathrm{T1}$). Event window: L2 days ($t = \mathrm{T1}+1\ldots \mathrm{T2}$), contains day 0.
  The test window [tau1, tau2] lies inside the event window; $L = \mathrm{tau2} - \mathrm{tau1} + 1$ counts both ends.
- Null H0: mean abnormal return is zero on the tested day, or mean CAR over [tau1, tau2] is zero.
- Market model $R_{it} = \alpha _{i} + \beta _{i} R_{mt} + e_{it}$, fitted by OLS on $\operatorname{E}_{i}$ only. The exact small-sample results below need
  iid normal $e_{it}$ and no event effect on the estimation window; the Z statistics are asymptotic (N large).

atoms.title: Event study (method): market model, abnormal returns and CAAR, Patell, BMP and Kolari-Pynnonen tests / Inputs and units
atoms.text:
## Inputs and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $R_{it}, R_{mt}$ | firm and market returns (simple or log, as the task says; 2% is `0.02`) | per day |
| L1, L2, L | estimation, event and test-window lengths in trading days | days |
| $N$ | number of events with valid data ($N_{t}$ on day t if some are missing) | count |

atoms.title: Event study (method): market model, abnormal returns and CAAR, Patell, BMP and Kolari-Pynnonen tests / Market model and abnormal returns (means and sums over the estimation window E_i)
atoms.text:
## Market model and abnormal returns (means and sums over the estimation window E_i)

$$
\begin{gathered}
S_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sum _{\operatorname{E}} (R_{mt} - \bar{R}_{m})^{2},  \beta _{i} = \sum _{\operatorname{E}} (R_{mt} - \bar{R}_{m})(R_{it} - \bar{R}_{i}) / S_{\mathrm{xx}},  \alpha _{i} = \bar{R}_{i} - \beta _{i} \bar{R}_{m} \\
e_{it} = R_{it} - \alpha _{i} - \beta _{i} R_{mt} (t \in  \operatorname{E}),   s_{i}^{2} = \sum _{\operatorname{E}} e_{it}^{2} / (\mathrm{L1} - 2) \\
\mathrm{AR}_{it} = R_{it} - \alpha _{i} - \beta _{i} R_{mt} (\mathrm{event} \;\text{window}\;),   \mathrm{CAR}_{i} = \sum _{t=\mathrm{tau1}}^{\mathrm{tau2}} \mathrm{AR}_{it} \\
\mathrm{AAR}_{t} = (1/N) \sum _{i} \mathrm{AR}_{it},   \mathrm{CAAR} = (1/N) \sum _{i} \mathrm{CAR}_{i}
\end{gathered}
$$

Forecast-error (prediction-error) correction, since $\alpha _{i}$, $\beta _{i}$ are estimates:

$$
C_{it} = 1 + 1/\mathrm{L1} + (R_{mt} - \bar{R}_{m})^{2} / S_{\mathrm{xx}}
$$

$$
\mathrm{SAR}_{it} = \mathrm{AR}_{it} / (s_{i} \sqrt{C_{it}})
$$

Exact $t(\mathrm{L1}-2)$, with variance $(\mathrm{L1}-2)/(\mathrm{L1}-4)$.

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{CAR}_{i}) = s_{i}^{2} [ L + L^{2}/\mathrm{L1} + ( \sum _{t=\mathrm{tau1}}^{\mathrm{tau2}} (R_{mt} - \bar{R}_{m}) )^{2} / S_{\mathrm{xx}} ]
$$

$$
\mathrm{SCAR}_{i} = \mathrm{CAR}_{i} / \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{CAR}_{i})}
$$

Exact $t(\mathrm{L1}-2)$. The equivalent matrix expression is $\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{CAR}_i)=s_i^2 1'(I+X^{*}(X'X)^{-1}(X^{*})')1$, with $X$ and $X^{*}$ the $[1,R_m]$ regressor matrices of E and of the window.

atoms.title: Event study (method): market model, abnormal returns and CAAR, Patell, BMP and Kolari-Pynnonen tests / Patell (1976) Z
Event study (method): market model, abnormal returns and CAAR, Patell, BMP and Kolari-Pynnonen tests / Boehmer-Musumeci-Poulsen (1991) standardized cross-sectional test
atoms.text:
## Boehmer-Musumeci-Poulsen (1991) standardized cross-sectional test

$$
t_{\mathrm{BMP}} = \sqrt{N} \cdot  \mathrm{Xbar} / S_{X},   \mathrm{Xbar} = (1/N) \sum _{i} X_{i},   S_{X} = \sqrt{\sum _{i} (X_{i} - \mathrm{Xbar})^{2} / (N - 1)}
$$

$X_{i} = \mathrm{SAR}_{\mathrm{i0}}$ for a single day. For a window, $X_{i}$ is the same window statistic chosen for the Patell test above: $\mathrm{CSAR}_{i} = \sum_{t} \mathrm{SAR}_{it} / \sqrt{L}$ (version b) when the task standardizes each event day with its own correction $C_{it}$, or $\mathrm{SCAR}_{i} = \mathrm{CAR}_{i} / \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{CAR}_{i})}$ (version a) when it standardizes the window CAR by one window-level variance; the Kolari–Pynnönen adjustment multiplies this same BMP t. Reference t(N-1) (N(0,1) for large N). Robust to event-induced variance.

atoms.title: Event study (method): market model, abnormal returns and CAAR, Patell, BMP and Kolari-Pynnonen tests / Kolari-Pynnonen (2010) adjustment for cross-sectional correlation (clustered event dates)
atoms.text:
## Kolari-Pynnonen (2010) adjustment for cross-sectional correlation (clustered event dates)
$\bar{r}$ is the average over the $N(N-1)/2$ pairs $i < j$ of $\mathrm{corr}(e_{i}., e_{j}.)$, the Pearson correlation of the two firms' estimation-window residuals over their common calendar dates (diagonal 1's excluded).
Same reference as BMP:

$$
t_{\mathrm{KP}} = t_{\mathrm{BMP}} \cdot  \sqrt{(1 - \bar{r}) / (1 + (N - 1) \bar{r})}
$$

What the adjustment does: positive cross-correlation $\bar{r}$ inflates the variance of the average standardized statistic by the factor $1 + (N - 1)\bar{r}$, so the adjustment divides the BMP t by $\sqrt{1 + (N - 1)\bar{r}}$ (and multiplies it by $\sqrt{1 - \bar{r}}$). A sentence saying the adjustment "scales BMP by $\sqrt{1 + (N - 1)\bar{r}}$" names this variance-inflation factor; it does not ask to multiply the t-statistic by it. Check: for $\bar{r} > 0$ the adjusted statistic is smaller in absolute value than $t_{\mathrm{BMP}}$; print both and the factor.

Adjusted Patell: software implementations multiply $Z_{\operatorname{P}}$ by the same factor; the variance of $Z_{\operatorname{P}}$ under equicorrelation
gives $Z_{\operatorname{P}}$ / $\sqrt{1 + (N - 1) \bar{r}}$. They differ by $\sqrt{1 - \bar{r}}$; use the one the task names.

atoms.text:

atoms.title: Event study (method): market model, abnormal returns and CAAR, Patell, BMP and Kolari-Pynnonen tests / Common variants and mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common variants and mistakes
- Randomization p-values (sign-flip, permutation, bootstrap) count draws whose statistic is at least as extreme as the observed one. The draw that reproduces the observed sample (all signs +1, the identity permutation) gives the observed statistic only up to floating-point round-off, so an exact comparison such as `abs(t_star) >= abs(t_obs)` can drop it or keep it by chance. Compare with a relative tolerance, for example `abs(t_star) >= abs(t_obs) * (1 - 1e-12)`, and check that the reproducing draw is counted.
- $s_{i}^{2}$ divisor: L1 - 2 (market model), L1 - 1 (constant-mean model, where $C_{it} = 1 + 1/\mathrm{L1}$ and
  $\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{CAR})=s^2(L+L^2/\mathrm{L1})$), L1 (MLE). Market-adjusted model ($\mathrm{AR} = R - R_{m}$): no estimation, $C_{it} = 1$.
- Forecast-error correction omitted ($C_{it} = 1, \operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{CAR}) = L s_{i}^{2}$) is a common simpler variant; it changes the number.
- Patell window version a vs b, and BMP on SCAR vs on CSAR, give different numbers; follow the task's wording.
- BMP compared with t(N-1) vs N(0,1); one-sided vs two-sided p-values; p = 2 * (1 - F(|stat|)) for two-sided.
- Off-by-one windows: (-1, +1) is three days; the estimation window must end before the event window starts.
- Lagged regressors: compute the change series once and shift it by exactly one row; re-deriving lagged differences with nested index offsets shifts twice and can leave the earliest windows empty.
- A lagged fit inside a window (y_t on y_{t-1}, as in an AR(1) of daily changes): take the positions `js` of the window's responses in the full series and pair each with its own previous value, `y = series[js]`, `x = series[js - 1]`, then fit once and reuse the coefficients for the forecast. Cutting the window out first and offsetting it (`w[1:]` against `w[:-1]`) drops the window's first response, whose previous value lies just before the window. If the task requires both values of a pair to lie inside the window, follow the task.
- When a window is stated as the n valid observations before an event → keep the rows where every field the window needs is valid, then take the last n of them before the event (`valid = frame.dropna(subset=needed_fields); window = valid[valid.index < event_date].iloc[-n:]`); n positions of the raw index span invalid rows and give a different window. Check the window length and its first and last dates.

atoms.title: Event study (method): market model, abnormal returns and CAAR, Patell, BMP and Kolari-Pynnonen tests / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- Our null simulation (validation.md): all tests are near nominal size with iid normal residuals. Fat-tailed residuals
  make Patell over-reject (about 7% at nominal 5%); BMP and Corrado stay near nominal.
- Event-induced variance (higher variance in the event window): Patell and Corrado over-reject strongly; BMP does not.
- Same event date for all firms with correlated residuals: Patell and BMP over-reject badly even for small rbar;
  KP-adjusted BMP and the variance-algebra adjusted Patell restore the size; Corrado stays close to nominal.
- KP adjustment without clustering adds noise from rbar and slightly over-rejects; compute rbar on overlapping
  calendar dates and adjust only when event windows overlap in calendar time.
- Patell version b over-rejects for long windows (daily SARs share the estimation error); version a is exact.
- The multi-day Corrado statistic under-rejects as L grows (ranks within a firm are dependent).

Economics 23(2):385-395; Corrado & Zivney (1992) J. Financial and Quantitative Analysis 27(3):465-478; Cowan (1992)
