atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / overview
atoms.text:
# Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen)

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Setting and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Setting and assumptions
- Work with LOSSES, large = bad: $x_{t} = -r_{t}$ (or `-(P&L)`). Fit the right tail of x. A task that keeps returns must flip the sign; VaR/ES are then reported as positive loss numbers.
- Pickands-Balkema-de Haan: above a high threshold u, the excess $Y = X - u \vert  X > u$ is approximately generalized Pareto (GPD).
  Data are treated as i.i.d. (or as GARCH-standardized residuals, McNeil & Frey 2000; then scale back with the forecast mean and $\sigma$).
- Threshold u: given by the task, or an empirical quantile, or "the k largest losses" (then u = the (k+1)-th largest loss and $N_{u} = k$).
  Diagnostics: mean-excess plot $e(v) = \operatorname{mean}(x_{i} - v \vert  x_{i} > v)$ approximately linear for $v\ge u$ (slope $\xi/(1-\xi)$); fitted $\xi$ stable when u is moved.
  Exceedances use strict $x_{i} > u$; ties at u are not exceedances unless the task says otherwise.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $n$ | number of loss observations | count |
| $u, N_{u}$ | threshold, number of $x_{i} > u; y_{i} = x_{i} - u$ for those i | loss units, count |
| $\xi$ | shape (tail index $1/\xi$ when $\xi>0$); $\xi>0$ heavy tail, $\xi  = 0$ exponential, $\xi  < 0$ bounded tail | none |
| $\beta$ | $\mathrm{GPD} \mathrm{scale}, \beta  > 0$ | loss units |
| $p$ | VaR/ES confidence level (99% is 0.99); tail probability is 1 - p | none |

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / GPD (exceedance y >= 0)
atoms.text:
## GPD (exceedance y >= 0)
When $\xi  \ne  0$:

$$
G(y) = 1 - (1 + \xi  y / \beta )^{-1/\xi}
$$

$$
g(y) = (1/\beta ) (1 + \xi  y / \beta )^{-1/\xi  - 1}
$$

When $\xi  = 0$:

$$
G(y) = 1 - \exp (-y / \beta )
$$

$$
g(y) = (1/\beta ) \exp (-y / \beta )
$$

Support: $y \ge  0$ if $\xi  \ge  0$; $0 \le  y \le  -\beta /\xi$ if $\xi  < 0$.Log-likelihood of the $N_{u}$ exceedances:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\xi  \ne  0:  l(\xi , \beta ) = -N_{u} \ln (\beta ) - (1 + 1/\xi ) \cdot  \sum _{i} \ln (1 + \xi  y_{i} / \beta ) \\
\xi   = 0:  l(\beta )     = -N_{u} \ln (\beta ) - \sum _{i} y_{i} / \beta
\end{gathered}
$$

MLE constraints: $\beta  > 0$ and $1 + \xi  y_{i} / \beta  > 0$ for every i (return -inf otherwise; this matters for $\xi  < 0$).
Maximize numerically (e.g. Nelder-Mead on -l from a method-of-moments start $\mathrm{xi0} = (1 - m^{2}/s^{2})/2$, $\mathrm{beta0} = m (1 + m^{2}/s^{2})/2$, $m, s^{2} = \operatorname{mean}$, variance of y).
Use the $\xi  = 0$ branch (or |$\xi$| tiny) to avoid dividing by zero. MLE is regular for $\xi  > -1/2$; for $\xi  \le  -1$ the likelihood is unbounded (Smith 1985).
Library check: `scipy.stats.genpareto` uses the same sign of $\xi$ ($c = \xi$), fit with $\mathrm{floc}=0$ on the $y_{i}$.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Tail estimator, VaR and ES (McNeil & Frey 2000)
atoms.text:
## Tail estimator, VaR and ES (McNeil & Frey 2000)
For $x > u$: $\hat{F}(x) = 1 - (N_{u} / n) (1 + \xi  (x - u) / \beta )^{-1/\xi}$. Inverting at level p:

When $\xi  \ne  0$:

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{p} = u + (\beta  / \xi ) \cdot  ( ((n / N_{u}) (1 - p))^{-\xi} - 1 )
$$

When $\xi  = 0$:

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{p} = u - \beta  \cdot  \ln ( (n / N_{u}) (1 - p) )
$$

Valid only for $\xi  < 1$ (ES is infinite for $\xi  \ge  1$):

$$
\operatorname{ES}_{p} = \operatorname{VaR}_{p} / (1 - \xi ) + (\beta  - \xi  u) / (1 - \xi )
$$

Valid only when $1 - p < N_{u} / n$ ($\operatorname{VaR}_{p}$ above u); otherwise use the empirical quantile. Mean excess over $v \ge  u$: $(\beta  + \xi  (v - u)) / (1 - \xi )$.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Variant: Hill estimator (xi > 0, positive losses only)
atoms.text:
## Variant: Hill estimator (xi > 0, positive losses only)
Sort descending $X_{1} \ge  \ldots  \ge  X_{n}$; with k upper order statistics (all $X_{i} > 0$):

$$
\xi _{H} = (1/k) \cdot  \sum _{i=1}^{k} \ln  X_{i} - \ln  X_{k+1}
$$

Tail index:

$$
\alpha _{H} = 1 / \xi _{H}
$$

Weissman quantile:

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{p} = X_{k+1} \cdot  ( (n / k) (1 - p) )^{-\xi _{H}}
$$

For $\xi _{H} < 1$:

$$
\operatorname{ES}_{p} = \operatorname{VaR}_{p} / (1 - \xi _{H})
$$

Some texts use $X_{(k)}$ as the threshold with divisor k - 1 or k; follow the task. Hill assumes a Pareto-type tail and is biased when the tail is not exactly Pareto.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / VaR backtests (hit sequence $I_t=1$ if $\mathrm{loss}_t>\operatorname{VaR}_t$, else 0; $t
atoms.text:
## VaR backtests (hit sequence $I_t=1$ if $\mathrm{loss}_t>\operatorname{VaR}_t$, else 0; $t=1,\ldots,T$)
p0 = expected violation probability = 1 - (VaR confidence). $x = \sum  I_{t}, \hat{\pi} = x / T$. Convention: $0 \cdot  \ln (0) = 0$.

Kupiec POF:

$$
\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}} = -2 [ (T - x) \ln (1 - \mathrm{p0}) + x \ln (\mathrm{p0}) ] + 2 [ (T - x) \ln (1 - \hat{\pi}) + x \ln (\hat{\pi}) ] \sim \mathrm{chi2}(1)
$$

For $x = 0$:

$$
\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}} = -2 T \ln (1 - \mathrm{p0})
$$

For $x = T$:

$$
\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}} = -2 T \ln (\mathrm{p0})
$$

Christoffersen independence: count transitions over $t = 2\ldots T$, $n_{ij}$ = #$\{I_{t-1} = i, I_{t} = j\}$:

$$
\pi _{01} = \mathrm{n01} / (\mathrm{n00} + \mathrm{n01})
$$

$$
\pi _{11} = \mathrm{n11} / (\mathrm{n10} + \mathrm{n11})
$$

$$
\pi  = (\mathrm{n01} + \mathrm{n11}) / (\mathrm{n00} + \mathrm{n01} + \mathrm{n10} + \mathrm{n11})
$$

Null: no clustering.

$$
\ln  \mathrm{L0} = (\mathrm{n00} + \mathrm{n10}) \ln (1 - \pi ) + (\mathrm{n01} + \mathrm{n11}) \ln (\pi )
$$

Alternative: first-order Markov.

$$
\ln  \mathrm{L1} = \mathrm{n00} \ln (1 - \pi _{01}) + \mathrm{n01} \ln (\pi _{01}) + \mathrm{n10} \ln (1 - \pi _{11}) + \mathrm{n11} \ln (\pi _{11})
$$

$$
\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}} = -2 (\ln  \mathrm{L0} - \ln  \mathrm{L1}) \sim \mathrm{chi2}(1)
$$

$$
\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{cc}} = \mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}} + \mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}} \sim \mathrm{chi2}(2)
$$

Edge cases: no hits $\to  \mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}} = 0; \mathrm{n10} + \mathrm{n11} = 0$(only hit is the last observation) -> $\pi _{11}$ terms drop out; n11 = 0 -> $\mathrm{n11} \ln (\pi _{11}) = 0$ and $\mathrm{n10} \ln (1) = 0$.
p-value = $1 - \mathrm{chi2}.\operatorname{cdf}(\mathrm{LR}, \mathrm{df})$; reject at level a if p-value < a. $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ equals the G-test of independence on the 2x2 table [[n00, n01], [n10, n11]].
$\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{cc}}$ variants: (a) $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}}$ on all T plus $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ (common), (b) $-2 (\ln  L(\mathrm{p0}) - \ln  \mathrm{L1})$ on the T-1 transitions, which equals $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{POF}}$ on $I_2,\ldots,I_T$ plus $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ exactly. Results differ slightly; follow the task.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Common variants and mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common variants and mistakes
- Several models in one session: the GPD scale $\beta$, a normal or GARCH volatility $\sigma$ and a t scale are different parameters. Keep each under its own name (for example `gpd_beta`, `normal_sigma`), pass the intended one to each formula, and when a fitted parameter changes, recompute every VaR, ES and derived result that uses it before writing outputs.
- Level labels built from a confidence level p: take the digits after the decimal point (0.99 → "99", 0.995 → "995", 0.999 → "999"), for example `format(p, "g").split(".")[1]` or the string the task lists. A fixed multiplier fails for one of them: `int(p * 100)` turns 0.995 into "99", `int(p * 1000)` turns 0.99 into "990", and floating point can make `int(0.29 * 100)` 28.
- Sign: fitting the GPD to returns (left tail as negative numbers) or forgetting $y = x - u$ (fitting x itself) gives nonsense $\beta$.
- $N_{u}$ / n vs (1 - threshold quantile): use the actual count $N_{u}$ when u is an empirical quantile.
- Violation as $\ge$ vs $>$, and `return < -VaR` vs $\mathrm{loss} > \operatorname{VaR}$: same thing if VaR is positive; follow the task.
- Basel traffic light (BCBS 1996): with T daily 99% VaR hits, yellow zone starts at the smallest x with $\mathrm{BinomCDF}(x; T, 0.01) \ge  0.95$, red at $\ge  0.9999$.
- Kupiec has low power in small samples, and its exact size differs from nominal because x is discrete; $\mathrm{LR}_{\mathrm{ind}}$ is oversized when few hits are expected.

atoms.title: Extreme value theory: peaks-over-threshold (GPD), Hill estimator, and VaR backtests (Kupiec, Christoffersen) / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- GPD needs enough exceedances and a high enough u; too low u biases $\xi$ (e.g. a Student-t tail fitted at a moderate quantile gives $\xi$ below $1/\nu$), too high u inflates variance.
- ES formula requires $\xi  < 1$; second moments need $\xi  < 1/2$. Clustered (non-i.i.d.) losses: filter first (GARCH) or decluster.

# EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this document to estimate exponentially weighted return covariance and attribute a linear portfolio's volatility or normal VaR to its assets. It distinguishes conditional EWMA forecasts from centered weighted sample covariance, and marginal risk from component risk. It does not cover nonlinear portfolio revaluation or risk-parity optimization.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / Contents
atoms.text:
## Contents

1. [Shared Foundations](#1-shared-foundations)
2. [EWMA Covariance and Estimation Conventions](#2-ewma-covariance-and-estimation-conventions)
3. [Portfolio Volatility and Normal VaR](#3-portfolio-volatility-and-normal-var)
4. [Euler Risk Decomposition](#4-euler-risk-decomposition)
5. [Checks and Scope](#5-checks-and-scope)
6. [References](#6-references)

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 1. Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared Foundations

Map the task's notation, definitions and units to the quantities here. Explicit task conventions take precedence; if they conflict or leave an estimator unspecified, identify the ambiguity and state the interpretation. A parameter's name alone does not define its statistical role.

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| n; i, j | Number of assets; asset indices |
| $t$ | Observation index, increasing from oldest to newest |
| $r_{t}$ | Column vector of simultaneous one-period returns, in decimals |
| $m_{t}$ | Conditional mean of $r_{t}$, specified using information available before t |
| $e_{t}$ | Return innovation $r_{t}$ - $m_{t}$ |
| $C_{t}$ | Covariance forecast after incorporating observation t, for the next period |
| $\lambda$ | Decay factor, normally $0 < \lambda  < 1$ |
| $w$ | Asset weights, in exactly the same order as $C_{t}$'s rows and columns |
| $C; \mu$ | Covariance matrix and mean-return vector for the risk horizon being measured |
| $\sigma _{p}$ | Portfolio volatility in return units |
| $\alpha$; $\Phi$ | Confidence probability in (0,1); standard normal cumulative distribution |
| $A$ | Number of observation periods per year |

For simple returns and beginning-of-period weights, the portfolio return is the weighted asset return. A weighted sum of log returns is generally only an approximation to a portfolio's log return.

$$
r_{p,t} = w^{T} r_{t}
$$

Here superscript T means transpose. Changes from decimal returns to percentage-point returns multiply covariance by $100^2$ and volatility by 100. Asset order, units and observation dates must agree before combining covariance with weights. Missing observations require a specified policy; they are not zero returns.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 2. EWMA Covariance and Estimation Conventions
atoms.text:
## 2. EWMA Covariance and Estimation Conventions

### Conditional covariance forecast

Use this branch for a RiskMetrics-style conditional forecast. Under the zero-conditional-mean approximation, $e_{t} = r_{t}$. If a nonzero conditional mean model is specified, use its innovations. Subtracting the full sample mean instead defines a different estimator and can introduce future information into historical forecasts.

The innovation outer product supplies one variance or covariance update for each asset pair; it is an n-by-n matrix, not the scalar sum of squared innovations.

The $(i,j)$ entry of $e_{t} e_{t}^{T}$ is $e_{t,i} \cdot  e_{t,j}$.

The covariance forecast weights the previous forecast and the latest outer product.

$$
C_{t} = \lambda \cdot C_{t-1} + (1-\lambda )\cdot e_{t} e_{t}^{T}
$$

Given an initial forecast $C_{0}$ before the m observations being incorporated, expanding the recursion gives its finite-history form.

$$
C_{m} = \lambda ^{m}\cdot C_{0} + (1-\lambda )\cdot \sum _{j=1}^{m}[\lambda ^{m-j}\cdot e_{j} e_{j}^{T}]
$$

The initial condition remains with weight $\lambda^{m}$. A zero matrix, a first-observation outer product and an initial sample covariance are distinct seeds; EWMA alone does not choose between them. When the input includes code to be repaired (a template or starter script the task asks you to fix), the seed, window and normalization that this code already uses are the chosen convention unless the task lists one of them as a defect: keep them, and change only the lines that correspond to a stated defect. A first-observation seed already incorporates that observation, so the next update incorporates the next observation. A sample-covariance seed also requires its own sample interval, centering and divisor conventions.

**Estimation window and initialization window are different.** A trailing estimation window selects which recent observations enter an estimate at a particular date. An initialization window supplies a starting matrix, after which subsequent observations update it. An expanding recursive history retains older information through the previous matrix. Neither a window length nor a decay factor specifies all three choices. Preserve the stated sample interval, seed and normalization together.

### Recursive EWMA over an estimation window

This block is the first-observation-seeded convention, as in `ewm(adjust=False)`, applied to the most recent $L$ observations. Use it only when that initialization is selected; a window length and decay factor alone do not choose the seed. A zero-seed finite-history alternative is $C=(1-\lambda)\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}\lambda^k e_{t-k}e_{t-k}^T$, which is not renormalized and gives a different oldest-observation weight.

Window from oldest to newest: $e_{t-L+1}, \ldots , e_{t}$.

$$
C = e_{t-L+1} e_{t-L+1}^{T}
$$

For $s = t-L+2, \ldots , t$:

$$
C = \lambda \cdot C + (1-\lambda )\cdot e_{s} e_{s}^{T}
$$

The result is the forecast after the newest observation. It is not centered, renormalized or divided by $(1-\lambda^L)$. A window length given in the configuration applies even when existing code ignores it; observations older than the window do not enter.

### Normalized finite-window moments

Use this branch only when the specification explicitly requests exponentially weighted moments whose weights sum to one. A window length for a recursive EWMA does not by itself request this branch. Let k be the age of an observation ($k=0$ is newest), and L the window length.

The normalized observation weight is:

$$
p_k=\frac{\lambda^k}{\sum_{a=0}^{L-1}\lambda^a},\qquad k=0,\ldots,L-1
$$

For a zero-mean model, the finite-window second moment is:

$$
C_{\mathrm{zero}} = \sum _{k=0}^{L-1}[p_{k}\cdot r_{t-k} r_{t-k}^{T}]
$$

If instead a centered weighted sample covariance is requested, first define the weighted sample mean.

$$
\bar{r} = \sum _{k=0}^{L-1}[p_{k}\cdot r_{t-k}]
$$

The centered population-form weighted covariance is:

$$
C_{\mathrm{centered}} = \sum _{k=0}^{L-1}[p_{k}\cdot (r_{t-k}-\bar{r})\cdot (r_{t-k}-\bar{r})^{T}]
$$

For fixed deterministic weights and independent observations with a common mean and covariance, the usual unbiased correction divides $C_{\mathrm{centered}}$ by $1-\sum (p_{k}^{2})$, when positive. That correction is not part of the conditional EWMA recursion. The normalization and centering choices in a statistical covariance routine cannot be assumed to match a requested forecast.

With zero initialization, uncentered recursion over L observations equals $(1-\lambda^L)C_{\mathrm{zero}}$. Dividing a recursion with a nonzero seed by this factor does not remove the seed and is not the same finite-window estimator.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 3. Portfolio Volatility and Normal VaR
atoms.text:
## 3. Portfolio Volatility and Normal VaR

For a linear portfolio, variance is the covariance quadratic form.

$$
v_{p} = w^{T} C w
$$

Portfolio volatility is its nonnegative square root.

$$
\sigma _{p} = \sqrt{v_{p}}
$$

The normal quantile is determined by the confidence probability, not by a fixed rounded constant.

$$
z_{\alpha} = \Phi ^{-1}(\alpha )
$$

When loss is minus return, the normal loss quantile includes the portfolio mean. A zero-mean specification sets $\mu$ to zero. Here $\mu$ is the conditional mean forecast that goes with $C$. The RiskMetrics EWMA method takes the conditional mean of daily returns as zero, consistent with its uncentered recursion, so with an EWMA covariance a full-sample average return is not $\mu$ unless the task says to use one.

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha} = z_{\alpha}\cdot \sigma _{p} - w^{T} \mu
$$

This is a return-unit quantile; for a positive portfolio value P, currency VaR is $P\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha$. A convention that floors VaR at zero is an additional convention, not part of this formula.

Under the conventional unchanged per-period covariance and uncorrelated additive-return assumptions, annualized volatility is:

$$
\sigma _{\mathrm{annual}} = \sqrt{A}\cdot \sigma _{p}
$$

The corresponding annualized covariance is A*C. These are horizon-scaling assumptions, not exact laws for compounded returns or serially correlated returns. An already annualized covariance must not be annualized again.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 4. Euler Risk Decomposition
atoms.text:
## 4. Euler Risk Decomposition

Use this block for attribution of volatility with C fixed and $\sigma _{p} > 0$. Derivatives vary one weight while holding other weights fixed; renormalizing weights during differentiation measures a different sensitivity.

The covariance exposure vector has one element per asset.

$$
b = C\cdot w
$$

Marginal risk is the derivative of portfolio volatility with respect to an asset weight.

$$
\mathrm{MRC}_{i} = \partial (\sigma _{p})/\partial (w_{i}) = b_{i}/\sigma _{p}
$$

Component risk multiplies that derivative by the position's weight.

$$
\mathrm{RC}_{i} = w_{i}\cdot \mathrm{MRC}_{i}
$$

Fractional contribution divides component risk by total volatility; multiply by 100 only when reporting percent rather than a fraction.

$$
\mathrm{PRC}_{i} = \mathrm{RC}_{i}/\sigma _{p} = w_{i}\cdot b_{i}/v_{p}
$$

Euler's identity for the degree-one volatility function gives full allocation.

$$
\sum _{i} \mathrm{RC}_{i} = \sigma _{p};  \sum _{i} \mathrm{PRC}_{i} = 1
$$

Negative contributions can represent hedging and need not be clipped. Weights need not all be positive or sum to one for the algebraic identity to hold. Replacing them by absolute values changes the portfolio.

If the requested risk measure is variance, an additive variance allocation has different units.

$$
\mathrm{VC}_{i} = w_{i}\cdot b_{i};  \sum _{i} \mathrm{VC}_{i} = v_{p}
$$

Variance is homogeneous of degree two, so its literal Euler derivative contributions sum to twice the variance; they are not the volatility components above.

$$
\partial (v_{p})/\partial (w_{i}) = 2\cdot b_{i}
$$

For normal VaR with fixed C and $\mu$, the component allocation also includes the mean term.

$$
\mathrm{RC}_{\mathrm{VaR}},i = w_{i}\cdot (z_{\alpha}\cdot \mathrm{MRC}_{i} - \mu _{i})
$$

These components sum to $\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}$. With zero mean they are $z_{\alpha}$ times the volatility components. Multiplication by a positive portfolio value converts them to currency; it does not change fractional contributions when the total is nonzero. A zero total VaR has no defined percentage allocation.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 5. Checks and Scope
atoms.text:
## 5. Checks and Scope

A common $\lambda$ and a positive-semidefinite seed preserve symmetry and positive semidefiniteness in exact arithmetic. Applying unrelated decay factors separately to matrix entries need not do so. Materially negative eigenvalues or variance indicate a problem; small roundoff negatives require a scale-aware tolerance rather than arbitrary changes to the estimate.

The expanded-history formula checks the recursion, including the seed and observation order. With $\lambda =0$ the next forecast is the latest outer product; with $\lambda =1$ it remains the seed. Finite-window normalization and the unbiased correction have separate edge cases; one observation has no unbiased centered covariance estimate.

The Euler sum identities check allocation algebra **but cannot establish that the covariance estimator, window, asset ordering or horizon is correct**. Independent checks include a diagonal covariance case, consistent asset permutations, the expanded-history result, and volatility derivatives with C held fixed. A scalar rank-one update cannot reproduce differing asset variances and cross-covariances.

If $\sigma _{p}=0$, the displayed MRC and PRC ratios are undefined; adding an arbitrary positive denominator changes their meaning. A singular covariance can still produce positive portfolio volatility, in which case these formulas remain valid.

EWMA responds to squared innovations; it does not by itself establish normal tails, remove serial dependence, or describe a nonlinear payoff. Quantile risk and volatility attribution are distinct from identifying equal-risk portfolio weights.

atoms.title: EWMA Covariance and Euler Portfolio Risk Decomposition / 6. References
atoms.text:
## 6. References

J.P. Morgan / Reuters, *RiskMetrics — Technical Document*, fourth edition (1996), §5.2.1 and §5.2.1.1: exponential variance and covariance forecasts. The matrix expansion and estimator distinctions above follow by algebra under the explicitly stated seed and mean conventions. [Publisher PDF](https://www.msci.com/documents/10199/5915b101-4206-4ba0-aee2-3449d5c7e95a).

Dirk Tasche, *Capital Allocation to Business Units and Sub-Portfolios: the Euler Principle*, arXiv:0708.2542, revised 2008, §2 and §3.1: homogeneous risk allocation and standard-deviation contributions. The weight-coordinate and normal-quantile forms above follow by differentiation. [Author paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.2542).

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / overview
atoms.text:
# Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this reference to interpret execution costs, signed spread measures and quantity allocations. An execution schedule is a target; a fill record is a realized or explicitly modeled outcome. A volume cap alone is not a model of queue priority, available liquidity or market impact.

**Two checks before writing a volume profile or a schedule:**

1. Lag order of exponential weights. With lag 0 = most recent, the weights must line up with the window's order. A window sliced as `data[i - n:i]` runs oldest to newest, so pairing it with `np.arange(n)` as lags gives the oldest day the largest weight. Reverse exactly one side: keep the window oldest to newest and reverse the lags (`np.arange(n)[::-1]`), as in the code below. Reversing both the lags and the window cancels, and the largest weight lands on the oldest day again. Then check that the largest weight sits on the newest day.
2. A target day with no rows in the data. The day an order is scheduled on can be missing from the input (the data end before it, or cleaning removed it). Its bars are then generated from the session hours and the bar length, never taken from the data, and an empty schedule is not an answer: check that the scheduled quantities add up to the order quantity.

1. Exponentially weighted profile over a window of $n$ rows ordered oldest to newest: lag $= n - 1 - i$ for row $i$ (the newest row has lag 0), weight $w_i = \exp(-\ln 2\cdot\mathrm{lag}_i/h)$ normalized to sum 1, profile $= \sum_i w_i\cdot\mathrm{row}_i$; the largest weight is on the newest row.
2. Remaining bars of the target day: the session's bar starts strictly after the order time.
3. Integer allocation of a quantity $Q$ over those bars: take $\lfloor \text{share}\cdot Q\rfloor$ per bar and give the rounding remainder one unit at a time to the first bars, or by the task's rule; the allocations sum to $Q$.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Reference prices and time
atoms.text:
## Reference prices and time

Map the trade side, quantity units, reference clock and quote-selection rule first. Transaction time, exchange publication time and local receipt time can differ. A quote known just before a decision and a quote first observed after it answer different questions. A retrospective specification can prescribe either; only information already available can drive a live decision.

For positive quantities $q_{i}$ and fill prices $p_{i}$, execution weighting uses quantities, not the count of fills.

**Average execution price**

$$
\bar{p}=\frac{\sum_i q_i p_i}{\sum_i q_i}
$$

Market VWAP uses the same weighted-price operation on its specified eligible market trades, which may differ from the order's fills. Both averages are undefined when the denominator is zero.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Signed cost and spreads
atoms.text:
## Signed cost and spreads

Let $s=+1$ for a buy and $s=-1$ for a sell, $m_{0}$ a positive benchmark midpoint and $m_{H}$ a later midpoint. Positive cost denotes a worse price for the investor. The following expressions use one fixed reference denominator; definitions using different denominators must not be mixed.

**Executed-price slippage in basis points**

$$
\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{bps}} = 10000\cdot s\cdot (\bar{p}-m_{0})/m_{0}
$$

**Two-sided effective spread**

$$
\mathrm{effective}_{\mathrm{bps}} = 20000\cdot s\cdot (\bar{p}-m_{0})/m_{0}
$$

**Two-sided realized spread at the specified later benchmark**

$$
\mathrm{realized}_{\mathrm{bps}} = 20000\cdot s\cdot (\bar{p}-m_{H})/m_{0}
$$

**Signed reference-price movement**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{movement}_{\mathrm{bps}} = 10000\cdot s\cdot (m_{H}-m_{0})/m_{0} \\
\mathrm{effective}_{\mathrm{bps}} = \mathrm{realized}_{\mathrm{bps}}+2\cdot \mathrm{movement}_{\mathrm{bps}}
\end{gathered}
$$

The identity is arithmetic, not evidence of causal impact. Arrival-reference order averages differ from measures using each fill's own reference midpoint. Averaging individual percentages is generally not equal to a percentage formed from aggregated prices when denominators vary. Fixing a later horizon does not establish permanent versus temporary impact economically.

Executed-price slippage excludes fees and nonexecution opportunity cost unless explicitly added. Full implementation shortfall can include both, relative to a stated decision portfolio. A report containing only the fills does not measure the cost of the unfilled balance.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Participation and residual quantity
atoms.text:
## Participation and residual quantity

If a rule limits a child order by remaining quantity R, participation fraction p times eligible market volume v, and size cap M, its allowable quantity is the minimum of those nonnegative quantities. A filled amount can be smaller under a separate fill model. Distinguish target quantity, permitted order quantity and actual quantity. No-volume intervals do not imply zero price; they imply no observed volume for that interval.

Volume known only at the end of an interval cannot be used as a forecast at its beginning. Ex-post participation reconstructions are valid descriptive calculations but are not automatically implementable trading strategies.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Intraday share estimates
atoms.text:
## Intraday share estimates

For historical session d and bucket b, let $v_{d,b}$ be volume and $V_{d}$ its full-session total, assumed positive.

**A session's volume fractions**

$$
s_{d,b} = v_{d,b}/V_{d}
$$

Averages of s give each session equal influence. Dividing pooled bucket volumes by pooled session volume instead weights high-volume sessions more heavily. Coordinatewise medians or winsorized means need not sum to one.

For historical lag l and positive half-life H, exponential weighting has:

**Decay weight by age**

$$
a_{l} = \exp (-\ln (2)\cdot l/H)
$$

A finite weighted average divides by the sum of the included weights. This is not automatically the same as a recursive infinite-history estimator with a particular initialization.

Given nonnegative predicted bucket scores $u_{b}$ and eligible set E with positive total mass:

**Conditional allocation over the remaining opportunities**

$$
w_b=\frac{u_b}{\sum_{j\in E}u_j},\qquad b\in E
$$

If E is empty or its total mass is zero, no proportional schedule is defined by these scores. A fallback requires an explicit convention. A bar timestamp can label its beginning or its end; that convention determines whether the bar is eligible at a decision time.

For integer total Q, allocations $Qw_b$ can be rounded down, then the remaining units assigned in descending fractional-remainder order with a specified tie rule. This preserves nonnegativity and the total; it does not guarantee participation constraints. Conflicting constraints require a different allocation problem.

When trades are resampled to fixed bars, `sum` and `count` return 0 for an empty interval while `first`, `last`, `max` and `min` return NaN. Identify empty bars by a NaN price column or a zero observation count, not by NaN volume, before counting bars per session; otherwise weekends, holidays and early-close afternoons appear as full-length days of zero volume.

A reference time defined by a horizon (the end of a window plus h, say) is that computed time; the quote matched at or after it has its own transaction and event times, which belong in their own fields. When several quotes share a timestamp, the earliest quote at or later than t is the earliest in the file's event order: pandas `sort_values` is not stable by default, so sort with `kind="stable"` or by (time, update id) before matching.

When a benchmark takes the earliest quote at or later than a time t and quotes can share a timestamp → match on a stably sorted copy:

Quote at or after time $t$: keep each quote's original file row, sort by time with a stable sort (ties keep file order), and take the first row with time $\ge t$ (`searchsorted` with `side="left"`); among quotes with the same time this is the earliest row in the file.


When trade records are aggregated trades (each row has its own aggregate id and also the first and last ids of the individual trades it groups) and an output asks for the first or last eligible trade's id in a set of rows → write the aggregate id of the first or last eligible row; the row's own first/last trade-id columns describe the trades inside that one row → check that the written ids are values of the aggregate-id column.

When a profile is an exponentially weighted average over a window stored oldest to newest and the weights are defined by lag (lag 0 = most recent) → build the lags from the window order so the newest day gets lag 0:

Weights with the window ordered oldest to newest: lags run from $n-1$ (oldest) down to 0 (newest), $w = \exp(-\ln 2\cdot\mathrm{lag}/h)$, and the profile is $\sum_i w_i\,\mathrm{row}_i/\sum_i w_i$; the newest day carries the largest weight.

When an order's quantity is scheduled over the bars of its own day that follow the order time → build that day's bar grid from the session hours and the bar length (not from the days kept for model fitting, which may exclude it), take the bars strictly after the order time, allocate, round as the task states, and check the result before writing:

Schedule after an order: build the session's bar-start grid for the order date from the session open to the last bar start at the bar frequency, keep the bars strictly after the order time (there must be at least one; otherwise check the session hours and the order time), key them by bar time into the profile, convert the shares to integer quantities as the task states, and check that the scheduled quantities sum to the order quantity.

When a bucket has no eligible trades and so no child order → it has no fill, and every fill-linked field (fill price, the benchmark quote's bid and ask, its ids and times) is left empty as the task specifies, not filled with the quote found for the bucket → check those fields on every empty-bucket row before writing.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Checks and scope
atoms.text:
## Checks and scope

Quantity reconciliation connects executed and residual quantities to the target. Conditional shares sum to one only on their declared eligible set. Out-of-sample profile R-squared can be negative; it is not bounded below by zero, and a flat realized profile needs a specified zero-denominator convention. Similar-looking timestamp or volume columns are different economic objects when their availability or aggregation differs.

atoms.title: Execution benchmarks, participation and volume profiles / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources

[SEC staff FAQ on Rule 605, execution-quality statistics](https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/staff-guidance/trading-markets-frequently-asked-questions/frequently-asked-questions-rule-605-regulation-nms), for benchmark-time and quantity-weighting distinctions. The formulas here state generic conventions, not a claim that every market or contract follows US equity reporting rules. Spread reconciliation and conditional allocation follow directly from the definitions above.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution / overview
atoms.text:
# Factor regressions and covariance attribution

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this reference to interpret linear factor exposures and additive variance contributions. It distinguishes fitted return components from risk contributions and robust inference from changing the fitted model. It does not identify causal risk premia from correlated proxies.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Definitions and conventions
atoms.text:
## Definitions and conventions

Map return frequency, units, information dates and the intercept convention to the task. A stock excess return subtracts its matching-period risk-free return; an already excess or zero-investment factor is not reduced by that rate again. Percentage-point spreads and decimal returns are different units. Explicit definitions govern annualization, missing observations and covariance divisors.

Let y contain T observations, F contain K factor columns, X include the intercept and F, b contain regression coefficients, and e denote residuals. A prime denotes transpose. These identities concern an unweighted, unpenalized OLS fit with an intercept, full column rank and a common sample.

**Fitted regression and residual**

$$
\begin{gathered}
b = (X'X)^{-1}\cdot X'\cdot y \\
\hat{y} = X\cdot b \\
e = y-\hat{y}
\end{gathered}
$$

The inverse expresses the mathematical solution; near collinearity makes coefficients unstable. Singular designs do not identify unique individual exposures. Robust standard errors cannot remedy identification failure.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Components of a fitted observation
Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Covariance allocation of variance
atoms.text:
## Covariance allocation of variance

Use sample covariances over exactly the fitted observations and one shared divisor. Assume $\operatorname{Var}(y)>0$. Covariance allocation shares correlated contributions; it is not a decomposition into independent factor variances.

**Fraction of total variance assigned to a fitted component**

$$
a_{j} = \operatorname{Cov}(c_{j},y)/\operatorname{Var}(y)
$$

OLS orthogonality makes the residual contribution equal to its variance fraction on that same sample.

**Residual variance share and coefficient of determination**

$$
\begin{gathered}a_e=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(e)}{\operatorname{Var}(y)}\\ R_{\mathrm{squared}}=1-\frac{\sum_t e_t^2}{\sum_t(y_t-\operatorname{mean}(y))^2}\\ a_e=1-R_{\mathrm{squared}}\end{gathered}
$$

**Exhaustiveness of the allocation**

$$
\sum _{j} a_{j} + a_{e} = 1
$$

To see why, center the level identity, take covariance with y, and use $X'e=0$. Shares can be negative or exceed one; replacing them with absolute values or clipping changes this allocation. With no intercept, shrinkage, out-of-sample residuals or unequal covariance samples, the identity need not hold. A zero total variance gives an undefined fraction.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Inference versus estimation
atoms.text:
## Inference versus estimation

HAC inference retains the OLS coefficients but estimates their sampling covariance allowing serial dependence and heteroskedasticity. It does not whiten the data or eliminate serial dependence. Lag bandwidth, finite-sample correction and t versus asymptotic-normal reference distributions are distinct choices. Fixed observation spacing is the usual HAC assumption; deleting an internal month and treating the neighboring rows as adjacent changes the meaning of a lag. It is not necessary for trading-day observations to be adjacent calendar days.

Multiplying y by a positive constant multiplies coefficients and their standard errors by that constant; t-statistics and R-squared remain unchanged. Rescaling a factor instead rescales its coefficient inversely, leaving fitted components unchanged. An annualized $\alpha$ based on arithmetic scaling is not a compounded investment return.

For overlapping windows the estimates share observations; consecutive estimates are not independent. A low rolling R-squared is a descriptive signal, not by itself a statistical test of structural change. Carrying a discontinued proxy forward is an explicit imputation convention, not new information about the underlying risk.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Checks and scope
atoms.text:
## Checks and scope

Check reconstruction including the intercept, residual orthogonality, allocation totals before rounding, and invariance to consistent unit changes. Risk contribution does not establish causality or tradability of a proxy. This reference supplements rather than replaces the HAC and GRS definitions; their distributional assumptions differ.

atoms.title: Factor regressions and covariance attribution / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources

Newey and West (1987), [A Simple, Positive Semi-Definite, Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix](https://www.nber.org/papers/t0055), for robust covariance estimation. [Statsmodels HAC documentation](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.stats.sandwich_covariance.cov_hac.html), for the single-series, ordered-observation assumption. The reconstruction, covariance allocation and unit-invariance identities above follow directly from the OLS normal equations; they are algebraic derivations, not empirical error guarantees.

atoms.title: Factor models and regressions: conventions and self-checks / overview
atoms.text:
# Factor models and regressions: conventions and self-checks

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this when a task regresses returns on factors or characteristics (time series or cross section), compresses features with PCA, or scores forecasts with an IC. Each rule names the quantity, shows code, and gives an assert.

atoms.title: Factor models and regressions: conventions and self-checks / 1. Training windows and time labels
atoms.text:
## 1. Training windows and time labels
A forecast made at row t may use only rows before t for fitting. With a RangeIndex, `.iloc[a:b]` excludes b but `.loc[a:b]` includes b, so `.loc[t-W:t]` holds W+1 rows and leaks row t.
The training window for date $t$ is the $W$ rows immediately before row $t$ (rows $t-W$ to $t-1$); check that it has exactly $W$ rows and that its last date is before date $t$.
"Mean of the previous N values": `s.rolling(N, min_periods=N).mean().shift(1)`. Rows before N values exist are undefined: keep them NaN and do not rank or trade on them; `fillna(0)` turns "no signal" into a tradable value.

atoms.title: Factor models and regressions: conventions and self-checks / 2. One regression per model
atoms.text:
## 2. One regression per model
Models with different regressor sets (nested or not) are separate fits, each on the rows complete for its own regressors and target. Coefficients of a larger model are not those of a smaller one.
For each model, drop the rows with a missing value in the target or in that model's regressors, then fit OLS of the target on those regressors with a constant (for example `statsmodels` OLS with `add_constant`).
An out-of-sample forecast is intercept plus every slope times its regressor, controls included, standardized as in the fit.

atoms.title: Factor models and regressions: conventions and self-checks / 3. Counting periods
atoms.text:
## 3. Counting periods
"Start after the n-th month" can count calendar periods of the sample (periods with no estimate still count) or estimated periods only. They differ when early periods are skipped; compute the start date under the reading the wording supports and assert it.

atoms.title: Factor models and regressions: conventions and self-checks / 4. PCA orientation
atoms.text:
## 4. PCA orientation
Fit scaler and PCA on the training block only. An eigenvector's sign is arbitrary: decide the sign once from the training scores and multiply both training and new scores by the same s.
Principal-component sign: project the standardized training rows and the test row on the first component (with the scaler and PCA fitted on the training window); if the training projections are negatively correlated with the reference series, flip the sign of both the training and the test projection.
Flipping `components_` and also negating the score flips twice.

atoms.title: Factor models and regressions: conventions and self-checks / 5. HAC (Newey-West) and GRS
atoms.text:
## 5. HAC (Newey-West) and GRS
Bartlett weights 1 - l/(L+1), autocovariances divided by T. statsmodels `fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": L})` matches this; `use_correction=True` multiplies the covariance by T/(T-k). GRS has two consistent forms: (T-N-K)/N with residual covariance /T, or (T/N)(T-N-K)/(T-K-1) with residual covariance /(T-K-1); factor covariance /T in both. Mixing pairs changes the statistic.

atoms.title: Factor models and regressions: conventions and self-checks / 6. IC, turnover, annualization
atoms.text:
## 6. IC, turnover, annualization
Spearman IC = Pearson correlation of ranks; undefined (NaN) when either side is constant. Per-period cross-sectional IC averaged over time differs from one pooled correlation. Turnover and cost reported for a period refer to the executed weights; assert `cost == rate * sum|w_final - w_prev|`. When a neutralizing projection is re-applied to a blend of old and new weights, two supports are possible: every name the blend holds (old names kept) or only this period's selected names (old names dropped); check which one lets the names the text says may carry over keep weight. Annualized return can be arithmetic (mean x P) or geometric ((prod(1+r))^(P/n) - 1); state which.

atoms.title: Factor models and regressions: conventions and self-checks / 7. Task wording -> API arguments
atoms.text:
## 7. Task wording -> API arguments
| call | argument and effect | wording it usually matches |
|---|---|---|
| `Series.std`/`np.std` | `ddof=0` population (numpy, StandardScaler), `ddof=1` sample (pandas) | "population" / "sample", "z-score" |
| `sm.OLS` | no intercept unless `sm.add_constant(X, has_constant="add")` | "with an intercept/constant" |
| `.fit(cov_type="HAC")` | `maxlags=L`; `use_correction`; `use_t` normal vs t p-values | "Newey-West, L lags", "small-sample" |
| `np.linalg.lstsq` | `rcond=None` machine-precision cutoff; minimum-norm on rank deficiency | "least squares", "pseudo-inverse" |
| `rolling` | `min_periods` (default = window); window includes current row unless `closed="left"` (same as `.shift(1)`) | "trailing N" vs "previous N" |
| `pct_change` / `shift` | first row NaN; `shift(-1)` = next-period value | "forward return", "drop first row" |
| `PCA` | centers, never scales; `whiten=False`; sign arbitrary; `random_state` only for randomized solvers | "z-normalize then PCA" |
| `np.median`/`np.percentile`/`quantile` | linear interpolation default | "median", "1st/99th percentile" |
| `np.random.default_rng(s)` vs `np.random.seed(s)` | different streams (PCG64 Generator vs legacy MT19937); the draw order also changes the numbers | the task names the generator; when it only says "use seed s", no reading is standard: numpy recommends the Generator API (`default_rng`) for new code, while code written with the legacy API seeds `np.random.seed(s)`; when a result sits on a discrete step the choice decides it, so say which one is used and keep one generator for every draw |
| `to_csv` | index written as unnamed column unless `index=False`; name it with `rename_axis(name).reset_index()` | first column named in the spec |

Read every written CSV back and assert its header equals the specified column list.

atoms.title: Factor models and regressions: conventions and self-checks / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources
Cochrane, *Asset Pricing* (rev. 2005), ch. 12.1 (GRS, time-series regressions) and 12.3 (Fama-MacBeth); Fama & MacBeth (1973) JPE 81(3); Newey & West (1987) Econometrica 55(3); Gibbons, Ross & Shanken (1989) Econometrica 57(5), sec. 2; Grinold & Kahn, *Active Portfolio Management* (2000), ch. 6 (IC); Jolliffe, *Principal Component Analysis* (2002), ch. 2-3; statsmodels `RegressionResults.get_robustcov_results`; pandas `DataFrame.loc`, `rolling`, `to_csv`; scikit-learn `PCA`, `StandardScaler`; NumPy `random.default_rng`, `linalg.lstsq`.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions: per-period slopes, standard errors, Newey-West, forecasts, Shanken correction, standardized characteristics and residual momentum / overview
atoms.text:
# Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions: per-period slopes, standard errors, Newey-West, forecasts, Shanken correction, standardized characteristics and residual momentum

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Read the topics relevant to the task; a task usually needs several of them.

Notation used in every topic:

| symbol | meaning |
|---|---|
| $y_{it}$ | dependent variable of asset $i$ for period $t$ (e.g. return from $t$ to $t+1$; align dates exactly as the task says) |
| $x_{it}$ | $K$ regressors of asset $i$ observed at $t$ (characteristics, or estimated betas $\hat{\beta}_{i}$) |
| $N_{t}$ | number of assets with complete data at $t$ (must exceed $K + 1$) |
| $T$ | number of periods with a valid cross-sectional regression (NOT the number of stock-month observations) |
| $\hat{\lambda}_{t}$ | $(K+1)$-vector of per-period coefficients (intercept first) |
| $L, h$ | Newey-West lag; return horizon in periods when returns overlap |

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions: per-period slopes, standard errors, Newey-West, forecasts, Shanken correction, standardized characteristics and residual momentum / Topic 1: Per-period cross-sectional regressions, one per model
atoms.text:
## Topic 1: Per-period cross-sectional regressions, one per model

**Purpose:** Estimate, for each period, the cross-sectional relation between outcomes and regressors known at the forecast date, so that the slopes form a time series.

**When to use:** A panel of assets $i$ over periods $t = 1 \ldots T$, and the task asks for Fama-MacBeth slopes, risk premia or characteristic returns, possibly for several models with different regressor sets.

**Constraints:**
- Regressors are known at the forecast date: firm characteristics, or betas estimated in a first pass.
- One regression per model. When the task compares models with different regressor sets (nested or not), run a separate cross-sectional regression for each model each period, on the rows complete for that model's own target and regressors. The coefficients of a smaller model are not a subset of a larger model's; copying them gives wrong slopes, wrong valid-period counts and wrong forecasts.
- Store the full fitted coefficient vector (intercept and every regressor, controls included) for each period, even when the deliverable reports only some slopes; the forecast step (Topic 4) needs all of them.

**How to implement:**
1. Check the inputs and print them: the date column, the target and its date alignment, each model's regressor list, and the minimum number of observations per regression.
2. Only if the regressors are betas (pass 1): for each asset, over the beta window, regress $R_{it} = a_{i} + b_{i}' f_{t} + e_{it}$ to get $\hat{\beta}_{i}$.
3. Pass 2, as a line-by-line algorithm:
   - `lam = {name: {} for name in models}`
   - `for date, month in panel.groupby(date_col):`
   - `    for name, cols in models.items():`
   - `        sub = month.dropna(subset=[target] + cols)`
   - `        if len(sub) < min_obs: continue`
   - `        lam[name][date] = sm.OLS(sub[target], sm.add_constant(sub[cols], has_constant="add")).fit().params`
   - after the loop, check `all(len(lam[m]) > 0 for m in models)`: each model keeps its own valid-period list.
4. Each fit is $X_{t} = [1, x_{\cdot t}]$ of shape $N_{t} \times (K+1)$ and $\hat{\lambda}_{t} = (X_{t}' X_{t})^{-1} X_{t}' y_{t}$.

**Limitations and cautions:** Unbalanced panels are fine; $T$ counts only periods actually regressed. Small $N_{t}$ makes per-period slopes noisy. With estimated betas the slopes have errors-in-variables bias in finite $T$ (Topic 5).

**Double check:** Print, per model, the number of valid periods and the first period's coefficient names; models with different regressors must show different counts or different coefficients, not copies.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions: per-period slopes, standard errors, Newey-West, forecasts, Shanken correction, standardized characteristics and residual momentum / Topic 2: Fama-MacBeth estimate and standard error
atoms.text:
## Topic 2: Fama-MacBeth estimate and standard error

**Purpose:** Average the per-period slopes and measure their uncertainty from their time-series variability.

**When to use:** The task asks for average slopes, their standard errors, t-statistics, p-values or an average $R^2$.

**Constraints:**
- The standard error is NOT the per-period OLS standard error, not an average of per-period standard errors, and not the standard error of one pooled regression.
- This handles cross-sectional correlation of returns automatically; it assumes the slopes are uncorrelated over time (otherwise Topic 3).

**How to implement:**
1. Estimate: $\bar{\lambda} = (1/T) \sum_{t} \hat{\lambda}_{t}$, with `numpy.mean` over the slope series.
2. Standard error: $s_{j}^{2} = (1/(T-1)) \sum_{t} (\hat{\lambda}_{jt} - \bar{\lambda}_{j})^{2}$ and $\mathrm{se}_{j} = s_{j} / \sqrt{T}$.
3. t-statistic $t_{j} = \bar{\lambda}_{j} / \mathrm{se}_{j}$; p-value from $t(T-1)$ or the normal, as the task says.
4. Covariance: $V_{\mathrm{FM}} = (1/(T(T-1))) \sum_{t} (\hat{\lambda}_{t} - \bar{\lambda})(\hat{\lambda}_{t} - \bar{\lambda})'$.
5. Average $R^2$: average the per-period $R^2$ values.

**Limitations and cautions:** Robust to cross-sectional correlation but not to serial correlation of $\hat{\lambda}_{t}$ (persistent characteristics, overlapping returns); then use Topic 3. With estimated betas, see Topic 5.

**Double check:** $T$ equals the number of valid periods of that model (Topic 1), not the number of rows in the panel.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions: per-period slopes, standard errors, Newey-West, forecasts, Shanken correction, standardized characteristics and residual momentum / Topic 3: Newey-West standard errors for persistent or overlapping slopes
atoms.text:
## Topic 3: Newey-West standard errors for persistent or overlapping slopes

**Purpose:** Correct the Fama-MacBeth standard error for serial correlation of the slopes.

**When to use:** Overlapping returns, persistent characteristics, or the task asks for Newey-West (HAC) t-statistics.

**Constraints:**
- With $h$-period overlapping returns the slopes are serially correlated up to lag $h - 1$: use $L \ge h - 1$ unless the task sets $L$.
- A task asking for the textbook Newey-West form with the $1/T$ autocovariance denominator means the formula below, computed directly.

**How to implement:**
1. Average slope $\bar{\lambda}_{j}$ with `numpy.mean` of the slope series.
2. $\gamma_{l} = (1/T) \sum_{t=l+1}^{T} (\hat{\lambda}_{jt} - \bar{\lambda}_{j})(\hat{\lambda}_{j,t-l} - \bar{\lambda}_{j})$.
3. $\mathrm{se}_{\mathrm{NW},j} = \sqrt{[\gamma_{0} + 2 \sum_{l=1}^{L} (1 - l/(L+1)) \gamma_{l}] / T}$ and $t_{\mathrm{NW},j} = \bar{\lambda}_{j} / \mathrm{se}_{\mathrm{NW},j}$.
4. Before reporting, check that each reported average slope equals `numpy.mean` of its monthly series.

**Implementation tips:** If the mean and its HAC standard error are obtained instead by regressing the slope series on a constant, the design matrix must hold exactly one column of ones: `sm.add_constant(np.ones(T))` adds a second, identical constant column, and OLS then splits the mean between the two columns, so the reported average slope is half the true one while its t-statistic is unchanged. See the Newey-West entry for lag rules.

**Limitations and cautions:** $L = 0$ gives the standard deviation with divisor $T$, slightly smaller than the plain Fama-MacBeth standard error.

**Double check:** Step 4; and $\mathrm{se}_{\mathrm{NW}}$ at $L = 0$ equals $\mathrm{se}_{j}\sqrt{(T-1)/T}$.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions: per-period slopes, standard errors, Newey-West, forecasts, Shanken correction, standardized characteristics and residual momentum / Topic 4: Forecasts from averaged slopes
atoms.text:
## Topic 4: Forecasts from averaged slopes

**Purpose:** Predict each asset's outcome at a date from slopes estimated before that date.

**When to use:** The task asks for out-of-sample forecasts, predicted returns or portfolios ranked on the fitted model.

**Constraints:**
- Calendar periods versus estimated periods: a start rule stated in calendar periods ("forecasts begin after the $n$-th month") counts the sample's calendar periods, including periods that produced no regression. Test the date's position in the full date list, not its position among estimated periods.
- An expanding average at a forecast date uses every slope estimated before that date.
- The forecast uses the whole fitted model: averaged intercept plus averaged slopes times every regressor of that model, controls included, standardized exactly as in the fit. Leaving the controls out ranks the assets on a different model.

**How to implement:**
1. `all_dates = sorted(panel[date_col].unique())` and `pos = {d: i for i, d in enumerate(all_dates)}`.
2. For each `d` in `all_dates`: skip it when `pos[d] < n`.
3. `past = [lam[name][e] for e in lam[name] if e < d]` and `avg = sum(past) / len(past)`.
4. `z = month_d[cols]` (standardized as in the fit) and `pred = avg["const"] + z @ avg[cols]`.
5. Check `list(avg.index) == ["const"] + cols`.

**Limitations and cautions:** Early forecast dates average few slopes and are noisy; this is part of the method, not an error to fix.

**Double check:** The first forecast date is the $(n+1)$-th calendar date of the sample; print it with the number of slopes averaged there.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions: per-period slopes, standard errors, Newey-West, forecasts, Shanken correction, standardized characteristics and residual momentum / Topic 5: Shanken (1992) correction for estimated betas
atoms.text:
## Topic 5: Shanken (1992) correction for estimated betas

**Purpose:** Inflate the Fama-MacBeth covariance for the estimation error of first-pass betas.

**When to use:** Only when the pass-2 regressors are ESTIMATED betas and the task asks for Shanken-corrected standard errors. Not for observed characteristics (they are not estimated).

**Constraints:**
- $\Gamma = (\gamma_{0}, \gamma_{a}')'$, with $\gamma_{a}$ the $K$ factor premia (per period, same frequency as returns).
- $c = \gamma_{a}' \Sigma_{f}^{-1} \gamma_{a}$, with $\Sigma_{f}$ the $K \times K$ covariance of the factors $f_{t}$ over the pass-1 sample; $c$ is not annualized when the data are monthly.
- $\Sigma_{f}^{*}$ is block-diagonal: 0 for the intercept, $\Sigma_{f}$ for the factors.

**How to implement:**
1. Compute $V_{\mathrm{FM}}$ (Topic 2) and $c$.
2. Practical form: $V_{\mathrm{Shanken}} = (1 + c)(V_{\mathrm{FM}} - \Sigma_{f}^{*} / T) + \Sigma_{f}^{*} / T$.
3. Without an intercept in pass 2, drop its row and column.

**Implementation tips:** The asymptotic form it comes from is $\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\Gamma}) = (1/T) [(1 + c) A \Sigma A' + \Sigma_{f}^{*}]$, $A = (X'X)^{-1} X'$, $X = [1, \hat{\beta}]$, $\Sigma$ = pass-1 residual covariance. Both forms agree asymptotically, not exactly.

**Limitations and cautions:** The non-factor variance component receives the multiplier $1 + c$; the corresponding standard-error multiplier is $\sqrt{1 + c}$, not $1 + c$. The full covariance also contains the separate factor component.

**Double check:** Corrected standard errors are at least as large as the uncorrected ones.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions: per-period slopes, standard errors, Newey-West, forecasts, Shanken correction, standardized characteristics and residual momentum / Topic 6: Cross-sectional standardization of characteristics
atoms.text:
## Topic 6: Cross-sectional standardization of characteristics

**Purpose:** Put characteristics on a common scale within each date before the cross-sectional regression.

**When to use:** The task asks for z-scored, standardized or ranked characteristics.

**Constraints:**
- $z_{it} = (x_{it} - \operatorname{mean}_{t}(x)) / \operatorname{sd}_{t}(x)$, mean and standard deviation over the $N_{t}$ assets present at date $t$.
- Standardize within each date (groupby date), never over the pooled panel (look-ahead).

**How to implement:**
1. Drop or fill missing values and winsorize first if the task says so.
2. Standardize over exactly the assets used in that date's regression.
3. Set ddof explicitly: population sd divides by $N_{t}$ (ddof 0), sample sd by $N_{t} - 1$ (ddof 1). numpy `std` defaults to ddof 0, pandas `.std()` to ddof 1; the z-scores differ by the factor $\sqrt{N_{t}/(N_{t}-1)}$.
4. Rank variant: replace $x$ by its cross-sectional rank (often scaled to $[0, 1]$ or demeaned) before regressing.

**Limitations and cautions:** On dates with few assets the sd is noisy; a constant characteristic on a date has sd 0 and its z-scores are undefined, so follow the task's rule for such dates.

**Double check:** Each date's z-scores have mean 0 and the standard deviation 1 under the chosen ddof.

atoms.title: Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions: per-period slopes, standard errors, Newey-West, forecasts, Shanken correction, standardized characteristics and residual momentum / Topic 7: Residual momentum (Blitz, Huij and Martens 2011)
atoms.text:
## Topic 7: Residual momentum (Blitz, Huij and Martens 2011)

**Purpose:** Rank stocks on past factor-model residual returns scaled by their residual volatility, instead of total returns.

**When to use:** The task asks for residual momentum or idiosyncratic momentum.

**Constraints:**
- Residuals exclude $\alpha$; factor betas use only data up to $t - 1$.
- Scale by the residual sd over the same formation months (standardization as in Gutierrez and Prinsky 2007), unless the task defines it otherwise.

**How to implement:** For each stock $i$ and formation date $t$ (ranking for the holding period that starts at $t$):
1. Over the $W$ months $t - W \ldots t - 1$ regress excess returns on the factor model (BHM: Fama-French three factors) with an intercept: $r_{is} = \alpha_{i} + \beta_{i}' f_{s} + \varepsilon_{is}$; keep only stocks with a complete window.
2. Residuals: $\hat{\varepsilon}_{is} = r_{is} - \hat{\alpha}_{i} - \hat{\beta}_{i}' f_{s}$ (do not add $\alpha$ back).
3. Formation months: $s = t - J \ldots t - 1 - S$ ($S$ = skip months; BHM use the past year and skip the most recent month).
4. Score: $\sum \hat{\varepsilon}_{is} / \operatorname{sd}(\hat{\varepsilon}_{is})$ over the formation months (sd over the SAME months; ddof per task). mean/sd ranks identically when every stock has the same number of formation months.
5. Sort stocks on the score each date (e.g. deciles), long the top, short the bottom, weighting as the task says. Unless the task gives its own bucketing rule, quantile groups are equal-count bins of the sorted values: `pd.qcut(score, q, labels=False)` (group 0 is the lowest), with `score.rank(method='first')` passed instead of the score when ties would make the edges repeat. A percentile-rank threshold such as `(rank - 1) / (n - 1) < 0.2` is a different rule: it changes how many names fall in the end groups when $n$ is not a multiple of $q$.

**Limitations and cautions:** Common mistakes: regressing without an intercept; including month $t - 1$ when it should be skipped; using betas estimated with data after $t - 1$; scaling by total-return volatility or by the whole $W$-month residual sd (only if the task defines it that way).

**Double check:** Print, for one stock and date, the window months, the formation months and the score.

References: Fama and MacBeth (1973), Journal of Political Economy 81(3):607-636; Shanken (1992), Review of Financial Studies 5(1):1-33; Shanken and Zhou (2007), Journal of Financial Economics 84(1):40-86 (eq. 9); Newey and West (1987), Econometrica 55(3):703-708; Blitz, Huij and Martens (2011), Journal of Empirical Finance 18(3):506-521; Gutierrez and Prinsky (2007), Journal of Financial Markets 10(1):48-75 (cited via BHM; original not read).
