atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes / 1. Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared Foundations

Read these definitions once; revisit them when the contract or parameter convention changes. Symbols in other references may mean different things.

| Symbol | Definition |
|---|---|
| $S$ | Positive spot at valuation |
| $K$ | Positive fixed strike |
| $r, q$ | Constant annual continuously compounded domestic rate and dividend yield; for FX, q is the foreign rate |
| $\sigma$ | Positive annual volatility, expressed as a decimal |
| $t_{j}$ | Strictly increasing future observation times in years; $t_{0}=0$ |
| $T, T_{p}$ | Last observation time and payment time; $T_{p} \ge  T$ |
| $w_{j}$ | Deterministic nonnegative weights; include historical weights when normalizing the full average |
| $Z_{j}$ | Independent standard normal draws for one path |
| $D$ | Discount factor $\exp (-r\cdot T_{p})$ |
| $g$ | Undiscounted contractual payoff |
| $H$ | A single-path discounted payoff D*g |
| $M$ | Number of independent observations used to estimate a mean |
| $\Phi , \phi$ | Standard normal CDF and density |

For constant-parameter risk-neutral GBM, define $b=r-q-\sigma ^{2}/2$. Then
**Construct observation times, Brownian values and stock paths**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{d}t_{j} = t_{j} - t_{j-1} \\
W_{j} = \sum _{k\le j}(\sqrt{\mathrm{d}t_{k}}\cdot Z_{k}) \\
S_{j} = S\cdot \exp (b\cdot t_{j} + \sigma \cdot W_{j})
\end{gathered}
$$

**Option value as an expected discounted payoff**

$$
V = \operatorname{E}[H]
$$

A log drift supplied as b already includes the variance correction. The Z array has one row per path and one column per future increment. European-only simulation can use one increment ending at T.

Greek definitions used here are $\Delta=\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}S$, $\Gamma=\mathrm{d}^{2}V/\mathrm{d}S^{2}$, $\mathrm{Vega}=\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}\sigma$ and $\mathrm{Rho}=\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}r$. Other inputs stay fixed. These are derivatives per unit of the decimal input. Multiply Vega or Rho by 0.01 to quote the approximate change for a one-percentage-point increase; a 1% relative change in volatility is a different shock. Do not scale twice.

For a European option with payment at expiry, hold spot and other constant model inputs fixed. Let $T$ and $h$ be measured in years, with $0<h<T$. The backward difference below estimates maturity sensitivity:

$$
V_T=\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}
\approx-\frac{V(T-h)-V(T)}{h},
\qquad
\Theta=-V_T.
$$

Compare this difference with negative BS calendar Theta in the same annual units. A one-day bump $h=1/B$, where $B$ is the specified days-per-year basis, does not itself make the quotient a daily sensitivity. Divide both the estimate and its SE by $B$ only when converting to daily units; reversing the sign leaves SE unchanged. Follow explicitly specified formulas and scaling; distinguish their meaning from their labels.

Zero volatility or expired contracts need deterministic/limit handling; score formulas that divide by $\sigma$ or time do not apply there.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes / 2. Samples, Variance and Standard Error
atoms.text:
## 2. Samples, Variance and Standard Error

For every estimator, first compute one random contribution $G_{i}$ per independent observation. Then
**Estimation and standard error from independent path contributions**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{estimate} = \operatorname{mean}(G_{i}) \\
\;\text{sample}\;_{\mathrm{variance}} = \sum _{i}((G_{i}-\mathrm{estimate})^{2})/(M-1) \\
\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\;\text{sample}\;_{\mathrm{variance}}/M}
\end{gathered}
$$

The variance of individual contributions is not the variance of their mean. A variance comparison must use the same level of aggregation for both methods. For antithetic sampling, average each pair before applying these formulas; M counts independent pairs. Do not use an IID standard error for correlated observations without accounting for dependence.

When comparing two estimates on shared paths, calculate paired differences $G_{i}$-$J_{i}$ and their SE; independent-error addition ignores their covariance. A confidence interval describes sampling uncertainty, not finite-difference bias, discretization error or a wrong contract.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes / 3. Finite Differences
atoms.text:
## 3. Finite Differences

Use [Shared Foundations](#1-shared-foundations) for the derivative and [Section 2](#2-samples-variance-and-standard-error) for its SE.

For parameter a and bump $h>0$, evaluate discounted payoffs on the same base random draws at a+h, a and a-h:
**Central finite-difference contribution for a first derivative**

$$
G_{\mathrm{first},i} = (H_{i}(a+h)-H_{i}(a-h))/(2\cdot h)
$$

**Central finite-difference contribution for a second derivative**

$$
G_{\mathrm{second},i} = (H_{i}(a+h)-2\cdot H_{i}(a)+H_{i}(a-h))/h^{2}
$$

Their means estimate first and second derivatives. Their sample standard deviations give the SEs. Computing only the bumped price means loses the information needed for the paired SE; subtract the per-path payoffs first.

Common random numbers couple scenarios, reducing noise for many option sensitivities. Reusing a seed is insufficient if different branches consume different draws. Keep the same path index aligned across bumps. Recompute everything that depends on the bumped parameter, including drift, diffusion, discount factors and any affected fixing times; hold unrelated contract terms fixed.

Central differences have second-order bump bias when the price has the required smooth derivatives. Smaller h can increase sampling noise or floating-point cancellation, especially for $\Gamma$. Compare more than one sensible bump size when the result is suspect, without changing a bump explicitly prescribed by the task. For ordinary calendar Theta, a central maturity bump gives
**Calendar-Theta finite-difference contribution**

$$
G_{\theta,i} = -(H_{i}(T+h)-H_{i}(T-h))/(2\cdot h)
$$

This central approximation requires $T>h$ and the payment/observation-time convention defined in Section 1; apply the same convention to each path contribution.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes / 4. Pathwise Estimators
atoms.text:
## 4. Pathwise Estimators

Use PW for the supported continuous vanilla or arithmetic-average call/put payoffs below, when differentiation under expectation is valid. Keep the base normal draws fixed. First select call or put in the following definition; then select terminal or arithmetic-average dependence. These are separate decisions. A density score belongs to LR, not this block.

### Shared payoff and sign definition

For an average or terminal value U, define
**Call payoff and its pathwise derivative**

$$
g_{\mathrm{call}}(U) = \max (U-K,0);  g_{\mathrm{call},\mathrm{prime}}(U) = \operatorname{indicator}(U>K)
$$

**Put payoff and its pathwise derivative**

$$
g_{\mathrm{put}}(U)  = \max (K-U,0);  g_{\mathrm{put},\mathrm{prime}}(U)  = -\operatorname{indicator}(U<K)
$$

At a kink, almost-sure differentiation alone is not sufficient: exchanging differentiation and expectation also needs regularity/integrability. Ordinary GBM call/put first sensitivities satisfy the needed conditions away from degenerate cases. Digital payoffs and barrier indicators require separate treatment.

### Path derivatives used by both supported payoff branches

Differentiating $S_{j}$ and D yields
**Path sensitivity to initial spot**

$$
\mathrm{d}S_{j}/\mathrm{d}S = S_{j}/S
$$

**Path sensitivity to volatility**

$$
\mathrm{d}S_{j}/\mathrm{dsigma} = S_{j}\cdot (W_{j}-\sigma \cdot t_{j})
$$

**Path sensitivity to the interest rate**

$$
\mathrm{d}S_{j}/\mathrm{d}r = t_{j}\cdot S_{j}
$$

**Discount-factor sensitivity to the interest rate**

$$
\mathrm{d}D/\mathrm{d}r = -T_{p}\cdot D
$$

### Payoff depends only on the terminal stock price

For a European payoff $g(S_T)$, with fixed strike and payment date $T_{p} \ge  T$, use $W_{T}=\sqrt{T}\cdot Z$. The explicit pathwise contributions are
**European pathwise Delta contribution**

$$
G_{\Delta} = D\cdot g_{\mathrm{prime}}(S_{T})\cdot S_{T}/S
$$

**European pathwise vega contribution**

$$
G_{\mathrm{vega}} = D\cdot g_{\mathrm{prime}}(S_{T})\cdot S_{T}\cdot (\sqrt{T}\cdot Z - \sigma \cdot T)
$$

**European pathwise Rho contribution, including discounting**

$$
G_{\mathrm{Rho}} = D\cdot (g_{\mathrm{prime}}(S_{T})\cdot T\cdot S_{T} - T_{p}\cdot g(S_{T}))
$$

For a call, $g_{\mathrm{prime}}(S_{T})=\operatorname{indicator}(S_{T}>K)$; for a put, $g_{\mathrm{prime}}(S_{T})=-\operatorname{indicator}(S_{T}<K)$. For each Greek, apply Section 2 to its per-path contributions to obtain the mean and standard error, then apply any requested unit conversion to both.

### Payoff depends on a weighted arithmetic average

Use this block when several fixing prices enter the average. Retain the original full-contract weights and fixed history. For a weighted arithmetic average with already fixed observations,
**Arithmetic payoff underlying with known past fixings**

$$
U = a_{\mathrm{past}} + \sum _{\mathrm{future}}(w_{j}\cdot S_{j})
$$

**Arithmetic-average spot sensitivity**

$$
U_{S} = \sum _{\mathrm{future}}(w_{j}\cdot S_{j}/S)
$$

**Arithmetic-average volatility sensitivity**

$$
U_{\sigma} = \sum _{\mathrm{future}}(w_{j}\cdot S_{j}\cdot (W_{j}-\sigma \cdot t_{j}))
$$

**Arithmetic-average rate sensitivity**

$$
U_{r} = \sum _{\mathrm{future}}(w_{j}\cdot t_{j}\cdot S_{j})
$$

Here $a_{\mathrm{past}}$ is constant, and weights retain their original full-contract normalization. Future weights need not sum to one. Historical prices do not change when current spot is bumped. If the payoff explicitly contains today's spot as a variable, include that extra derivative instead of treating it as a frozen fixing.

The arithmetic-average single-path contributions, using U and its derivatives just above and the shared signed payoff derivative, are
**Asian pathwise Delta contribution**

$$
G_{\Delta} = D\cdot g_{\mathrm{prime}}(U)\cdot U_{S}
$$

**Asian pathwise vega contribution**

$$
G_{\mathrm{vega}} = D\cdot g_{\mathrm{prime}}(U)\cdot U_{\sigma}
$$

**Asian pathwise Rho contribution, including discounting**

$$
G_{\mathrm{Rho}} = D\cdot (g_{\mathrm{prime}}(U)\cdot U_{r} - T_{p}\cdot g(U))
$$

The negative discount term is necessary for Rho. Put Greeks require the negative put payoff derivative, not the call indicator.

PW differentiates the payoff along each simulated path; LR multiplies the payoff by a density score. Do not interchange these contributions. Differentiate discounting separately where required.

### Time sensitivity: select the schedule convention first

For a European option with $T_{p}=T$ and fixed Z,
**Terminal-stock maturity sensitivity**

$$
U_{T} = S_{T}\cdot (b + \sigma \cdot Z/(2\cdot \sqrt{T}))
$$

**European calendar-Theta contribution**

$$
G_{\Theta} = D\cdot (r\cdot g(S_{T}) - g_{\mathrm{prime}}(S_{T})\cdot U_{T})
$$

For a fresh Asian whose dates scale as $t_{j}=\lambda _{j}\cdot T$ and payment scales as $T_{p}=\lambda _{p}\cdot T$, keeping lambdas fixed,
**Average maturity sensitivity when fixing dates scale**

$$
U_{T} = \sum _{j}(w_{j}\cdot S_{j}\cdot (b\cdot \lambda _{j} + \sigma \cdot W_{j}/(2\cdot T)))
$$

**Negative maturity sensitivity with scaled payment time**

$$
G_{\mathrm{minus},\mathrm{maturity}} = D\cdot (r\cdot \lambda _{p}\cdot g(U) - g_{\mathrm{prime}}(U)\cdot U_{T})
$$

This is minus the derivative of that scaled-schedule family, not automatically calendar decay of a seasoned fixed-date contract.

Naively differentiating the vanilla pathwise $\Delta$ again gives an invalid $\Gamma$ estimator: it misses the exercise-boundary contribution. Use FD, LR, or a separately derived smoothing/hybrid method. Pathwise $\Gamma$ is not generally zero. A task may request that some otherwise computable sensitivities be left unavailable; distinguish a task restriction from a mathematical impossibility.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes / 5. Likelihood Ratio Estimators
atoms.text:
## 5. Likelihood Ratio Estimators

Use [Shared Foundations](#1-shared-foundations) and [Section 2](#2-samples-variance-and-standard-error).

Let X have density $p_{a}$(x), with a parameter-independent support and sufficient regularity to differentiate its integral. Hold x fixed when differentiating log density. Write $L_{a}=\partial _{a} \log  p_{a}(x)$. Then
**First-derivative likelihood-ratio identity**

$$
d/\mathrm{d}a \operatorname{E}_{a}[f(X,a)] = \operatorname{E}_{a}[\partial _{a} f(X,a) + f(X,a)\cdot L_{a}]
$$

For parameter-independent f, the second derivative uses
**Second-derivative likelihood-ratio identity**

$$
d^{2}/\mathrm{d}a^{2} \operatorname{E}_{a}[f(X)] = \operatorname{E}_{a}[f(X)\cdot (L_{a}^{2} + \partial _{a} L_{a})]
$$

A first-order score squared alone is not the second-order weight. Explicit parameter dependence in a payoff or discount factor adds derivative terms; it cannot be hidden inside a density score.

### European terminal density

Use this block when the payoff depends only on $S_{T}$ and the assumptions below hold. If several fixing prices affect the payoff, use the joint-path block instead.

For a payoff $g(S_T)$ with no explicit dependence on S, $\sigma$ or r, set $a=\sigma \cdot \sqrt{T}$, and
**Standardize the terminal log return**

$$
Z = (\ln (S_{T}/S)-b\cdot T)/a
$$

**Terminal-density spot score**

$$
L_{S} = Z/(S\cdot a)
$$

**Terminal-density volatility score**

$$
L_{\sigma} = (Z^{2}-1)/\sigma  - Z\cdot \sqrt{T}
$$

**Terminal-density rate score**

$$
L_{r} = Z\cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma
$$

**Terminal-density second-spot-derivative weight**

$$
W_{\mathrm{SS}} = (Z^{2}-1-a\cdot Z)/(S^{2}\cdot a^{2})
$$

These follow by differentiating the lognormal log density: $-\ln (S_{T})-\ln (a)-Z^{2}/2$ plus a constant. For example, $\partial _{S} Z=-1/(S\cdot a)$; combining $\partial_SL_S$ with $L_{S}^{2}$ gives $W_{\mathrm{SS}}$.

**European LR Delta contribution**

$$
G_{\Delta} = D\cdot g(S_{T})\cdot L_{S}
$$

**European LR Gamma contribution**

$$
G_{\Gamma} = D\cdot g(S_{T})\cdot W_{\mathrm{SS}}
$$

**European LR vega contribution**

$$
G_{\mathrm{vega}} = D\cdot g(S_{T})\cdot L_{\sigma}
$$

**European LR Rho contribution, including discounting**

$$
G_{\mathrm{Rho}} = D\cdot g(S_{T})\cdot (L_{r}-T_{p})
$$

These weights are for derivatives with respect to S and $\sigma$, not $\log  S$ and $\log  \sigma$. Rho includes differentiation of discounting. This reference does not provide an LR time estimator; do not assume the time Greek is universally impossible.

### Discretely observed paths

Use this block when the payoff depends on multiple observed stock prices and has the supported parameter dependence below. Do not obtain an Asian estimator by changing only the payoff in the terminal-density formula. Use the joint density of all observations affecting the payoff. With $t_{1}>0$, define
**Standardized path transition innovations**

$$
Z_{j} = (\ln (S_{j}/S_{j-1})-b\cdot \mathrm{d}t_{j})/(\sigma \cdot \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t_{j}})
$$

**Joint density of the observed path**

$$
p(S_{1},\ldots ,S_{n} \vert  S) = \prod _{j} p(S_{j} \vert  S_{j-1})
$$

When observed prices are held fixed, initial S occurs only in the first transition. Consequently,
**Joint-path spot score**

$$
L_{S,\mathrm{path}} = Z_{1}/(S\cdot \sigma \cdot \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t_{1}})
$$

**Joint-path second-spot-derivative weight**

$$
W_{\mathrm{SS},\mathrm{path}} = (Z_{1}^{2}-1-\sigma \cdot \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t_{1}}\cdot Z_{1})/(S^{2}\cdot \sigma ^{2}\cdot \mathrm{d}t_{1})
$$

**Joint-path volatility score**

$$
L_{\sigma,\mathrm{path}} = \sum _{j}((Z_{j}^{2}-1)/\sigma  - Z_{j}\cdot \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t_{j}})
$$

**Joint-path rate score**

$$
L_{r,\mathrm{path}} = \sum _{j}(Z_{j}\cdot \sqrt{\mathrm{d}t_{j}}/\sigma )
$$

With g the full path payoff and $D=\exp (-r\cdot T_{p})$, the contributions are
**Path-dependent LR Delta contribution**

$$
G_{\Delta} = D\cdot g\cdot L_{S,\mathrm{path}}
$$

**Path-dependent LR Gamma contribution**

$$
G_{\Gamma} = D\cdot g\cdot W_{\mathrm{SS},\mathrm{path}}
$$

**Path-dependent LR vega contribution**

$$
G_{\mathrm{vega}} = D\cdot g\cdot L_{\sigma,\mathrm{path}}
$$

**Path-dependent LR Rho contribution, including discounting**

$$
G_{\mathrm{Rho}} = D\cdot g\cdot (L_{r,\mathrm{path}}-T_{p})
$$

Apply Section 2 to each contribution for its estimate and SE. These formulas cover a weighted arithmetic Asian with fixed historical contributions and no other explicit parameter dependence. For $n=1$ they reduce to the terminal formulas. An initial fixing that varies with S or a spot-linked strike introduces explicit payoff derivatives; use the general identity rather than these shortened products.

Very small first observation times can make LR spot weights noisy. The volatility score also accumulates contributions from all increments. Increasing the number of dates can increase LR variance; it does not automatically improve accuracy.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes / 6. Analytic Benchmarks and Checks
atoms.text:
## 6. Analytic Benchmarks and Checks

Use [Shared Foundations](#1-shared-foundations); compare the same contract, units, payment date, derivative variable and sign convention. Convert both estimates to the same convention before comparing; maturity sensitivity and calendar Theta have opposite signs under the stated European convention.

For a European call/put with payment at T,
**Black–Scholes benchmark thresholds**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{d1} = (\ln (S/K)+(r-q+\sigma ^{2}/2)\cdot T)/(\sigma \cdot \sqrt{T}) \\
\mathrm{d2} = \mathrm{d1}-\sigma \cdot \sqrt{T}
\end{gathered}
$$

**European call benchmark**

$$
C = S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d1})-K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T)\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d2})
$$

**European put benchmark**

$$
\operatorname{P} = K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T)\cdot \Phi (-\mathrm{d2})-S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)\cdot \Phi (-\mathrm{d1})
$$

**Call Delta benchmark**

$$
\Delta _{C} = \exp (-q\cdot T)\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d1})
$$

**Put Delta benchmark**

$$
\Delta _{\operatorname{P}} = \exp (-q\cdot T)\cdot (\Phi (\mathrm{d1})-1)
$$

**$\Gamma$ benchmark**

$$
\Gamma  = \exp (-q\cdot T)\cdot \phi (\mathrm{d1})/(S\cdot \sigma \cdot \sqrt{T})
$$

**Vega benchmark**

$$
\mathrm{Vega} = S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)\cdot \phi (\mathrm{d1})\cdot \sqrt{T}
$$

**Call Rho benchmark**

$$
\mathrm{Rho}_{C} = K\cdot T\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T)\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d2})
$$

**Put Rho benchmark**

$$
\mathrm{Rho}_{\operatorname{P}} = -K\cdot T\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T)\cdot \Phi (-\mathrm{d2})
$$

**Call calendar-Theta benchmark**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\Theta _{C} = -S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)\cdot \phi (\mathrm{d1})\cdot \sigma /(2\cdot \sqrt{T}) \\
+ q\cdot S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d1})-r\cdot K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T)\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d2})
\end{gathered}
$$

**Put calendar-Theta benchmark**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\Theta _{\operatorname{P}} = -S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)\cdot \phi (\mathrm{d1})\cdot \sigma /(2\cdot \sqrt{T}) \\
- q\cdot S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)\cdot \Phi (-\mathrm{d1})+r\cdot K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T)\cdot \Phi (-\mathrm{d2})
\end{gathered}
$$

For payment delayed to $T_{p}$, price is $\exp (-r\cdot (T_{p}-T))$ times the price payable at T. Differentiating that factor adds terms for rate or time sensitivities. Do not blindly multiply every Greek by the same factor.

Differentiating put-call parity at fixed T gives
**Greek identities obtained by differentiating European put-call parity**

$$
\begin{gathered}
\Delta _{C}-\Delta _{\operatorname{P}} = \exp (-q\cdot T) \\
\Gamma _{C}-\Gamma _{\operatorname{P}} = 0 \\
\mathrm{Vega}_{C}-\mathrm{Vega}_{\operatorname{P}} = 0 \\
\mathrm{Rho}_{C}-\mathrm{Rho}_{\operatorname{P}} = K\cdot T\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T) \\
\Theta _{C}-\Theta _{\operatorname{P}} = q\cdot S\cdot \exp (-q\cdot T)-r\cdot K\cdot \exp (-r\cdot T)
\end{gathered}
$$

For an Asian average, start from $C_{A}-\operatorname{P}_{A}=D\cdot (\operatorname{E}[A]-K)$ and differentiate its actual schedule and weights. European parity derivatives do not automatically apply.

For any LR score with fixed support, $\operatorname{E}[L_{a}]=0$; likewise $\operatorname{E}[W_{\mathrm{SS}}]=0$. Test these identities and simple payoffs with known derivatives. Passing them does not prove the whole pricer correct. Compare European Greeks with the analytic benchmark and Asian PW/FD estimates with paired errors, accounting for bump bias. For an exact geometric-average benchmark, use the same fixing schedule and payment date as the simulation.

Neither Asian versus European price or Delta ordering nor PW versus LR variance ordering is a universal law across contracts and parameters. Larger M reduces standard error at rate $1/\sqrt{M}$ for IID finite-variance estimators; individual estimates need not approach the truth monotonically.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes / 7. Numerical considerations and scope
atoms.text:
## 7. Numerical considerations and scope

Uncertainty is computed from per-path estimator contributions. Counts, means and centered sums of squares suffice for batched variance estimation without retaining all paths. Stable variance accumulation and matched random draws across bumps preserve the intended estimator; estimates sharing draws are correlated.

An analytic Greek is not an MC estimator. An uncomputed estimator is distinct from a zero estimate or a mathematically unavailable Greek.

The formulas assume constant-parameter GBM, deterministic dates/weights and the stated payoff dependence. Stochastic volatility, jumps, continuous monitoring, early exercise, discontinuous payoffs or parameter-dependent support require separate derivations. For Asian pricing, seasoned reduction and geometric control prices, consult the Asian-options reference; the Monte Carlo arithmetic price itself does not require a Curran approximation.

atoms.title: Monte Carlo Greeks under Black–Scholes / 8. References
atoms.text:
## 8. References

- Broadie and Glasserman (1996), *Estimating Security Price Derivatives Using Simulation*, Management Science 42(2), 269–285. [Author-hosted paper](https://www.columbia.edu/~mnb2/broadie/Assets/bg_ms_1996.pdf).
- Martin Haugh, *Monte-Carlo Simulation: Estimating the Greeks*. [Columbia lecture slides](https://www.columbia.edu/~mh2078/MonteCarlo/MCS_Greeks_MasterSlides.pdf), sections on FD, pathwise estimators, joint-density scores and second derivatives.
- Glasserman (2004), *Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering*, Chapter 7: sensitivity estimation and estimator variance.

The GBM formulas above are explicit differentiations of the displayed transition density and simulated path. They use the conventions stated here; particular task conventions must be mapped separately.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / overview
atoms.text:
# Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

This reference explains the valuation of deposits, fixed and floating swap legs, and curve sensitivities when discounting and rate projection use different curves. It also covers the single-curve limit and the dependence of bootstrapping on interpolation. It does not specify market calendars, quote corrections or a universal currency convention.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 1. Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared Foundations

Map the task's notation to economic quantities and units. Explicit definitions of accrual, curve time, settlement and shocks take precedence. If requirements conflict, state the ambiguity and interpretation; do not infer conventions from a currency or field name alone.

Let v be the valuation date and $\operatorname{P}_{d}$(v,t) the discount factor for a payment at t, under the chosen collateral/funding convention. $Q_{x}$(v,t) is a positive projection-curve parameter for index tenor x; it need not be a tradable zero-coupon bond price. N denotes notional, k a fixed coupon rate, and b a spread, all rates in decimals. A basis point of rate is 0.0001. The curve coordinate u(t) is a year fraction measured from v; coupon accrual fractions are separate quantities.

For a positive discount factor and $u(t)>0$, the continuously compounded zero rate is:

$$
\begin{gathered}
z_{d}(t) = -\ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,t))/u(t) \\
\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,v) = 1
\end{gathered}
$$

Positive discount factors need not decrease with maturity when forward rates can be negative. At $u=0$ a quoted zero rate requires a limiting or short-end convention; the logarithmic quotient is undefined.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 2. Rate projection and known fixings
atoms.text:
## 2. Rate projection and known fixings

For a simple rate accruing from a to c with index accrual $\delta _{x}$(a,c), the projection-curve definition is:

$$
F_{x}(v;a,c) = (Q_{x}(v,a)/Q_{x}(v,c)-1)/\delta _{x}(a,c)
$$

The reverse relation recovers an end-date projection factor from a forward quote and a known start-date factor.

$$
Q_{x}(v,c) = Q_{x}(v,a)/(1+\delta _{x}(a,c)\cdot F_{x}(v;a,c))
$$

The denominator must be positive. A simple deposit discount identity uses the same algebra only when the quoted instrument's start/end values and relevant curve justify it. At $a=v$, the start factor is one. A spot-starting instrument has a later start date, so setting its start factor to one is a distinct assumption.

For an already fixed coupon, its rate is the contractual fixing, not the forward currently implied by the curve. If fixing is still ahead, $F_{x}$ denotes the model's projected rate appropriate to that payment. In a full stochastic multiple-curve model, measure changes may require adjustments; the curve-ratio formula alone is not a universal expectation under every measure. The conventional cash-flow framework separates projection from discounting [1].

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 3. Fixed and floating leg values
atoms.text:
## 3. Fixed and floating leg values

For fixed payments on dates $t_{i}$ with fixed-leg accrual fractions $\alpha _{i}$, the discounted annuity per unit notional is:

$$
A_{d} = \sum _{i} \alpha _{i}\cdot \operatorname{P}_{d}(v,t_{i})
$$

For a constant fixed coupon k, the fixed-leg value before assigning the holder's receive/pay sign is:

$$
\mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{fixed}} = N\cdot k\cdot A_{d}
$$

For floating accrual intervals ($a_{j}$,$c_{j}$), payment dates $p_{j}$, accrual fractions $\delta _{j}$ and rates $H_{j}$ (known fixings or projected rates), the floating-leg value before assigning the holder's receive/pay sign is:

$$
\mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{float}} = N\cdot \sum _{j} \delta _{j}\cdot (H_{j}+b)\cdot \operatorname{P}_{d}(v,p_{j})
$$

The two legs may use different accrual bases, frequencies and dates. Payment lag changes the discount date, not the accrual interval. Principal exchanges, amortization and accrued-interest treatment are contractual additions; an ordinary fixed-for-floating swap does not acquire principal exchanges merely because a bond representation is useful.

From the holder's perspective, paying fixed and receiving floating gives:

$$
\begin{gathered}
V_{\mathrm{pay},\mathrm{fixed}} = \mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{float}}-\mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{fixed}} \\
V_{\mathrm{receive},\mathrm{fixed}} = -V_{\mathrm{pay},\mathrm{fixed}}
\end{gathered}
$$

The par fixed rate sets this value to zero, assuming a nonzero annuity and the floating-leg spread already included.

$$
k_{\mathrm{par}} = \mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{float}}/(N\cdot A_{d})
$$

In the single-curve case only, with $Q_{x}=\operatorname{P}_{d}$, consecutive accrual intervals, payment at each interval end and no floating spread, algebra makes the floating coupons telescope:

$$
\mathrm{PV}_{\mathrm{float}} = N\cdot (\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,a_{1})-\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,c_{\mathrm{last}}))
$$

Using this expression with distinct curves, historical off-market fixings, payment lag or nonconcatenating intervals generally changes the valuation.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 4. Overnight coupons and product definitions
atoms.text:
## 4. Overnight coupons and product definitions

An overnight compounded coupon over observations l, with annualized overnight fixings $r_l$ published daily and accrual fractions $d_l$ (for example, elapsed days divided by 360), has a realized accumulation factor [2]. Nonbusiness days may enter through a multi-day $d_{l}$; observation shifts and lookbacks are contract-specific.

$$
\begin{gathered}
G_{\mathrm{ON}} = \prod _{l} (1+r_{l}\cdot d_{l}) \\
\mathrm{coupon}_{\mathrm{ON}} = N\cdot (G_{\mathrm{ON}}-1)
\end{gathered}
$$

The equivalent simple coupon rate over an accrual $\delta$ is:

$$
R_{\mathrm{ON}} = (G_{\mathrm{ON}}-1)/\delta
$$

An arithmetic overnight average is another payoff. A simple single-payment instrument can be defined instead of a compounded OIS; its stated payoff determines its pricing equation. The word OIS by itself does not make every quoted pillar a deposit or impose one fixed accrual schedule. Adding a contractual spread outside compounding differs from compounding the spread with each daily rate.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 5. Interpolation and calibration equations
atoms.text:
## 5. Interpolation and calibration equations

A curve fitted to quotes must value every instrument with its contractual cash flows and the same interpolant. Let $\theta$ contain curve parameters, $q_{j}$ a market quote and $\mathrm{model}_{\mathrm{quote},j}$ the corresponding par rate or price. Exact calibration requires:

$$
\mathrm{model}_{\mathrm{quote},j}(\theta ) = q_{j}
$$

For a par coupon bond with unit redemption at $T_{n}$, coupons $c\alpha_j$, and payment dates on already determined knots except for the final date, the last factor solves:

$$
\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,T_{n}) = (1-c\cdot \sum _{j<n} \alpha _{j}\cdot \operatorname{P}_{d}(v,t_{j}))/(1+c\cdot \alpha _{n})
$$

If earlier coupon dates lie between the previous and new knots, their interpolated factors may depend on the new unknown. The equation is then implicit. A nonlocal interpolant can also change earlier intervals when later knots are added; fitting one knot at a time does not by itself establish final repricing.

For two knots $u_{a}<u_{b}$ and weight $w=(u-u_{a})/(u_{b}-u_{a})$, interpolation linear in log discount factors gives:

$$
\ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(u)) = (1-w)\cdot \ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(u_{a}))+w\cdot \ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(u_{b}))
$$

Interpolation linear in continuous zero rates gives a different curve:

$$
\begin{gathered}
z_{d}(u) = (1-w)\cdot z_{d}(u_{a})+w\cdot z_{d}(u_{b}) \\
\operatorname{P}_{d}(u) = \exp (-u\cdot z_{d}(u))
\end{gathered}
$$

The first has a constant instantaneous forward on each interval. A spline applied to the exponent $g(u)=u\cdot z_{d}(u)$ is yet another choice. Positivity of factors, calibration and local shape are separate properties; a smooth interpolant does not guarantee nonnegative forwards.

The continuously compounded average forward over a curve-coordinate interval is:

$$
f_{\mathrm{average}}(a,c) = \ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,a)/\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,c))/(u(c)-u(a))
$$

This is not the instantaneous forward except in a constant-forward interval. The instantaneous forward, where differentiable, is:

$$
f_{\mathrm{instant}}(u) = -d \ln (\operatorname{P}_{d}(u))/\mathrm{d}u
$$

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / 6. Risk definitions and checks
atoms.text:
## 6. Risk definitions and checks

Let $V(\theta)$ be value and e specify the shocked curve/risk factor. The central sensitivity to an absolute rate change h is:

$$
\mathrm{d}V_{\mathrm{dtheta},e} \approx  (V(\theta +h\cdot e)-V(\theta -h\cdot e))/(2\cdot h)
$$

The signed change for a positive one-basis-point bump is distinct from a derivative or its absolute value:

$$
\mathrm{change}_{\mathrm{up},1\mathrm{bp}} = V(\theta +0.0001\cdot e)-V(\theta )
$$

A projection-zero shock at coordinate u changes $Q_{x}$ by a factor $\exp (-h\cdot u)$ while an unshocked discount curve stays fixed. A market-quote shock instead changes an input quote and recalibrates affected curves. These are different risks, and recalibration may change multiple parameters. Risk terminology alone does not identify the shock definition.

Useful identities are zero PV at the par fixed rate, opposite signs for opposite swap positions, single-curve telescoping under its conditions, and recovery of the original forward after converting to factor ratios and back. Repricing checks must include earlier quotes when a nonlocal interpolant changes. Small residuals do not validate a wrong day-count or cash-flow model.

This reference does not cover stochastic basis calibration, caplet volatility stripping, FX-reset notionals, or historical short-rate estimation. LIBOR is an index label in historical models here, not a recommendation for a present-day trading convention.

When a task defines a swap's NPV from the perspective of the fixed payer or receiver → compute it from the two leg values by that direction and check its sign:

Swap value: a payer swap (pays fixed, receives floating) is worth the floating leg's present value minus the fixed leg's; a receiver is the opposite. A payer swap has positive value exactly when the floating leg is worth more.

A provided script that computes the NPV another way is checked against this before its output is used.

When curves are bootstrapped from quotes (by your code or a provided script) → reprice every input instrument on the finished curves and stop on any residual above the task's stated tolerance (without one, report the residuals and fix only clear errors); a nonzero residual means a remaining error in the bootstrap (pillar dates, day count, which curve discounts, the order the curves are built in):

Repricing check: the largest absolute difference between each input quote and the model rate, in basis points, must be below the tolerance the task states; otherwise the curve does not reprice its inputs.

atoms.title: Discount curves, projection curves and interest-rate cash flows / References
atoms.text:
## References

[1] Ametrano and Bianchetti (2009), Bootstrapping the Illiquidity: Multiple Yield Curves Construction for Market Coherent Forward Rates Estimation, Sections 2–5. [Author manuscript](https://www.bianchetti.org/finance/bootstrappingtheilliquidity-v1.0.pdf). Bianchetti (2009), Two Curves, One Price, distinguishes forwarding/discounting measures and possible quanto adjustments. [Author paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.2770).

[2] Alternative Reference Rates Committee (2019), A User's Guide to SOFR, discussion of simple versus compound averaging. [Official guide hosted by the New York Fed](https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/Microsites/arrc/files/2019/Users_Guide_to_SOFR.pdf). Actual contractual calendars and accrual conventions govern a trade.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / overview
atoms.text:
# Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Model and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Model and assumptions
- A smooth parametric curve for the zero-coupon (spot) rate z(m) and the instantaneous forward rate f(m) at time to maturity m,
  for ONE trade date. Nelson-Siegel (NS) has 3 betas + 1 decay; Svensson (NSS) adds a second hump: 4 betas + 2 decays.
- In both papers the rates are CONTINUOUSLY compounded: discount factor $\mathrm{DF}(m) = \exp (-z(m) \cdot  m)$, and
  $z(m) = (1/m) \cdot  \int _{0}^{m} f(u) \mathrm{d}u$, i.e. $f(m) = d[m z(m)]/\mathrm{d}m$. Not arbitrage-free; a fitting device, not a dynamic model.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $m$ | time to maturity (years unless the task says months) | years |
| beta0 | long-run level: z and f tend to beta0 as $m \to  \infty$(either sign is allowed; positivity is an optional fitting restriction) | rate, decimal (5% = 0.05) |
| beta1 | $\mathrm{slope}: z(0) = f(0) = \mathrm{beta0} + \mathrm{beta1}$ | rate |
| beta2 | first hump/trough, decay tau1 | rate |
| beta3 | second hump/trough, decay tau2 (Svensson only) | rate |
| tau1, tau2 | decay times (> 0), same time unit as m | years |
| $\lambda$ | an ambiguous name: Diebold-Li use it for the decay RATE $1/\tau$ (loadings in $\lambda m$); other texts and tasks use it for the decay TIME $\tau$ itself (loadings in $m/\lambda$). See "Which parameterization" below | depends |

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Formulas (x1 = m/tau1, x2 = m/tau2)
atoms.text:
## Formulas (x1 = m/tau1, x2 = m/tau2)
Loadings (write them once and reuse):

$$
\begin{gathered}
S(x) = (1 - \exp (-x)) / x\quad (\mathrm{slope} \mathrm{loading}; S(0) = 1) \\
C(x) = S(x) - \exp (-x)\quad (\mathrm{curvature}/\mathrm{hump} \mathrm{loading}; C(0) = 0, C(\infty ) = 0)
\end{gathered}
$$

Svensson zero rate and forward rate:

$$
\begin{gathered}
z(m) = \mathrm{beta0} + \mathrm{beta1} \cdot  S(\mathrm{x1}) + \mathrm{beta2} \cdot  C(\mathrm{x1}) + \mathrm{beta3} \cdot  C(\mathrm{x2}) \\
f(m) = \mathrm{beta0} + \mathrm{beta1} \cdot  \exp (-\mathrm{x1}) + \mathrm{beta2} \cdot  \mathrm{x1} \cdot  \exp (-\mathrm{x1}) + \mathrm{beta3} \cdot  \mathrm{x2} \cdot  \exp (-\mathrm{x2})
\end{gathered}
$$

- beta1 AND beta2 both use tau1; ONLY beta3 uses tau2. Nelson-Siegel = the same formulas with $\mathrm{beta3} = 0$(no tau2).
- Limits: $m \to  0$: $z = f = \mathrm{beta0} + \mathrm{beta1}$(the "instantaneous short rate"); m -> infinity: $z = f = \mathrm{beta0}$.
  z approaches beta0 slowly (like 1/m); f approaches it exponentially. At $m = 0$ use $S = 1, C = 0$(no 0/0).
- Discount factor $\mathrm{DF}(m) = \exp (-z(m) m)$; $\mathrm{bond\ price}=\sum_j\mathrm{CF}_j\mathrm{DF}(t_j)$; forward between $\mathrm{m1} < \mathrm{m2}$:
  $F(\mathrm{m1}, \mathrm{m2}) = [z(\mathrm{m2}) \mathrm{m2} - z(\mathrm{m1}) \mathrm{m1}] / (\mathrm{m2} - \mathrm{m1})$ (continuous).
- Original NS (1987) zero form: $z = \mathrm{beta0} + (\mathrm{beta1} + \mathrm{beta2}) \cdot  S(x) - \mathrm{beta2} \cdot  \exp (-x)$ is algebraically identical to the above.
- Diebold-Li (2006) form: $y(m) = \mathrm{L1} + \mathrm{L2} \cdot  S(\lambda  m) + \mathrm{L3} \cdot  C(\lambda  m)$ = NS with $\tau  = 1/\lambda$,
  L1 = level, L2 = slope, L3 = curvature. DL measure m in MONTHS and fix $\lambda$ for all dates at the value they say puts the
  peak of C at 30 months. Use the $\lambda$ value the task gives: solving dC/dm = 0 at exactly 30 months gives a value slightly
  below the one DL print. A $\lambda$ per month becomes per year by multiplying by 12. With $\lambda$ fixed the model is linear in
  L1..L3, so fit by ordinary least squares on each date.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Which parameterization the task uses
atoms.text:
## Which parameterization the task uses
- The same curve can be written with decay times ($x = m / \tau$) or decay rates ($x = \lambda  m, \lambda  = 1/\tau$). The name of a
  parameter does not decide which: some texts and tasks write the decay TIME as $\lambda$.
- Decide from the task's formula for the loadings, or from units the task states explicitly. If the task gives neither, report
  the parameter in the form you fitted and say which form it is; do not take a reciprocal only because an output field is named $\lambda$.
- Before writing the outputs, plug the parameters you will report into the formula you used and check that they reproduce your
  fitted curve and the fit error you report.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Fitting (estimate the betas and taus)
atoms.text:
## Fitting (estimate the betas and taus)
- Yield errors: minimize $\sum _{i} (z_{\mathrm{model}}(m_{i}) - z_{\mathrm{obs}}(m_{i}))^{2}$ over zero yields, or over model-implied vs observed YTMs of coupon bonds.
- Price errors: model price $\operatorname{P}_{i} = \sum _{j} \mathrm{CF}_{ij} \exp (-z(t_{ij}) t_{ij})$, minimize $\sum _{i} w_{i} (\operatorname{P}_{i} - \operatorname{P}_{\mathrm{obs},i})^{2}$. Unweighted price errors
  have a different scale from yield errors. Locally, $\Delta P_i \approx -P_i D_i \Delta y_i$ with $D_i$ the modified duration under the yield compounding convention, so weights proportional to $1/(P_iD_i)^2$ approximate squared yield errors for currency price residuals; for relative price residuals, use $1/D_i^2$.
  Use full (dirty) prices for cash flows; if clean prices are given add accrued interest.
- Nonlinear least squares (e.g. bounded trust-region) requires positive decay times $\tau_1,\tau_2$. Positive short- and long-end limits do not guarantee positive yields or forwards between them. Decay times need not lie inside the observed maturity range; additional bounds are fitting restrictions, not model identities. The objective is non-convex with local minima (Gilli et al. 2010):
  use several starting points (e.g. beta0 from the longest yield, beta1 from shortest minus longest, $\mathrm{betas2}/3 = 0$, a few $\tau$ pairs)
  and keep the lowest objective; or profile: grid over (tau1, tau2), OLS for the betas at each grid point, keep the best.
- Near-equal decay times can make hump loadings nearly collinear and parameter estimates unstable. A decay ordering or minimum gap is an additional constraint and must not silently replace an unconstrained specification. Similar fitted curves need not identify individual parameters.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Compounding conversions (apply to OUTPUTS only if the task asks)
atoms.text:
## Compounding conversions (apply to OUTPUTS only if the task asks)
- Annual: $R_{a} = \exp (z) - 1$, $z = \ln (1 + R_{a})$. Periodic k per year: $R_{k} = k (\exp (z/k) - 1)$, $z = k \ln (1 + R_{k}/k)$.
- If the observed yields are annual / semi-annual (e.g. bond-equivalent) convert them to continuous BEFORE fitting, or fit in
  their convention and say so; never mix. Percent vs decimal: keep one unit throughout.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common mistakes
- Pairing beta3 with tau1, or giving beta2 its own tau2: wrong curve (the error can be hundreds of basis points).
- Using forward loadings ($\exp (-x), x \exp (-x)$) in the zero-rate formula or vice versa.
- Switching between decay time and decay rate (taking 1/x) when the task's parameter is already in the form you fitted;
  reporting parameters that do not reproduce your own fitted curve; using a $\lambda$ calibrated for months with maturities in years.
- Evaluating S(0) as 0/0 (NaN) at $m = 0$.
- Reporting fitted parameters from one local optimum without checking the fit residuals.

atoms.title: Nelson-Siegel (1987), Svensson (1994) and Diebold-Li (2006) yield-curve parameterizations / Applicability and limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and limits
- Good for smoothing and interpolation inside the observed maturity range; extrapolation is governed by beta0.
- Does not reprice every bond exactly (a least-squares fit); if exact repricing is required, bootstrap instead.
- Parameters are unstable when the problem is ill-conditioned (Gilli et al. 2010); compare fitted curves, not parameters.

Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / overview
atoms.text:
# Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Setting and assumptions
atoms.text:
## Setting and assumptions
- Linear regression $y_{t} = x_{t}' b + u_{t}$, $t = 1\ldots T, k$ regressors (constant included in k). The errors may be heteroskedastic and
  serially correlated; correlation is assumed to die out with the lag. OLS point estimates are unchanged; only the covariance changes.
- A sample mean is the special case $x_{t} = 1$ ($k = 1$): use it for the mean of a return series, of Fama-MacBeth slopes, of a strategy P&L.
- Time order matters: rows must be sorted by time with no gaps; HAC is not for a pure cross-section.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning |
|---|---|
| $T, k$ | number of time observations; number of regressors including the constant |
| $L$ | maximum lag ("maxlags", "truncation lag"); integer >= 0; L = 0 means White (no autocorrelation) |
| $w_{l}$ | Bartlett weight of lag l |
| $\hat{u}_{t}$ | OLS residual; for a mean, $y_{t} - \bar{y}$ |
The covariance is in squared units of the coefficient per the data frequency; do not annualize unless the task says so.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Formulas (OLS)
atoms.text:
## Formulas (OLS)

$$
\hat{b} = (X'X)^{-1} X'y
$$

The score vector has $k$ components:

$$
g_{t} = x_{t} \cdot  \hat{u}_{t}
$$

A $k$ by $k$ SUM, not divided by $T - l$:

$$
\Gamma _{l} = \sum _{t=l+1}^{T} g_{t} g_{t-l}'
$$

$$
w_{l} = 1 - l / (L + 1)
$$

For $l = 0\ldots L$.

$$
S = \Gamma _{0} + \sum _{l=1}^{L} w_{l} (\Gamma _{l} + \Gamma _{l}')
$$

Sandwich covariance:

$$
V_{\mathrm{NW}} = (X'X)^{-1} S (X'X)^{-1}
$$

$$
\mathrm{se}_{j} = \sqrt{V_{\mathrm{NW}}[j,j]}
$$

$$
t_{j} = (\hat{b}_{j} - \mathrm{b0}_{j}) / \mathrm{se}_{j}
$$

With the small-sample scaling, $V_{\mathrm{NW},\mathrm{adj}} = T/(T-k) \cdot  V_{\mathrm{NW}}$ (Stata `newey` applies this factor; see below for statsmodels).

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Formulas (sample mean)
atoms.text:
## Formulas (sample mean)
Divisor $T$ for every $l$:

$$
\gamma _{l} = (1/T) \sum _{t=l+1}^{T} (y_{t} - \bar{y})(y_{t-l} - \bar{y})
$$

Long-run variance:

$$
\Omega  = \gamma _{0} + 2 \sum _{l=1}^{L} (1 - l/(L+1)) \gamma _{l}
$$

$$
\mathrm{se}(\bar{y}) = \sqrt{\Omega  / T}
$$

Optionally multiply by $\sqrt{T/(T-1)}$.

$$
t = (\bar{y} - \mathrm{mu0}) / \mathrm{se}(\bar{y})
$$

Note $\gamma _{0}$ uses divisor T, so with $L = 0$ this is $\operatorname{sd}_{\mathrm{pop}} / \sqrt{T}$, not the usual `sd(ddof=1) / sqrt(T)`.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Choosing L
atoms.text:
## Choosing L
- If the task gives L, use it. For overlapping h-period returns ($h > 1$ periods summed each observation) use at least $L = h - 1$.
- Rule of thumb: $L = \operatorname{floor}(4 (T/100)^{2/9})$ (statsmodels' default when no lag is given to $\mathrm{cov}_{\mathrm{hac}}$).
- Newey-West (1994) automatic lag (Bartlett): with a scalar series $v_{t}$ (the demeaned series for a mean) and
  $n = 4 (T/100)^{2/9}$ rounded to an integer (implementations differ: floor or ceil),
  $\sigma _{j} = (1/T) \sum _{t=j+1}^{T} v_{t} v_{t-j}$, $\mathrm{s0} = \sigma _{0} + 2 \sum _{j=1}^{n} \sigma _{j}$, $\mathrm{s1} = 2 \sum _{j=1}^{n} j \sigma _{j}$,
  $\gamma  = 1.1447 (\mathrm{s1}/\mathrm{s0})^{2/3}$, bandwidth $m = \gamma  T^{1/3}$, then $L = \operatorname{floor}(m)$(R sandwich) or ceil(m) (arch); weights 1 - l/(L+1).
  For a vector $g_{t}$ the series is a weighted sum of its components; the weighting is implementation-specific.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / statsmodels mapping (checked against the installed statsmodels)
atoms.text:
## statsmodels mapping (checked against the installed statsmodels)
- `sm.OLS(y, X).fit(cov_type='HAC', cov_kwds={'maxlags': L})` = $V_{\mathrm{NW}}$ above with Bartlett weights, **no** T/(T-k) factor
  (`use_correction` defaults to False in `fit`), p-values from the **normal** distribution (`use_t=False` by default).
- `cov_kwds={'maxlags': L, 'use_correction': True}` multiplies by T/(T-k). `kernel='uniform'` gives equal weights (not Newey-West).
- `statsmodels.stats.sandwich_covariance.cov_hac(results, nlags=None)` defaults differ: **`use_correction=True`** and
  nlags = floor(4(T/100)^(2/9)).
- HAC standard error of a mean = `sm.OLS(y, np.ones(T)).fit(cov_type='HAC', cov_kwds={'maxlags': L}).bse[0]`.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test of joint zero alphas
atoms.text:
## Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test of joint zero alphas
Time-series regressions $R_{it} = \alpha _{i} + \beta _{i}' f_{t} + e_{it}$ for N test assets (excess returns) on L' traded factors (excess returns),
$t = 1\ldots T$, errors iid normal over time with covariance $\Sigma$. H0: all $\alpha _{i} = 0$.

Unbiased residual covariance, $N$ by $N$:

$$
\hat{\Sigma} = (1/(T - L' - 1)) \sum _{t} e_{t} e_{t}'
$$

$\hat{\mu}$ denotes the factor sample means. Divisor $T$:

$$
\hat{\Omega} = (1/T) \sum _{t} (f_{t} - \hat{\mu})(f_{t} - \hat{\mu})'
$$

$$
\mathrm{GRS} = (T/N) \cdot  ((T - N - L')/(T - L' - 1)) \cdot  \hat{\alpha}' \hat{\Sigma}^{-1} \hat{\alpha} / (1 + \hat{\mu}' \hat{\Omega}^{-1} \hat{\mu})
$$

Under $\mathrm{H0}$:

$$
\mathrm{GRS} \sim F(N, T - N - L')
$$

The p-value is $1 - F_{\mathrm{cdf}}(\mathrm{GRS}; N, T - N - L')$.Equivalent form: $((T - N - L')/N) \cdot  \alpha ' \Sigma _{\mathrm{mle}}^{-1} \alpha  / (1 + \mu ' \hat{\Omega}^{-1} \mu )$ with $\Sigma _{\mathrm{mle}}$ = residual
cross-products / T. Do not mix the two ($\Sigma _{\mathrm{mle}}$ with the T/(T-L'-1) factor over-rejects). One factor: the denominator is
$1+(\mathrm{factor\ Sharpe})^2$, with mean and standard deviation at the data frequency and the standard deviation computed with divisor $T$ (`ddof=0`), consistent with $\hat\Omega$. Requires $T>N+L'$ and full rank of the design, factor covariance and residual covariance. The sample-size inequality alone does not ensure invertibility.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Common variants and mistakes
atoms.text:
## Common variants and mistakes
- Divisor of $\gamma _{l}$: T (Newey-West, PSD) vs T - l (not guaranteed PSD); weights 1 - l/(L+1), not 1 - l/L.
- Lag definition: L counts lags beyond 0; "L lags" includes lags 1..L. Some software instead takes a bandwidth b with weights 1 - l/b; then $b = L + 1$.
- Not demeaning the series for a mean, or forgetting the factor 2 on the autocovariances.
- Reporting statsmodels HAC p-values (normal) when the task asks for t(T - k) p-values, or vice versa.
- Asymptotic Wald alternative to GRS: $T \alpha ' \Sigma _{\mathrm{mle}}^{-1} \alpha  / (1 + \mu ' \hat{\Omega}^{-1} \mu ) \sim \mathrm{chi2}(N)$; use only if the task asks.

atoms.title: Newey-West (1987) HAC standard errors (OLS and sample mean) and the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (1989) test / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- NW is consistent as T grows with L growing slowly; in small samples with persistent series it understates the variance
  (our AR(1) simulations: coverage of nominal 95% intervals well below 95% when autocorrelation is strong and L is small).
- GRS is exact only under iid normal errors and traded factors; with non-normal or autocorrelated errors use a GMM/HAC Wald test.
