atoms.title: PCA risk factors, exposures and neutralization / overview
atoms.text:
# PCA risk factors, exposures and neutralization

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this reference for linear principal components of returns or curve changes, and for hedging exposures to a selected component subspace. Ordinary PCA does not estimate characteristic-dependent loadings in an instrumented latent-factor model.

atoms.title: PCA risk factors, exposures and neutralization / Meaning of the input
atoms.text:
## Meaning of the input

Let Y have T time observations and n assets or maturities. Decide whether entries represent levels, changes or returns. Covariance PCA centers columns; correlation PCA also divides each by its standard deviation. Those are different risk questions. Match the task's units, covariance divisor and sign convention; none is determined by the word PCA alone.

For an inference or investment exercise, the estimation sample determines the mean and axes; full-sample axes applied to earlier dates do not constitute a causal out-of-sample strategy.

atoms.title: PCA risk factors, exposures and neutralization / Covariance principal components
atoms.text:
## Covariance principal components

Here mean(Y) denotes the row vector of column means, Z is centered data, d is the selected positive covariance divisor, and $v_{j}$ is a unit column vector. I denotes an identity matrix.

**Centered observations and covariance**

$$
\begin{gathered}
Z = Y - 1\cdot \operatorname{mean}(Y) \\
C = Z'\cdot Z/d
\end{gathered}
$$

**Ordered component axes**

$$
\begin{gathered}
C\cdot v_{j} = \lambda _{j}\cdot v_{j} \\
\lambda _{1} \ge  \lambda _{2} \ge  \ldots  \ge  0 \\
v_{i}'\cdot v_{j} = \operatorname{indicator}(i=j)
\end{gathered}
$$

For singular values $s_{j}$ of Z, the covariance eigenvalues equal $s_{j}$ squared divided by d. PCA of the original centered observations and this covariance eigendecomposition describe the same axes. Feeding C as if it were an observation matrix to a routine that centers its input describes a different problem.

**Scores and explained variance fractions**

$$
\begin{gathered}
f_{j} = Z\cdot v_{j} \\
\mathrm{variance}_{\mathrm{fraction},j} = \lambda _{j}/\sum _{l} \lambda _{l}
\end{gathered}
$$

The denominator includes every covariance eigenvalue, not only the retained ones. If total variance is zero, these fractions are undefined. “Loadings” may mean unit axes or axes multiplied by square roots of eigenvalues; identify the convention before calculating exposure.

atoms.title: PCA risk factors, exposures and neutralization / Sign, scaling and identification
atoms.text:
## Sign, scaling and identification

An eigenvector may change sign if its score changes sign with it. Repeated eigenvalues identify a subspace rather than unique individual axes. A sign convention is applied per component: flip component k (and its scores) exactly when its own reference quantity, for example the sum of its loadings or its exposure at a stated maturity, is negative. Never flip all components together. Explained-variance shares are unchanged by any flip. A sign convention cannot make a mixed-sign vector have only positive entries; level, slope and curvature interpretations are empirical descriptions.

If all input values are multiplied by a constant a, covariance eigenvalues scale by a squared. Fractions and the eigenspaces are unchanged. Standardizing columns separately generally changes those spaces. Z-normalizing columns before PCA (a correlation-matrix PCA): when the task does not name the divisor, the convention is the population standard deviation (ddof=0), as scikit-learn `StandardScaler` and `scipy.stats.zscore` use; pandas `DataFrame.std()` divides by $n-1$ and scales every score by $\sqrt{(n-1)/n}$ (about 1.3 % for $n = 40$). Pass ddof explicitly and use the same choice in every window. Whitening rescales scores to unit variance and therefore changes what a coefficient on a score means.

atoms.title: PCA risk factors, exposures and neutralization / Portfolio exposure
atoms.text:
## Portfolio exposure

Let V contain k retained unit axes as columns and w be n portfolio weights. Assume returns are measured consistently across assets.

**Retained-factor reconstruction**

$$
Z_{\mathrm{retained}} = (Z\cdot V)\cdot V'
$$

**Portfolio coefficients on the retained scores**

$$
\begin{gathered}
b_{\mathrm{portfolio}} = V'\cdot w \\
Z_{\mathrm{retained}}\cdot w = (Z\cdot V)\cdot b_{\mathrm{portfolio}}
\end{gathered}
$$

The portfolio's mean return comes from mean(Y)*w, not from the centered scores alone. Zero exposure to retained axes leaves unmodeled covariance risk and does not guarantee a lower realized variance or a higher Sharpe ratio after additional constraints.

atoms.title: PCA risk factors, exposures and neutralization / Minimum-size hedge with linear constraints
atoms.text:
## Minimum-size hedge with linear constraints

Use this block when a hedge h must neutralize specified exposures while preserving selected linear quantities. Write $A\cdot h=b$ for those constraints. For example, a row of ones with right-hand side zero preserves the sum of portfolio weights. A superscript + denotes the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse.

**Minimum Euclidean-norm feasible hedge**

$$
h = A^{+}\cdot b
$$

This gives an exact constrained hedge only if b lies in the column space of A. Otherwise it is a minimum-norm least-squares residual solution, not a neutral portfolio. For independent rows the same feasible solution is A'*(A*A')^(-1)*b. Position limits, trading costs and a covariance-weighted objective define different optimization problems.

**Exposure and budget residual check**

$$
\mathrm{constraint}_{\mathrm{residual}} = A\cdot h-b
$$

Check the actual residual and numerical rank. Dependent constraints may be consistent or inconsistent; counting equations alone does not decide feasibility. Replacing V by V*Q for orthogonal Q, and transforming exposures consistently, preserves the hedge against that subspace.

atoms.title: PCA risk factors, exposures and neutralization / Neutrality after scaling, clipping and turnover control
atoms.text:
## Neutrality after scaling, clipping and turnover control

Let $B$ be the current asset-by-exposure matrix, possibly including a column of ones. For common asset ordering, the orthogonal projection onto its neutral subspace is:

$$
P=I-B(B'B)^+B',\qquad B'Pw=0.
$$

The pseudoinverse handles dependent exposure columns; numerical rank still matters. Any common scalar multiple of a neutral vector stays neutral. Thus dividing a nonzero neutral vector by its gross exposure preserves linear neutrality, but can violate position limits or a turnover cap. If gross exposure is zero, that normalization is undefined.

For old holdings $w_{\mathrm{old}}$ and a neutral target $w_{\mathrm{target}}$, consider a turnover-controlled blend with $0\le a\le1$:

$$
w(a)=(1-a)w_{\mathrm{old}}+a w_{\mathrm{target}},\qquad
B'w(a)=(1-a)B'w_{\mathrm{old}}.
$$

The blend stays neutral only if the right side is zero. In particular, a portfolio neutral to an earlier exposure matrix need not be neutral to today's $B$. Align old and new positions on one declared universe; an omitted exiting position is not zero turnover.

For the one-way convention, the blend's turnover from the old allocation is:

$$
\frac12\lVert w(a)-w_{\mathrm{old}}\rVert_1
=a\,\frac12\lVert w_{\mathrm{target}}-w_{\mathrm{old}}\rVert_1.
$$

This identity precedes any further projection, clipping or gross normalization. Those subsequent transformations can change turnover again. Componentwise clipping generally destroys linear neutrality; repeated projection and clipping is not automatically the solution of a constrained allocation problem. A prescribed sequence of transformations defines its own portfolio and should not be replaced by an extra normalization intended to improve one diagnostic. These are algebraic properties, not a guarantee of lower realized risk.

atoms.title: PCA risk factors, exposures and neutralization / Yield interpretation
atoms.text:
## Yield interpretation

PCA of yield changes measures co-movement, not a term-premium decomposition. Par rates generally are not zero rates. If a stated approximation treats them as zero yields z(t) with continuous compounding, the finite-interval forward is an average over the interval, not an instantaneous forward.

**Continuously compounded forward over an interval**

$$
f_{a,b} = (b\cdot z(b)-a\cdot z(a))/(b-a)
$$

Both endpoints use a common time unit, and rates retain their input scale. The instantaneous rate is the derivative of t*z(t), obtained only as the interval shrinks under differentiability.

atoms.title: PCA risk factors, exposures and neutralization / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources

[Scikit-learn PCA documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/decomposition.html#pca), for centering, scaling and SVD semantics. Jolliffe and Cadima (2016), [Principal component analysis: a review and recent developments](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.2015.0202), for PCA terminology and covariance/SVD equivalence. Portfolio exposure, unit transformation and constrained-hedge formulas above are direct linear-algebra derivations; they do not assert an empirical performance improvement.

atoms.title: Perpetual funding carry: cash flows, rate units and mean reversion / overview
atoms.text:
# Perpetual funding carry: cash flows, rate units and mean reversion

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this note for periodic funding payments and carry from a spot/perpetual hedge. Distinguish a funding-rate-only return model from the complete trade P&L. Settlement timing, notional definition, return denominator and estimation conventions follow the contract.

atoms.title: Perpetual funding carry: cash flows, rate units and mean reversion / Funding cash flows
atoms.text:
## Funding cash flows

Let $f_{j}$ be a decimal funding rate at settlement j and $N_{j}$ the positive position notional in settlement currency. Under the positive-long-pays convention, the short receives the following cash flow.

$$
\mathrm{cash}_{\mathrm{short},j} = N_{j}\cdot f_{j}
$$

The long has the opposite cash flow. The signed funding rate and the signed fee shown in an account ledger need not use the same sign convention. One basis point is an absolute $0.0001$ in decimal rate units, or $0.01\%$, not a relative fraction of the current rate.

For constant notional N and capital denominator N, simple accumulated funding return is additive.

$$
R_{\mathrm{funding}} = \sum _{j} f_{j}
$$

For varying notionals or a different capital denominator C, the cash-flow return changes.

$$
R_{\mathrm{cash}} = \sum _{j} N_{j}\cdot f_{j} / C
$$

Thus funding return on notional differs from return on posted margin. Spot/perpetual basis movement, financing, trading fees, slippage and liquidation exposure remain in the complete trade even if the price $\delta$ is approximately hedged. Positive expected funding alone does not imply a riskless arbitrage.

With A settlements per year and H included settlements, a simple annualized rate is a rescaling, not compounded wealth growth.

$$
R_{\mathrm{annual}} = (A/H)\cdot R_{\mathrm{funding}}
$$

Settlement indices decide whether the known initial rate is included; phrases such as starting rate and first realized payment must refer to the same convention.

atoms.title: Perpetual funding carry: cash flows, rate units and mean reversion / OU estimation conventions
Perpetual funding carry: cash flows, rate units and mean reversion / Risk of accumulated funding
atoms.text:
## Risk of accumulated funding

For a covariance-stationary sequence with autocovariance $\gamma _{l}$ at lag l, the variance of the H-settlement sum includes cross-period dependence.

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\sum _{j=1}^{H} f_{j}) = H\cdot \gamma _{0} + 2\cdot \sum _{l=1}^{H-1} (H-l)\cdot \gamma _{l}
$$

The iid simplification retains only $H\gamma_0$. Positive weighted autocovariances increase the true sum variance; negative ones can decrease it. The variance of the mean divides this sum variance by H^2. These stationary formulas do not describe the initial transient conditional on a fixed $f_{0}$.

Loss is minus return. Quantile loss, a loss quantile floored at zero, and the mean strictly above that threshold are distinct risk definitions. A strict tail can be empty; it must not silently become a zero empirical estimate.

atoms.title: Perpetual funding carry: cash flows, rate units and mean reversion / Sources and scope
atoms.text:
## Sources and scope

[Bybit, Funding Fee Calculation](https://www.bybit.com/en/help-center/article/Funding-fee-calculation?category=cd60af6303161fd598) documents the payer direction, notional-based fee and contract-dependent settlement intervals. It is an example of an exchange convention, not a substitute for another venue's rules. OU mappings and the variance-of-sums identity are algebraic consequences of the SDE transition and covariance expansion. No specific funding cadence or fixed risk threshold is assumed here.

atoms.title: Holdings-based return attribution / overview
atoms.text:
# Holdings-based return attribution

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this entry to explain a portfolio's return relative to a benchmark through category allocation and within-category selection. This is a holdings-based accounting decomposition, not a regression estimate of factor exposures or a variance decomposition. Categories may be sectors, countries or asset classes.

Map the notation to the contract's definitions. Explicit conventions for rebalancing, cash, return measurement and multiperiod aggregation take precedence. Returns and weights below are decimal quantities; one unit of return equals 10,000 basis points.

atoms.title: Holdings-based return attribution / 1. What the weights and returns measure
atoms.text:
## 1. What the weights and returns measure

For one period, let $\mathrm{wP}_{i}$ and $\mathrm{wB}_{i}$ be the category's portfolio and benchmark weights at the period's beginning. Include cash and financing where applicable so both complete weight sets sum to one. Let $\mathrm{rP}_{i}$ and $\mathrm{rB}_{i}$ be the returns of the respective holdings within category i; these need not be the same even when the category labels agree. Let RP and RB be total portfolio and benchmark returns.

**Within-category return, for nonzero category weight $W_{i}$.** Security j has whole-portfolio weight $a_{j}$ and simple return $r_{j}$. Dividing by the category weight distinguishes a category return from its contribution to the whole portfolio.

$$
\begin{gathered}
W_{i} = \sum _{j \in  \mathrm{category} i} a_{j} \\
r_{i} = \sum _{j \in  \mathrm{category} i} a_{j}\cdot r_{j} / W_{i}
\end{gathered}
$$

When $W_{i}$ is zero, this quotient is undefined. A reference return convention is needed for any attribution term still involving that category. A zero contribution alone does not identify its hypothetical return.

**Portfolio return from category contributions.**

$$
\mathrm{RP} = \sum _{i} \mathrm{wP}_{i}\cdot \mathrm{rP}_{i}
$$

**Benchmark return from its own holdings.** A convenient market index is not interchangeable with a specified weighted benchmark.

$$
\mathrm{RB} = \sum _{i} \mathrm{wB}_{i}\cdot \mathrm{rB}_{i}
$$

atoms.title: Holdings-based return attribution / 2. Single-period Brinson–Fachler attribution
atoms.text:
## 2. Single-period Brinson–Fachler attribution

Use the following three-effect form when separating allocation, selection and their interaction. Other variants may combine selection and interaction; the labels alone do not establish which definition is intended. These identities assume comparable simple returns over the same period, with any costs treated consistently.

**Allocation effect $A_{i}$: overweighting a category relative to the benchmark's total return.**

$$
A_{i} = (\mathrm{wP}_{i}-\mathrm{wB}_{i})\cdot (\mathrm{rB}_{i}-\mathrm{RB})
$$

**Selection effect $S_{i}$: different holdings' performance at benchmark category weight.**

$$
S_{i} = \mathrm{wB}_{i}\cdot (\mathrm{rP}_{i}-\mathrm{rB}_{i})
$$

**Interaction effect $I_{i}$: allocation and selection differences together.**

$$
I_{i} = (\mathrm{wP}_{i}-\mathrm{wB}_{i})\cdot (\mathrm{rP}_{i}-\mathrm{rB}_{i})
$$

**Reconciliation to arithmetic active return for this period.** This follows by expansion and $\sum _{i}(\mathrm{wP}_{i}-\mathrm{wB}_{i})=0$, not by a fitted residual.

$$
\sum _{i} (A_{i}+S_{i}+I_{i}) = \mathrm{RP}-\mathrm{RB}
$$

The uncentered Brinson allocation expression uses $\mathrm{rB}_{i}$ instead of $\mathrm{rB}_i-\mathrm{RB}$. Its total allocation equals the centered total when both weight sets sum to one, but its category allocation contributions differ. Do not mix the two category definitions within a report.

**Off-benchmark cash under an explicit common cash-return convention.** If $\mathrm{wB}_{c}=0$ and $\mathrm{rB}_{c}=\mathrm{rP}_{c}=r_{\mathrm{cash}}$, the cash selection and interaction vanish. This conclusion requires the return convention; zero benchmark weight alone only forces selection to zero.

$$
\begin{gathered}
A_{c} = \mathrm{wP}_{c}\cdot (r_{\mathrm{cash}}-\mathrm{RB}) \\
S_{c} = 0 \\
I_{c} = 0
\end{gathered}
$$

atoms.title: Holdings-based return attribution / 3. Return timing and drifting weights
atoms.text:
## 3. Return timing and drifting weights

Use start-of-period weights to attribute the returns earned during that period. Under buy-and-hold within a period, with no external flows, trades or unmodelled fees, each position's wealth changes by its own gross return. Let $w_{i}$ be its initial weight and $r_{i}$ its holding return, with positive total ending wealth.

**Ending weight before any new rebalance.** This is also the next period's initial weight if no intervening trade occurs.

$$
w_{i,\mathrm{end}} = w_{i}\cdot (1+r_{i}) / (1+\sum _{j} w_{j}\cdot r_{j})
$$

A rebalance sets the subsequent weights to the new allocation; it does not retroactively change the weights that earned earlier returns. External flows require a flow-adjusted return convention.

**Simple total return from a total-return index J.** Both endpoints must refer to the same holding and consecutive period boundaries.

$$
r_{t} = J_{t}/J_{t-1}-1
$$

Ordinary price changes exclude distributions unless adjusted appropriately. Annualized cash quotes also need the stated accrual convention: simple rate times year fraction and effective-rate compounding are different definitions.

When beginning-of-period weights are stored in a table or dict keyed by period-end dates, the entry labelled with the end of period $m$ holds the weights at the start of period $m$; the weights at the beginning of $m$ are that entry, not the one labelled with the end of $m-1$. Check that a reported weight snapshot for period $m$ equals the weights used for period $m$'s effects, for example `assert all(np.isclose(snapshot[k], weights_used[m][k]) for k in snapshot)`.

atoms.title: Holdings-based return attribution / 4. Multiperiod meaning
atoms.text:
## 4. Multiperiod meaning

Let $\mathrm{RP}_{t}$ and $\mathrm{RB}_{t}$ be successive period returns; $A_{it}$, $S_{it}$ and $I_{it}$ are period attribution effects.

**Compounded portfolio return.**

$$
\mathrm{RP}_{\mathrm{total}} = \prod _{t} (1+\mathrm{RP}_{t})-1
$$

**Compounded benchmark return.**

$$
\mathrm{RB}_{\mathrm{total}} = \prod _{t} (1+\mathrm{RB}_{t})-1
$$

**Unlinked sums of effects explain the sum of period active returns.**

$$
\sum _{t} \sum _{i} (A_{it}+S_{it}+I_{it}) = \sum _{t} (\mathrm{RP}_{t}-\mathrm{RB}_{t})
$$

The right side generally differs from $\mathrm{RP}_{\mathrm{total}}$-$\mathrm{RB}_{\mathrm{total}}$. If unlinked period sums are requested, they remain unlinked sums. To explain compounded active return with linked effects requires a stated linking method; it is not achieved by relabelling the simple sums. Different linking conventions can allocate compounding differently, even when each reconciles overall.

atoms.title: Holdings-based return attribution / 5. Checks and scope
atoms.text:
## 5. Checks and scope

Identical portfolio and benchmark holdings and weights give zero active return and zero effects. Equal category weights eliminate allocation and interaction. Equal within-category returns eliminate selection and interaction. Wealth-based drift preserves total weight one under the assumptions above.

A return attribution identity does not imply causality or investment skill. This entry does not cover currency overlays, derivatives with exposure weights different from capital weights, or a complete fee attribution model.

atoms.title: Holdings-based return attribution / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources

[MathWorks, Brinson model documentation, “More About”](https://www.mathworks.com/help/finance/brinsonattribution.html): the centered three-effect identity and distinction between period attribution and linked multiperiod results. Labels here are A/S/I rather than the documentation's S/I/U.

[Lu and Kane (2013), Performance Attribution for Equity Portfolios, §3](https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RJ-2013-025/): holdings-based Brinson interpretation and uncentered allocation convention. Within-category returns above are explicitly normalized by category weight; they are not whole-portfolio contributions. The weight-drift and reconciliation formulas follow directly from wealth accounting and algebra.

atoms.title: Delta-gamma-vega risk: units, covariance and variance allocation / overview
atoms.text:
# Delta-gamma-vega risk: units, covariance and variance allocation

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use a local price expansion to relate market-factor shocks to portfolio P&L. Explicit contract definitions determine shock horizon, units and allocation convention. A local expansion is unreliable across a barrier crossing, discontinuity or large market move.

atoms.title: Delta-gamma-vega risk: units, covariance and variance allocation / Local portfolio response
atoms.text:
## Local portfolio response

For factor increments $x$, define $a$ as portfolio first derivatives, symmetric $G$ as portfolio second derivatives, and $c$ as deterministic carry. Derivatives include signed position sizes. The second-order P&L approximation is:

$$
Y=c+a'x+\frac12x'Gx
$$

For spot and annualized volatility as separate factors, their linear coefficients are position-scaled Delta and Vega. The spot diagonal of $G$ is position-scaled Gamma. A return shock must first be converted to a spot increment, approximately $\Delta S=S r$ for a small simple return. A volatility shock is an absolute change in annualized decimal volatility, not a percent return on volatility.

atoms.title: Delta-gamma-vega risk: units, covariance and variance allocation / Gaussian shock moments
atoms.text:
## Gaussian shock moments

When the task names the model volatility as the input for pricing and risk, take the spot shock from it: for a one-day horizon $\sigma_{S} = S\,\sigma_{\mathrm{model}}/\sqrt{252}$ with an annualized $\sigma_{\mathrm{model}}$. Sample moments of historical price changes are a different input. Under the Gaussian model below the gamma term contributes $\operatorname{Var}(\tfrac12\Gamma\Delta S^{2}) = \tfrac12\Gamma^{2}\sigma_{S}^{4}$; an empirical variance of $\Delta S^{2}$ from fat-tailed history is larger and changes every variance share.

Assume $x\sim N(m,C)$ and set $b=a+Gm$. Gaussian odd centered moments vanish; paired fourth moments give the mean and variance:

$$
\operatorname{E}[Y]=c+a'm+\frac12m'Gm+\frac12\sum_i(GC)_{ii}
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=b'Cb+\frac12\sum_i(GCGC)_{ii}
$$

With centered spot and volatility shocks, $\operatorname{Cov}((\Delta S)^2,\Delta S)=\operatorname{Cov}((\Delta S)^2,\Delta\sigma)=0$ under joint normality. Linear Delta and Vega components can still covary. Non-Gaussian shocks can introduce all these covariances.

atoms.title: Delta-gamma-vega risk: units, covariance and variance allocation / Component allocation
atoms.text:
## Component allocation

Let $Y_j$ denote a specified additive P&L component and $Y=\sum_jY_j$; constant carry has zero variance. Covariance allocation splits every pair covariance equally between its two components:

$$
A_j=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_j,Y),\qquad
\sum_j A_j=\operatorname{Var}(Y)
$$

For strictly positive total variance, its shares sum to one:

$$
p_j=\frac{A_j}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}
$$

A share can be negative when a component hedges the others. Standalone ratios $\operatorname{Var}(Y_j)/\operatorname{Var}(Y)$ need not sum to one. Under this convention, Euler contributions to portfolio standard deviation are $A_j/\operatorname{sd}(Y)$. They differ from variance allocations and from generic quantile allocations; an explicitly specified alternative must retain its own definition.

atoms.title: Delta-gamma-vega risk: units, covariance and variance allocation / Horizon and quantiles
atoms.text:
## Horizon and quantiles

If $v_t$ is an annualized conditional-volatility series observed daily, $\operatorname{sd}(v_t-v_{t-1})$ already measures daily shocks in annualized-volatility units. Annualizing that shock standard deviation by $\sqrt{B}$ and converting back to a one-day shock divides by the same $\sqrt{B}$; do not apply the second conversion to a quantity never annualized.

A moment-matched normal approximation for loss $L=-Y$ gives:

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_q(L)\approx-\operatorname{E}[Y]+\Phi^{-1}(q)\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}
$$

A quadratic function of normal factors is generally not normal. This quantile is an approximation, not an exact consequence of the moment formulas. Fitted physical variance, risk-neutral pricing volatility and volatility-shock variance are different quantities.

atoms.title: Delta-gamma-vega risk: units, covariance and variance allocation / References
atoms.text:
## References

[Tasche, Capital Allocation: the Euler Principle](https://arxiv.org/abs/0708.2542), homogeneous risk allocation. Gaussian moments above are direct consequences of the stated local model and normal second/fourth moments; covariance closure follows by bilinearity, without assuming independence.

atoms.title: Range-based (OHLC) volatility: Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang / overview
atoms.text:
# Range-based (OHLC) volatility: Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

atoms.title: Range-based (OHLC) volatility: Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang / Model and setting
atoms.text:
## Model and setting
- During trading the log price is a Brownian motion with constant vol $\sigma$ and drift $\mu$ (geometric Brownian motion for the price),
  monitored continuously. Each period $i$ (usually a day) has open $O_{i}$, high $H_{i}$, low $L_{i}$, close $C_{i}$; $C_{i-1}$ is the previous close.
- Between $C_{i-1}$ and $O_{i}$ the market is closed. Each log return is named by its start and end price (cc = previous close to close, co = previous close to open, oc = open to close):
  close-to-close return $r_{cc,i} = \ln (C_{i} / C_{i-1})$;
  overnight (opening-jump) return $r_{co,i} = \ln (O_{i} / C_{i-1})$;
  open-to-close (intraday) return $r_{oc,i} = \ln (C_{i} / O_{i})$.
  Identity for every period: $r_{cc,i} = r_{co,i} + r_{oc,i}$. So $r_{oc,i} = r_{cc,i}$ only when there is no opening gap ($O_{i} = C_{i-1}$); on real data they differ every day.
- Normalized high and low relative to the open: $u_{i} = \ln (H_{i}/O_{i}) \ge  0$, $d_{i} = \ln (L_{i}/O_{i}) \le  0$.

atoms.title: Range-based (OHLC) volatility: Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $O, H, L, C$ | open, high, low, close of one period (prices, not returns) | price |
| $r_{cc}, r_{co}, r_{oc}, u, d$ | log ratios defined above (natural log) | log units |
| $n$ | number of periods in the window ($r_{cc}$ and $r_{co}$ need the previous close, so the first row has none) | count |
| $f$ | fraction of the full period (close to close) during which the market is closed | none |
| $\operatorname{P}$ | periods per year for annualization (from the task; commonly 252 for daily bars) | $1/\mathrm{year}$ |

atoms.title: Range-based (OHLC) volatility: Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang / Per-period variance estimators
atoms.text:
## Per-period variance estimators
Close-to-close (the classical benchmark; uses closes only, includes the overnight part):

$$
r_{cc}^{2}, \quad r_{cc} = \ln (C_{i}/C_{i-1}) \quad \text{(not } r_{oc} = \ln (C_{i}/O_{i})\text{)}
$$

Window form: either the zero-mean form $(1/n) \sum_{i} r_{cc,i}^{2}$ or the sample variance $(1/(n-1)) \sum_{i} (r_{cc,i} - \operatorname{mean}(r_{cc}))^{2}$; use the one the task describes.

The range estimators below (Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell) estimate the variance of the open-to-close return $r_{oc}$ only; they use the same-period open, never the previous close.

Parkinson (1980):

$$
\sigma ^{2}_{\operatorname{P}} = (u - d)^{2} / (4 \ln  2) = [\ln (H/L)]^{2} / (4 \ln  2)
$$

Garman–Klass (1980), practical:

$$
\sigma ^{2}_{\mathrm{GK}} = 0.5 (u - d)^{2} - (2 \ln  2 - 1) r_{oc}^{2}
$$

Garman–Klass best analytic:

$$
\sigma ^{2}_{\mathrm{GK}^{*}} = 0.511 (u - d)^{2} - 0.019 [r_{oc} (u + d) - 2 u d] - 0.383 r_{oc}^{2}
$$

Rogers–Satchell (1991):

$$
\sigma ^{2}_{\mathrm{RS}} = u (u - r_{oc}) + d (d - r_{oc}) = \ln (H/C) \ln (H/O) + \ln (L/C) \ln (L/O)
$$

Garman-Klass with an opening jump (targets the full close-to-close variance; overnight treated as diffusion over fraction $f$):

$$
\sigma ^{2}_{\mathrm{GKo}} = a r_{co}^{2} / f + (1 - a) \sigma ^{2}_{\mathrm{GK}^{*}} / (1 - f)
$$

Variance-minimizing weight from Garman–Klass:

$$
a = 0.12
$$

atoms.title: Range-based (OHLC) volatility: Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang / Multi-period estimate and annualization
atoms.text:
## Multi-period estimate and annualization
- Window of $n$ periods: $\sigma ^{2} = (1/n) \sum _{i} \sigma ^{2}_{i}$ (mean of the per-period VARIANCES), annualized variance = $P\sigma^2$,
  annualized vol = $\sqrt{\operatorname{P} \cdot \sigma ^{2}}$. Do not average per-period volatilities, and do not annualize with $\operatorname{P}$ instead of $\sqrt{\operatorname{P}}$ on a vol.
- Yang-Zhang (2000), window of $n \ge  2$ periods, estimates the variance of the full close-to-close return (overnight + intraday):
Overnight returns, demeaned:

$$
V_{O} = (1/(n-1)) \sum _{i} (r_{co,i} - \operatorname{mean}(r_{co}))^{2}
$$

Open-to-close returns, demeaned:

$$
V_{C} = (1/(n-1)) \sum _{i} (r_{oc,i} - \operatorname{mean}(r_{oc}))^{2}
$$

$$
V_{\mathrm{RS}} = (1/n) \sum _{i} \sigma ^{2}_{\mathrm{RS},i}
$$

$$
k = (\alpha  - 1) / (\alpha  + (n + 1)/(n - 1))
$$

Yang–Zhang suggest $\alpha  = 1.34$, i.e.

$$
k = 0.34 / (1.34 + (n+1)/(n-1))
$$

$$
\sigma ^{2}_{\mathrm{YZ}} = V_{O} + k V_{C} + (1 - k) V_{\mathrm{RS}}
$$

  Rolling windows apply the whole formula (with its own means and $k$) inside each window.

atoms.title: Range-based (OHLC) volatility: Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang / Properties (continuous monitoring; verified by simulation, see Applicability)
atoms.text:
## Properties (continuous monitoring; verified by simulation, see Applicability)
| estimator | unbiased, no drift | unbiased with drift | handles opening jump | efficiency vs close-to-close $r_{cc}^{2}$ (no drift, no gap) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parkinson | yes | no (biased up) | no | about 4.9 (often quoted 5.2) |
| Garman-Klass (both forms) | yes | no (biased up, less than Parkinson) | no | about 7.4 |
| Rogers-Satchell | yes | yes | no | about 6.0 |
| Garman-Klass with jump | yes | no | yes (needs $f$) | about 8.4 |
| Yang-Zhang | yes | yes | yes | about 7 to 8 vs the demeaned close-to-close sample variance |
Efficiency = Var(benchmark) / Var(estimator) for the same number of periods.

Efficiency compares estimators of the variance. With rolling windows, form for every estimator the series of window variance estimates $\sigma^{2}_{w}$ (all on the same scale, daily or annualized), then $\mathrm{Efficiency} = \operatorname{Var}(\sigma^{2}_{w,\mathrm{benchmark}}) / \operatorname{Var}(\sigma^{2}_{w,\mathrm{estimator}})$, using the same windows and the same sample-variance definition for each series. The same ratio computed on the rolling volatility series $\sigma_{w} = \sqrt{\sigma^{2}_{w}}$ is a different number ($\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt{X}) \approx \operatorname{Var}(X) / (4 \operatorname{E}[X])$ brings in each estimator's mean level), so it does not replace the variance-based ratio. Rolling volatility is the series to report or plot; the efficiency uses the variance series.

atoms.title: Range-based (OHLC) volatility: Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang / Variants and common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Variants and common mistakes
- Parkinson uses $\ln (H/L)$ of the SAME period, squared, divided by $4 \ln  2 (= 2.7726\ldots )$; not $\ln (H/O)$, not log10, not divided inside a square root twice.
- Two different returns, never interchangeable: the close-to-close estimator uses $r_{cc} = \ln (C_{i}/C_{i-1})$ (previous close); Garman-Klass and Rogers-Satchell use $r_{oc} = \ln (C_{i}/O_{i})$ (same-period open). Rogers-Satchell needs all four prices of the same period.
- Check in your code: (1) each estimator reads the return its formula names: close-to-close and the Yang-Zhang overnight term need a shift of the close series by one row, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell and the Yang-Zhang open-to-close term do not; (2) one variable or column name per return ($r_{cc}$, $r_{co}$, $r_{oc}$), never one name such as `c` reused for two of them; (3) on the data, $r_{cc}$ equals $r_{co} + r_{oc}$ row by row and differs from $r_{oc}$ on days with an opening gap; if your close-to-close series equals your open-to-close series, it was built from the wrong prices.
- Opening gaps: Parkinson, Garman-Klass and Rogers-Satchell measure only open-to-close variance. If the target is close-to-close vol, add the overnight part (Yang-Zhang, or Garman-Klass with an opening jump);
  otherwise vol is understated by the overnight share of variance.
- Yang-Zhang: $n$ is the number of periods (overnight returns), not the number of prices; $V_{O}$ and $V_{C}$ are demeaned with $n-1$; $V_{\mathrm{RS}}$ is a plain mean.
  Some sources write $k$ with $T/(T-2)$ where $T$ counts prices; check which count the task uses.
- Yang-Zhang weights: $k$ multiplies $V_{C}$ and $1-k$ multiplies $V_{\mathrm{RS}}$; $V_{O}$ enters with weight 1. With $\alpha = 1.34$, $k$ rises from 0.078 at $n = 2$ toward $0.34/2.34 \approx 0.145$ as $n$ grows, so $V_{\mathrm{RS}}$ always carries most of the intraday weight.
  Two slips put a weight near 1 on $V_{C}$ and make Yang-Zhang about as noisy as close-to-close (its rolling efficiency can then fall below 1):
  writing $k = (n-1)/n$, and swapping $k$ and $1-k$ (that is, $k V_{\mathrm{RS}} + (1-k) V_{C}$). Also check the inputs: $V_{C}$ is built from $r_{oc}$, not $r_{cc}$, and the overnight term uses the previous close, $\ln(O_{i}/C_{i-1})$, not the previous open.
- Rogers-Satchell pairs each extreme with itself: $\ln(H/C)\ln(H/O) + \ln(L/C)\ln(L/O) \ge 0$ for every period. The cross pairing $\ln(H/O)\ln(L/O) + \ln(H/C)\ln(L/C)$ is $\le 0$ and is not a variance.
- Sanity check after computing rolling efficiencies: on ordinary daily data every range estimator, Yang-Zhang included, is expected to have a smaller rolling variance than close-to-close. A ratio below 1 for one of them almost always means its formula was built wrongly; recheck it before writing outputs.
- Output units: per-period vs annualized, variance vs volatility, decimal vs percent (30% is 0.30).

atoms.title: Range-based (OHLC) volatility: Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- All formulas assume continuous monitoring. Highs/lows from a finite number of trades or bars understate the true range, so range estimators are
  biased DOWN (simulation with a GBM sampled at only a few hundred points per period: about 6 to 9% low; with fewer points, more).
- Drift bias of Parkinson and Garman-Klass grows with $(\mu/\sigma)^2$ per period: negligible for daily bars of ordinary assets, large for long periods or strong trends.
- Simulation check (exact Brownian-bridge highs/lows): every estimator was within 0.4% of its target in the cases where the table says unbiased;
  Parkinson / Garman-Klass were +9% / +3.5% high at drift 0.5 $\sigma$ per period and +38% / +14% at drift 1 $\sigma$; Rogers-Satchell stayed within 0.2%;
  intraday-only estimators missed exactly the overnight share; the variance-minimizing $k$ from simulation matched the formula $k$ within 0.02.
- Stochastic volatility, jumps inside the period, and bid-ask bounce in $H$ and $L$ are not handled.

atoms.title: Range-based (OHLC) volatility: Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources
Parkinson (1980) J. Business 53(1):61-65; Garman & Klass (1980) J. Business 53(1):67-78; Rogers & Satchell (1991)
Annals of Applied Probability 1(4):504-512; Yang & Zhang (2000) J. Business 73(3):477-491.

atoms.title: Rate caplets and floorlets: fixing, payment and Black pricing / overview
atoms.text:
# Rate caplets and floorlets: fixing, payment and Black pricing

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this reference for European options on a single rate fixing and sums of such options into caps or floors. It distinguishes the option's uncertainty horizon from its payment date and accrual fraction. It does not value an option on a compounded realized rate by simply treating that payoff as a single term-rate fixing.

atoms.title: Rate caplets and floorlets: fixing, payment and Black pricing / 1. Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared Foundations

Map notation by meaning and units, following explicit contract conventions. Let v be today, $T_{f}$ the fixing date, $T_{p}$ the payment date, $\tau$ the year fraction from v to $T_{f}$, and $\delta >0$ the underlying coupon accrual fraction. The payment discount factor is $D=\operatorname{P}_{d}(v,T_{p})>0$, not a discount factor to $T_{f}$. $N\ge 0$ is notional, K the strike rate and F the projected fixing under the payment-date pricing measure. Rates are decimals. Values below are for a long option; a short position reverses their sign.

For an unfixed positive rate, Black's model assumes a lognormal fixing with total log variance w. Constant annual volatility $\sigma$ gives:

$$
w = \sigma ^{2}\cdot \tau
$$

The rate at fixing, expressed using a standard normal Z under that pricing measure, is:

$$
L_{\mathrm{fix}} = F\cdot \exp (-w/2+\sqrt{w}\cdot Z)
$$

This construction has mean F. A projection-curve quantity requires appropriate calibration/measure interpretation before being treated as F; do not add a second spot-to-forward drift to it.

atoms.title: Rate caplets and floorlets: fixing, payment and Black pricing / 2. Payoffs and pricing
atoms.text:
## 2. Payoffs and pricing

The caplet pays the excess of the fixed rate over strike at $T_{p}$.

$$
\;\text{payoff}\;_{\mathrm{caplet}} = N\cdot \delta \cdot \max (L_{\mathrm{fix}}-K,0)
$$

The floorlet pays the shortfall below strike at the same date.

$$
\;\text{payoff}\;_{\mathrm{floorlet}} = N\cdot \delta \cdot \max (K-L_{\mathrm{fix}},0)
$$

For $F>0, K>0$ and $w>0$, the normal-CDF arguments are:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{d1} = (\ln (F/K)+w/2)/\sqrt{w} \\
\mathrm{d2} = \mathrm{d1}-\sqrt{w}
\end{gathered}
$$

Writing $\Phi$ for the standard normal CDF, integration of the positive payoff gives the caplet value [1].

$$
V_{\mathrm{caplet}} = N\cdot \delta \cdot D\cdot (F\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d1})-K\cdot \Phi (\mathrm{d2}))
$$

The floorlet value follows from the complementary payoff region [1].

$$
V_{\mathrm{floorlet}} = N\cdot \delta \cdot D\cdot (K\cdot \Phi (-\mathrm{d2})-F\cdot \Phi (-\mathrm{d1}))
$$

Total variance w already includes the time horizon. It must not receive a second multiplication by $\tau$. Annual volatility is dimensionless per square root year, whereas $\delta$ scales the coupon amount and may use a different day-count basis.

atoms.title: Rate caplets and floorlets: fixing, payment and Black pricing / 3. Known fixings and degenerate cases
atoms.text:
## 3. Known fixings and degenerate cases

If the fixing is known, use the observed contractual rate $L_{\mathrm{known}}$ even if the forward curve has moved. Payment can still be in the future.

$$
V_{\mathrm{caplet},\mathrm{known}} = N\cdot \delta \cdot D\cdot \max (L_{\mathrm{known}}-K,0)
$$

The known floorlet is:

$$
V_{\mathrm{floorlet},\mathrm{known}} = N\cdot \delta \cdot D\cdot \max (K-L_{\mathrm{known}},0)
$$

For an unfixed rate with zero total variance, the same deterministic expressions apply with F in place of $L_{\mathrm{known}}$. At $K=0$ and nonnegative lognormal $L_{\mathrm{fix}}$, the caplet value is $N\delta DF$ and the floorlet is zero; negative strike extends this linear caplet branch. A deterministic zero forward can be handled by its deterministic payoff, but an unshifted lognormal model cannot represent a genuinely negative rate distribution.

A specified shifted-lognormal model applies Black to F+s and K+s, with positive shifted inputs and shift s; the payoff difference is unchanged. A normal-volatility model instead uses a different distribution and volatility units. Substituting an absolute value into $\ln (F/K)$ does not repair an invalid lognormal model.

atoms.title: Rate caplets and floorlets: fixing, payment and Black pricing / 4. Portfolios and checks
atoms.text:
## 4. Portfolios and checks

A cap is the sum of its component caplets, with each component's own accrual, fixing, payment, notional and volatility. A floor is the corresponding sum of floorlets. A quoted cap volatility reprices a cap as a whole and is not generally a term structure of individual caplet volatilities; stripping is a separate calibration problem [1].

Pointwise payoff subtraction gives exact caplet-floorlet parity with consistent inputs:

$$
V_{\mathrm{caplet}}-V_{\mathrm{floorlet}} = N\cdot \delta \cdot D\cdot (F-K)
$$

For known fixings replace F by the known rate. Summing this identity gives the corresponding floating-minus-fixed coupon stream, without inventing principal exchanges. A mixed portfolio of known and future fixings uses the correct rate for each component.

When $F=K>0$, the Black caplet simplifies to:

$$
V_{\mathrm{caplet},\mathrm{ATM}} = N\cdot \delta \cdot D\cdot F\cdot (2\cdot \Phi (\sqrt{w}/2)-1)
$$

Parity, the zero-variance limit and positive homogeneity in N are independent checks on signs and scaling. Under the positive-rate model, the caplet lies between zero and $N\delta DF$; the floorlet lies between zero and $N\delta DK$ for $K\ge 0$. These bounds are not the bounds of a normal model with negative rates.

atoms.title: Rate caplets and floorlets: fixing, payment and Black pricing / References
atoms.text:
## References

[1] OpenGamma quantitative research, Eight ways to strip your caplets: An introduction to caplet stripping, rate-option definitions and Black caplet valuation. [Author technical paper](https://quant.opengamma.io/Caplet-Stripping-OpenGamma.pdf). Black's forward-option framework originates in Fischer Black (1976), The Pricing of Commodity Contracts, Journal of Financial Economics 3, 167–179; [bibliographic record](https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X(76)90024-6).

atoms.title: Rate curves and swaps: working conventions / overview
atoms.text:
# Rate curves and swaps: working conventions

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this as a checklist when a task builds discount or projection curves, converts rates, shocks curves or values swaps. Where a task leaves a choice open, the common readings are listed with what each computes; pick one deliberately and say which.

atoms.title: Rate curves and swaps: working conventions / 1. Units and shifts
atoms.text:
## 1. Units and shifts

One basis point is 0.0001, so 100 bp is 0.01. Build every shift as a float array and check its extreme values before repricing.

Curve shifts on integer maturities: build the shift array as floating point (an integer array silently truncates a shift of 0.01 to 0); a parallel shift of 100 bp is 0.01 at every maturity; a tilt is linear between key points (for example +25 bp at 2 years to -25 bp at 10 years) and flat outside them.

Before repricing any scenario, check the shock itself and the direction of the result. `np.full_like(template, value)` and slice assignment `arr[:] = value` keep the template's dtype, so an integer maturity array turns a 0.01 shift into 0 with no error. Positive cash flows lose value when every rate rises.

Check every scenario before using it: the shift is floating point and non-zero, and a bond's value falls under an upward shift and rises under a downward one.

atoms.title: Rate curves and swaps: working conventions / 2. Rates from discount factors
atoms.text:
## 2. Rates from discount factors

Continuous zero rate z(t) = -ln P(t) / t. Continuous forward over (t1, t2]: ln(P(t1)/P(t2)) / (t2 - t1). Simple forward: (P(t1)/P(t2) - 1) / accrual.

A forward column with one row per maturity T has two readings that give different numbers:
- A: the period ending at T, (T_prev, T], where the first row uses P(0) = 1 and equals z of the first maturity.
- B: the period starting at T, (T, T_next], so the last row needs a factor beyond the curve.

With one row per maturity and no reading stated in the task, A (the period ending at T) is the usual one: it needs no point beyond the curve and fills every row. B leaves the last row undefined unless the task supplies or prescribes an extension.

If the chosen reading leaves a required cell empty, decide how to fill it (the other reading or a stated extrapolation) instead of writing NaN.

Forward rates between nodes from discount factors $P(T_i)$, with $P(0) = 1$:

1. Reading A (period ending at $T_i$): $f_i = \ln(P(T_{i-1})/P(T_i))/(T_i - T_{i-1})$; the first equals the first zero rate.
2. Reading B (period starting at $T_i$): $f_i = \ln(P(T_i)/P(T_{i+1}))/(T_{i+1} - T_i)$; undefined at the last node.

atoms.title: Rate curves and swaps: working conventions / 3. Bootstrapping par quotes
atoms.text:
## 3. Bootstrapping par quotes

Price each par instrument on its full coupon schedule, not only on the supplied maturities. A coupon date between two knots takes its factor from the interpolant, so the new knot appears on both sides and must be solved with a 1-D root finder (see bootstrap_immunization). A par instrument shorter than one coupon period pays once: P(T) = 1 / (1 + y T).

With a non-local interpolant (cubic spline), two readings: (a) solve knots in order with a local rule for in-between dates, then fit the spline through the knots; (b) solve all knots jointly so the final spline reprices every quote. Always reprice every quote from the final curve on its full schedule. Zero rates tens of bp away from par yields on a gently sloped curve usually mean coupons were skipped.

atoms.title: Rate curves and swaps: working conventions / 4. Swaps
atoms.text:
## 4. Swaps

Fixed leg PV $= N k \sum_i \alpha_i P_d(t_i)$ with the fixed-leg day count and frequency. Float leg PV $= N \sum_j \alpha_j F_j P_d(s_j)$, $F_j = (Q(s_{j-1})/Q(s_j) - 1)/\alpha_j$, with the float-leg day count. Discount factors P_d come from the discount (collateral) curve; forwards come from the projection curve Q. Build the discount curve first, then solve the projection curve with the discount curve held fixed. Payer (pay fixed) = float - fixed.

A compounded overnight leg on the discount curve itself has PV = P(s_0) - P(s_n), so its par rate is $(P(s_0) - P(s_n)) / \sum_i \alpha_i P(t_i)$; a single-payment pillar gives $P(e) = P(s) / (1 + r\alpha)$. For spot-starting quotes, two anchors: curve time from the valuation date with P(v) = 1 and P(s_0) < 1, or P(s_0) = 1 at the start date. They differ by the factor from v to s_0.

FX spot settles on the spot date s_0, so covered parity compares the two currencies over the same period from s_0 to delivery T: $F(T) = S \, P_f(s_0, T) / P_d(s_0, T)$. Some references write the spot value date as v; here v is the valuation date. With curves anchored at the valuation date, P_c(s_0, T) = P_c(v, T) / P_c(v, s_0). Using P_c(v, T) directly multiplies the forward by P_f(v, s_0) / P_d(v, s_0), which is not one when the two currencies' overnight rates or day counts differ. An implied basis annualised from the same forward uses a year fraction over the same period [s_0, T].

Covered-interest-parity forward from discount functions with $P(\text{valuation}) = 1$, for spot start $s_0$ and maturity $T$: $F = S\,\frac{P_f(T)/P_f(s_0)}{P_d(T)/P_d(s_0)}$.

OIS bootstrap:

1. Represent the curve by knots of $g = -\ln P$ against time from the valuation date, interpolated linearly, with a flat zero rate beyond the last knot.
2. Par OIS rate for a swap starting at $s_0$ with payment dates $t_k$ and accruals $\alpha_k$: $(P(s_0) - P(t_n))/\sum_k \alpha_k P(t_k)$.
3. Process the quotes in order of final payment date; for each, solve for the new knot value $g$ at its final payment date with a bracketing root finder (for example `scipy.optimize.brentq` on $[-1, 5]$) so that the par rate equals the quote, then add the knot.
4. Check that every quote reprices to within $10^{-12}$.

The value at a later date T0 of a payer swap paying fixed K per unit notional is $1 - \sum_i c_i P(T_0, t_i)$ with $c_i = K\alpha_i$ and $c_n = 1 + K\alpha_n$: the final principal is part of the coupon bond. At time 0 the same expression with $P(0, \cdot)$ is $P(0, T_0) - \sum_i c_i P(0, t_i)$, which is zero at the at-the-money rate.

atoms.title: Rate curves and swaps: working conventions / 5. Fixing a supplied pricing script
atoms.text:
## 5. Fixing a supplied pricing script

Read the whole file once, then list per function: day count, frequency, which curve each call receives, sign, build order and output path, against the convention contract. Write edits to a new writable file by exact text replacement and confirm each replacement matched. Keep the output directory the task names. After each run, reprice every input quote and look at the worst residual.

atoms.title: Rate curves and swaps: working conventions / 6. Task wording → API arguments
atoms.text:
## 6. Task wording → API arguments

Arguments that silently change results, with the task phrases they usually answer to.

- `scipy.optimize.brentq(f, a, b, xtol=2e-12, rtol=8.9e-16, maxiter=100)`: "solve on the interval [lo, hi]" means a = lo, b = hi; f(a) and f(b) must differ in sign or it raises ValueError. Widen a bracket only when the task fixes none. xtol is absolute, so the default suits rates; a non-converged run raises RuntimeError.
- `scipy.optimize.newton(func, x0, fprime=None, tol=1.48e-8, maxiter=50)`: "starting from" gives x0. Without fprime it runs the secant method; with fprime, Newton. It has no bracket and can leave the economic range, so check the root.
- `scipy.optimize.least_squares(fun, x0, bounds=(-inf, inf), loss='linear', ftol=xtol=gtol=1e-8)`: "least squares" or "squared errors" is loss='linear'; 'soft_l1' or 'huber' answer "robust". fun returns the residual vector, not its square.
- `scipy.optimize.minimize(fun, x0, method, bounds, constraints, options)`: name the method the task names. L-BFGS-B takes options ftol, gtol, maxiter; SLSQP takes ftol and maxiter (default 100). "Positive parameter" is a bound (small epsilon, None). Read res.success and res.message; "retry with a looser tolerance" means a second call.
- `numpy.interp(x, xp, fp, left=None, right=None)`: xp must increase; outside the range it returns the end values of fp. The interpolated quantity is the argument fp: "log-linear in discount factors" means fp = ln P; "linear in zero rates" means fp = z; "linear in g(T) = -ln P" means fp = g. Flat ln P beyond the end is a zero forward, not a flat zero rate; "flat zero-rate extrapolation" means extending z, so P = exp(-z_end t).
- `scipy.interpolate.interp1d(x, y, kind='linear', fill_value=...)`: fill_value='extrapolate' continues the last segment's slope; that is a stated extrapolation choice.
- `scipy.interpolate.CubicSpline(x, y, bc_type='not-a-knot')`: "not-a-knot" is the default; "natural" is bc_type='natural'; "clamped" fixes the end slopes. A task point such as g(0) = 0 must be passed as a node, and adding it changes the whole spline. `.derivative()(t)` of g gives the instantaneous forward.
- Day counts have no library default; write each one. ACT/360 = days/360; ACT/365F = days/365; ACT/365.25 = days/365.25. 30/360 variants differ at month ends: Bond Basis sets D1 = 30 if D1 = 31, and D2 = 30 if D2 = 31 and D1 >= 30; 30/360 US also treats the last day of February as 30; 30E/360 caps both days at 30. "Time in years ACT/365" is the curve coordinate for discounting; the accrual day count only sizes the coupon.
- Schedules: "generated backward from maturity" steps months back from the maturity date; "unadjusted" means no business-day roll. Month arithmetic (`pandas.DateOffset(months=n)`, `dateutil.relativedelta`) clips the 31st to the month end.

atoms.title: Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / overview
atoms.text:
# Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV

**If the task text defines the formula, inputs or conventions differently, the task text wins.**

atoms.title: Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / Model and setting
atoms.text:
## Model and setting
- Observed log price = efficient log price + noise: $y_{t} = x_{t} + \eta _{t}$. x is a continuous semimartingale with integrated variance
  

$$
\mathrm{IV} = \int  \sigma _{s}^{2} \mathrm{d}s
$$

 over the period (usually one trading day). $\eta$ is iid, mean 0, variance $\sigma _{\eta}^{2}$, independent of x.
- Intraday return j of day i: $r_{j} = y_{t_{j}} - y_{t_{j-1}} = (x_{t_{j}} - x_{t_{j-1}}) + \mathrm{eps}_{j}$, $\mathrm{eps}_{j} = \eta _{j} - \eta _{j-1}$.
  So $\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) = 2 \sigma _{\eta}^{2}$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(\mathrm{eps}_{j}, \mathrm{eps}_{j-1}) = -\sigma _{\eta}^{2}$: noise makes high-frequency returns negatively autocorrelated (MA(1)).
- Use LOG returns of consecutive prices inside one day. Do not include the overnight return or the jump from day i's last price to
  day i+1's first price. M = number of returns in the day = number of prices in the day minus 1 (zero returns count).

atoms.title: Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / Parameters and units
atoms.text:
## Parameters and units
| symbol | meaning | units |
|---|---|---|
| $r_{j}, j = 1\ldots M$ | intraday log returns of one day at the chosen sampling frequency | log units |
| $M$ | returns per day; $M^{*}$ = optimal count; interval = (trading-day length) / M | count |
| IV, Q | integrated variance and integrated quarticity $\int  \sigma ^{4} \mathrm{d}s$ of one day | per day, per day^2 |
| $\sigma _{\eta}^{2}$ | variance of the noise in the $\log  \mathrm{PRICE}$ | log units^2 |
| $\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}), \operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{4})$ | 2nd / 4th moment of the noise in RETURNS; $\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) = 2 \sigma _{\eta}^{2}$ | log units^2, ^4 |
| $N_{d}$ | number of days pooled | count |

atoms.title: Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / Formulas
atoms.text:
## Formulas
Realized variance of one day: $\mathrm{RV} = \sum _{j=1}^{M} r_{j}^{2}$. On a fixed efficient-price grid define $\mathrm{RV}_x=\sum_{j=1}^M(x_j-x_{j-1})^2$. Conditional on that path and independent price noise, the exact expectation is $\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{RV}\mid x]=\mathrm{RV}_x+2M\sigma_\eta^2$. For a continuous Ito process, $\mathrm{RV}_x$ converges to IV as the mesh vanishes, but need not equal it on a finite grid. Accordingly $\mathrm{E}[\widehat\sigma_\eta^2\mid x]=\sigma_\eta^2+\mathrm{RV}_x/(2M)$ for the estimator below. Adjacent return-noise covariance is $-\sigma_\eta^2$; non-iid or endogenous price noise changes these identities.

Bandi-Russell noise moments, from returns at the HIGHEST available frequency (every price change / tick):
Per day:

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) = \mathrm{RV} / M
$$

$$
\hat{\sigma}_{\eta}^{2} = \mathrm{RV} / (2 M)
$$

Pooled:

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) = \sum _{i} \sum _{j} r_{ij}^{2} / \sum _{i} M_{i}
$$

The denominator equals $N_{d} M$ when every day has $M$ returns.

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{eps}^{4}) = \sum _{i} \sum _{j} r_{ij}^{4} / \sum _{i} M_{i}
$$

$$
\hat{\sigma}_{\eta}^{2} = \widehat{\mathrm{E}}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) / 2
$$

Conditional on the efficient path, $\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{RV}/(2M)\mid x]-\sigma_\eta^2=\mathrm{RV}_x/(2M)$. This is an upward conditional-mean bias, not an inequality for every random estimate. For a continuous efficient price, $\mathrm{RV}_x$ approaches $\mathrm{IV}$ as sampling becomes fine, so this bias vanishes.

Quarticity (Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard), per day, from LOWER-frequency returns (Bandi & Russell 2006 use 15-minute returns), $M_{q}$ returns:

$$
\widehat Q= (M_{q} / 3) \cdot  \sum _{j=1}^{M_{q}} r_{j}^{4}
$$

MSE-optimal number of returns per day (Bandi & Russell 2006 Prop. 3; 2008):

$$
\mathrm{MSE}(M) \approx 2 Q / M + M \beta  + M^{2} \alpha
$$

$$
\alpha  = (\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}))^{2}
$$

$$
\beta  = 2 \operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{4}) - 3 (\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}))^{2}
$$

$M^{*}$ solves the exact first-order condition:

$$
2 M^{3} \alpha  + M^{2} \beta  - 2 Q = 0
$$

Rule of thumb (Prop. 4; good when $M^{*}$ is large):

$$
M^{*} \approx ( Q / (\operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}))^{2} )^{1/3}
$$

For one $M^{*}$ over many days, use the average of the daily Q^ (or compute M*_i per day with Q^_i). Optimal interval = day length / $M^{*}$.

Bipower variation (Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard 2004), per day:

$$
\mathrm{BV} = \mathrm{mu1}^{-2} \cdot  \sum _{j=2}^{M} \vert r_{j}\vert  \vert r_{j-1}\vert ,   \mathrm{mu1} = \operatorname{E}\vert Z\vert  = \sqrt{2/\pi},  \mathrm{so} \mathrm{mu1}^{-2} = \pi /2
$$

Jump part of quadratic variation: $\mathrm{RV} - \mathrm{BV}$ (often floored at 0). Without noise and jumps, BV and RV both estimate IV.

Two-scales realized variance (Zhang, Mykland & Ait-Sahalia 2005), one day with log prices $y_{0}$..$y_{n}$ (n returns):

$$
\mathrm{RV}_{\mathrm{all}} = \sum _{j=1}^{n} (y_{j} - y_{j-1})^{2}
$$

$\mathrm{RV}^{(k)}$ sums squared differences over consecutive points of subgrid $k$.

$$
\mathrm{subgrid}_{k} = \{y_{k-1}, y_{k-1+K}, y_{k-1+2K}, \ldots \}
$$

For $k = 1\ldots K$.

$$
\mathrm{RV}_{\mathrm{avg}} = (1/K) \sum _{k} \mathrm{RV}^{(k)}
$$

$$
\bar{n} = (n - K + 1) / K
$$

$$
\mathrm{TSRV} = \mathrm{RV}_{\mathrm{avg}} - (\bar{n} / n) \mathrm{RV}_{\mathrm{all}}
$$

Small-sample adjusted:

$$
\mathrm{TSRV}_{\mathrm{adj}} = \mathrm{TSRV} / (1 - \bar{n} / n)
$$

Noise variance (ZMA), same as Bandi–Russell per day:

$$
\hat{\sigma}_{\eta}^{2} = \mathrm{RV}_{\mathrm{all}} / (2 n)
$$

$K$ grows like $c n^{2/3}$.
Annualization: annual variance = (periods per year from the task, commonly 252 trading days) * mean of daily estimates;
volatility = sqrt of that. Average VARIANCES across days, then take the square root. Daily vol = $\sqrt{\text{daily RV}}$.

atoms.title: Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / Variants and common mistakes
atoms.text:
## Variants and common mistakes
- Price noise vs return noise: "noise variance" usually means $\sigma _{\eta}^{2} = \mathrm{RV}/(2M); \operatorname{E}(\mathrm{eps}^{2}) = \mathrm{RV}/M$ is twice that. The rule of thumb
  uses E(eps^2); plugging $\sigma _{\eta}^{2}$ instead makes $M^{*}$ too large by a factor 4^(1/3).
- n / M counts RETURNS, not prices. Pooled estimates divide the pooled sum by the total number of returns, not by days times a nominal M.
- Per-day vs pooled: per-day RV/(2M) gives one noise estimate per day; pooled (Prop. 1b) assumes the noise is iid across days. Use what the task asks.
- Q^ from the highest frequency is dominated by noise; compute it from sparse returns. Do not use $Q = \mathrm{RV}^{2}$ unless the task says so.
- BV and RV from the same returns are of the same size: by Cauchy-Schwarz $\sum|r_j||r_{j-1}| \le \mathrm{RV}$, so $\mathrm{BV} \le (\pi/2)\,\mathrm{RV}$; BV close to $(\pi/2)\,\mathrm{RV}$ on most days means the products are $|r_j|^2$. In pandas, `s.iloc[1:] * s.iloc[:-1]` aligns on index labels and multiplies each value by itself; use `np.abs(r.to_numpy())` slices or `s * s.shift(1)`.
- BV constant is $\pi/2$, not $2/\pi$. Some papers multiply BV by M/(M-1) (finite-sample variant). BV is robust to jumps, NOT to noise: compute it at a sparse frequency.
- Sparse RV at M returns: sample every (day length / M) using the last price at or before each grid time (previous tick), starting at the open.
- Simple returns, percentage returns, or including the overnight return all change the number.

atoms.title: Realized variance with microstructure noise: Bandi-Russell noise variance and optimal sampling, bipower variation, two-scales RV / Applicability and known limits
atoms.text:
## Applicability and known limits
- iid noise independent of the price is assumed. Serially dependent noise or noise correlated with x breaks RV/(2M) and the $M^{*}$ formula.
- With finite M a jump J still inflates BV by about $\vert J\vert  \sqrt{2 \pi  \mathrm{IV} / M}; \mathrm{RV} - \mathrm{BV}$ is then a noisy jump estimate.
- TSRV subgrids lose up to $K-1$ edge intervals. With driftless constant intraday volatility and an equidistant grid,

$$
\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{TSRV}]
=\mathrm{IV}\frac{(n-K+1)(K-1)}{nK}.
$$

  The unadjusted relative downward bias is about $K/n+1/K$, not just $K/n$. For the adjusted estimator,

$$
\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{TSRV}_{\mathrm{adj}}]
=\mathrm{IV}\frac{n-K+1}{n+1},
$$

  whose relative downward bias is $K/(n+1)$. These finite-grid expectations use the stated constant-volatility setup; changing endpoint handling changes the edge terms.
- In a simulation, separate the realized efficient-grid quantity from its continuous target: conditional on $x$, $\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{RV}\mid x]-\mathrm{RV}_x=M\mathrm{E}(\mathrm{eps}^2)$. Comparing against $\mathrm{IV}$ adds efficient-price discretization error; it is not an exact pathwise identity.

atoms.title: Backtest of a portfolio rebalanced from rolling estimates (regimes, inverse volatility, risk metrics): workflow / Topic 1: Choices to settle before coding
atoms.text:
## Topic 1: Choices to settle before coding

**Purpose:** Fix every choice that changes the numbers, from the task's wording.

**When to use:** Weights are set on scheduled dates from rolling-window estimates (correlation eigenvalues, a regime label, volatilities) and the realised strategy is then evaluated. Read the scenario table in the VaR and ES conventions card first: it says which rebalance dates, initial holdings and earning day fit the task's wording.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Settle each row of this table from the task text and print the choices:

| Topic | Choice | Options and the wording that selects them |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | Matrix for the eigenvalues | correlation (unit-free, trace $n$) or covariance (keeps scale, trace = total variance); "correlation" / "covariance" in the text decides |
| 3 | Estimate window | equal-weighted rolling window of $W$ rows, or exponentially weighted with a stated half-life; expanding window when the text says "all data to date" |
| 3 | Rows an estimate for day $t$ uses | rows before $t$ when it sets day $t$'s regime or weights; rows through $t$ when it is dated at the close of $t$ and used from $t+1$ |
| 3 | Regime rule | fixed thresholds with the stated comparison signs; thresholds that move with the indicator's own moving average and dispersion; a standardized shift (short minus long average over a long standard deviation); the text names which |
| 3 | Weights | inverse volatility $1/\sigma$, inverse variance $1/\sigma^2$, equal risk contribution, or equal weight; then scaled by a regime budget, by a volatility target, or not scaled. A budget below 1 leaves cash that earns nothing unless the text gives a cash rate |
| 4 | Rebalance calendar | month-end rows, month-start rows, weekly, every $N$ rows, or on regime changes; dates are rows present in the data |
| 4 | Last data row | excluded when weights set at a close earn from the next day; included when the text rebalances at the open of the same day |
| 5 | Holdings before the first rebalance | equal weights, cash, the first estimate, or start the evaluation at the first rebalance (scenario table) |
| 5 | When new weights earn | from the next day (set at a close) or the same day (set at the open); never both a loop delay and an extra shift |
| 5 | Costs | none unless stated; a proportional cost charges turnover $\sum_i\lvert w_i^{new}-w_i^{old}\rvert$ at each rebalance |
| 6 | Annualised return | arithmetic mean times periods per year, or geometric $(1+R_{total})^{P/n}-1$; "mean daily return x 252" or "CAGR" in the text |
| 6 | Sharpe ratio | zero risk-free rate unless given; `ddof` as stated |
| 6 | Drawdown | on the wealth path, as a positive magnitude unless the text reports it negative |
| 6 | VaR / CVaR of the strategy | one trailing window, the full evaluated sample, or a rolling series (then the text says which statistic of it); quantile rule and tail mean per the VaR and ES conventions card |
| 6 | Average weight of an asset | over all evaluated days (held weights) or over rebalance dates (target weights); "average weight" without a qualifier is the time average of the held weights |

atoms.title: Backtest of a portfolio rebalanced from rolling estimates (regimes, inverse volatility, risk metrics): workflow / Topic 2: Cleaning, counting and the estimation window
atoms.text:
## Topic 2: Cleaning, counting and the estimation window

**Purpose:** Build the return table that every later step uses, and count it correctly.

**When to use:** Always first.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Clean the raw returns with the rules of the VaR and ES conventions card (duplicate dates, missing values) and keep the cleaned table.

Step 2: The count of valid observations is the number of rows after cleaning.

Step 3: Cut the estimation window from the cleaned table (the last rows the task names, or all of them).

**Double check:**

1. The count of valid observations is at least the window length; a reported count of valid observations is the cleaned row count, not the window length.

atoms.title: Backtest of a portfolio rebalanced from rolling estimates (regimes, inverse volatility, risk metrics): workflow / Topic 3: Rolling estimates known before each day
atoms.text:
## Topic 3: Rolling estimates known before each day

**Purpose:** Estimate, for each evaluated day, the indicator, the regime and the target weights from data available at that time.

**When to use:** After Topic 2.

**Constraints:**

1. An estimate that sets day $t$'s regime or weights uses rows $t-W,\dots,t-1$ only.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: For each day $t$ from $W$ to the end, take the window of the previous $W$ rows.

Step 2: Eigenvalues of the window's correlation (or covariance) matrix with a symmetric solver (`np.linalg.eigvalsh`), sorted largest first; the share of the top $k$:

$$\mathrm{AR}_t=\frac{\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i}{\sum_i\lambda_i}$$

Step 3: Regime from the indicator with the thresholds and comparison signs exactly as the task states.

Step 4: Weights, for inverse volatility $w_i\propto1/\sigma_i$ (standard deviation with the task's `ddof`), normalized to sum to one, then times the regime budget.

Step 5: Random-matrix reference, when asked: the Marchenko-Pastur upper edge for a $W\times n$ correlation matrix,

$$\lambda_{+}=\left(1+\sqrt{n/W}\right)^2$$

**Double check:**

1. The number of evaluated days equals the number of rows minus $W$; the trace of each correlation matrix is $n$; $\lambda_+>1$. Summary statistics of these series use the task's `ddof` consistently.

atoms.title: Backtest of a portfolio rebalanced from rolling estimates (regimes, inverse volatility, risk metrics): workflow / Topic 4: Rebalance dates
atoms.text:
## Topic 4: Rebalance dates

**Purpose:** Choose rebalance dates that are rows of the data.

**When to use:** Scheduled rebalancing (month ends and similar).

**Constraints:**

1. Rebalance dates are dates present in the data and among the evaluated days; a calendar month end that is a weekend, or later than the last row, is not one.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Put the evaluated dates in a Series indexed by themselves and, per calendar month (`dt.to_period("M")`), keep the date equal to the group maximum (`groupby(...).transform("max")`). On a DatetimeIndex, `groupby` returns a plain dict of labels, so wrap the dates in a Series first.

Step 2: If `resample` is used instead, take its values, `resample("ME").last().dropna()`, which are the last dates present in each month, not its index, whose labels are calendar month ends.

Step 3: Drop the last data row when weights set at a close earn from the next day.

**Double check:**

1. Every rebalance date is an evaluated day; the number of rebalances is at most the number of calendar months in the evaluated period.

atoms.title: Backtest of a portfolio rebalanced from rolling estimates (regimes, inverse volatility, risk metrics): workflow / Topic 5: Holdings and the daily return loop
atoms.text:
## Topic 5: Holdings and the daily return loop

**Purpose:** Compute one return per evaluated day, with weights applied at the right time.

**When to use:** After Topics 3 and 4.

**Constraints:**

1. Delay the new weights exactly once: the loop below already applies them from the next day; no extra shift or forward fill on top.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Holdings before the first rebalance, by the reading the task supports (write it in a comment): equal weights; cash (zero weights); the first estimate; or start the evaluation after the first rebalance with its weights.

Step 2: Loop over the evaluated days in order:

1. record the weights held at the start of the day;
2. the day's return is the sum of held weights times that day's asset returns;
3. if the day is a rebalance date, replace the held weights by that day's target weights (they earn from the next day);
4. with a proportional cost, subtract the cost rate times the turnover on the rebalance day.

**Double check:**

1. The return series has one value per evaluated day.

atoms.title: Backtest of a portfolio rebalanced from rolling estimates (regimes, inverse volatility, risk metrics): workflow / Topic 6: Performance and risk of the strategy
atoms.text:
## Topic 6: Performance and risk of the strategy

**Purpose:** Summarize the realised strategy.

**When to use:** After Topic 5.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Annualised return (mean times periods per year, or geometric by Topic 1) and volatility (standard deviation with the task's `ddof` times $\sqrt{P}$); Sharpe ratio as their ratio with the stated risk-free rate.

Step 2: Wealth $W_t=\prod(1+r)$ (`cumprod`) and maximum drawdown $\max_t(1-W_t/\max_{s\le t}W_s)$, as a positive magnitude.

Step 3: VaR and CVaR on the sample Topic 1 chose (for one trailing window, its last rows of realised returns), with the quantile rule and tail mean of the VaR and ES conventions card.

Step 4: Win rate as the share of days with a positive return; average weights by the reading in Topic 1.

**Double check:**

1. The trailing window has the stated length; as losses, CVaR is at least VaR and VaR is positive; with a short window and a high level the tail may hold one observation, so state the quantile rule used.

atoms.title: Backtest of a portfolio rebalanced from rolling estimates (regimes, inverse volatility, risk metrics): workflow / Topic 7: Writing the deliverables
atoms.text:
## Topic 7: Writing the deliverables

**Purpose:** Write results that match the task's schema.

**When to use:** At the end of each stage that completes a deliverable.

**How to implement:**

Step 1: Write each file as soon as its values are computed.

Step 2: Read every file back.

**Double check:**

1. Every requested key is present, counts are integers, and magnitudes are reported as the task states (positive losses and drawdowns).
