| ES | strict tail mean | E[L \| L > VaR]; empty when VaR is the largest loss | only when the task writes "strictly greater than VaR" or a formula with a strict inequality |
| ES | inclusive tail mean | E[L \| L >= VaR]; always contains the VaR amount; the tail conditional expectation of Artzner et al. (1999), Definition 5.1 | the default when losses tie at VaR: "at or beyond VaR", and also "exceeding VaR", "beyond VaR" or "conditional on exceeding VaR" without "strictly" |
| ES | integrated quantile (tail mean) | the mean of exactly the worst (1 - a) share of probability, taking only the needed part of the VaR atom; equals min over c of c + E[max(L - c, 0)] / (1 - a) | "average of VaR over the tail", "coherent ES", "integrated quantile" |

How to choose when the wording does not decide:

- Without ties at VaR the strict and inclusive means are equal; on a grid, or with resampled or simulated losses that repeat, they can differ by a large amount and the inclusive mean is then the lower one. Report the inclusive mean unless the task writes a strict inequality or the word "strictly"; "beyond VaR" and "exceeding VaR", alone or inside a longer phrase, are not such a request. Print the strict mean and the mass at the VaR amount (`(L == var).mean()`) only as diagnostics; they do not change which value is written.
- A VaR that falls between two grid values is a sign of interpolation; a VaR equal to a grid value can come from any rule. Report `P(L <= VaR)` next to it so the reader can see which side of an atom it sits on.
- Use one quantile rule and one tail-mean rule for every level and every output that the same loss sample feeds.

On a loss grid (for example losses that are multiples of a fixed amount) at level $a$:

1. The order-statistic VaR (`numpy.quantile` with `method="inverted_cdf"`) equals the generalized inverse of the empirical CDF, the smallest grid value whose CDF reaches $a$; the default interpolated quantile can fall between grid values.
2. Three tail means differ on a grid: the mean of losses strictly above the VaR, the mean of losses at or above it, and the integrated tail mean over the worst $m = n(1-a)$ losses (the sum of the $\lfloor m\rfloor$ worst plus the fractional part of the next). The integrated mean lies between the inclusive and the strict means.
3. Report the CDF at the VaR and the probability mass at the VaR.

atoms.title: Simulated and discrete loss distributions: random streams, quantiles and tail means on a grid / Task wording -> API arguments
atoms.text:
## Task wording -> API arguments

Random numbers: np.random.seed(s) with np.random.normal / standard_normal / multivariate_normal uses the legacy RandomState; np.random.default_rng(s) returns a Generator whose normal, standard_normal and multivariate_normal give a different stream. Generator.multivariate_normal factorizes the covariance with method="svd" by default ("cholesky" and "eigh" change the draws).

atoms.title: Simulated and discrete loss distributions: random streams, quantiles and tail means on a grid / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources

Jorion, Value at Risk, 3rd ed. (2007), ch. 5 (historical simulation, parametric VaR) and ch. 6 (backtesting). Acerbi and Tasche (2002), J. Banking and Finance 26(7), 1487-1503 (tail mean and conditional means at atoms). Rockafellar and Uryasev (2002), J. Banking and Finance 26(7), 1443-1471 (CVaR minimization formula). Hyndman and Fan (1996), American Statistician 50(4), 361-365 (sample quantile definitions). Boudoukh, Richardson and Whitelaw (1998), Risk 11(5), 64-67 (age-weighted historical simulation). J.P. Morgan/Reuters, RiskMetrics Technical Document, 4th ed. (1996), sec. 5.2 (EWMA). Kupiec (1995), J. Derivatives 3(2), 73-84 (proportion of failures). J.P. Morgan, CreditMetrics Technical Document (1997), ch. 8 (simulation). Docs: NumPy numpy.quantile and Random Generator / legacy RandomState; SciPy rv_continuous.fit, stats.t, special.xlogy; pandas Series.ewm and Series.rolling.

atoms.title: Simulated and discrete loss distributions: random streams, quantiles and tail means on a grid / Loss by group in a simulated portfolio
atoms.text:
## Loss by group in a simulated portfolio

For groups that partition the portfolio (initial rating, sector), two "mean loss" figures exist per group: the mean over scenarios of the group's total loss, and the mean loss of one member, smaller by the group size. A table that reports a figure for each group next to the portfolio figure is a breakdown: use the group total, so that the groups add up to the portfolio mean loss. Use the per-member mean only when the task asks for it per name, per obligor or per member of the group. An input quantity stated per bond or per name, such as a notional or a recovery amount, does not ask for it.

Breakdown by group: for each scenario sum the losses of the names in each group, then average over scenarios; the group means add up to the portfolio mean loss.

atoms.title: Rating transition matrices: count matrices, cohort and pooled estimates, multi-year default probabilities, homogeneity tests and generator matrices / overview
atoms.text:
# Rating transition matrices: count matrices, cohort and pooled estimates, multi-year default probabilities, homogeneity tests and generator matrices

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Read the topics relevant to the task; a task usually needs several of them.

atoms.title: Rating transition matrices: count matrices, cohort and pooled estimates, multi-year default probabilities, homogeneity tests and generator matrices / Topic 1: Count matrices on a target rating scale
atoms.text:
## Topic 1: Count matrices on a target rating scale

**Purpose:** Turn published transition tables with a fine rating scale into count matrices on the target scale, one per cohort.

**When to use:** The inputs are rating transition tables (counts or rates) per year or cohort, possibly on a finer scale than the one the task asks for.

**Constraints:**
- Map every source rating to exactly one target rating, as the task states (for example notches and sub-grades of the lowest grades merged into one distressed bucket, and every default-type code into Default).
- Withdrawn or not-rated outcomes are censored: they leave the sample and are not a destination, unless the task says otherwise; they enter neither the numerators nor the row totals.
- Default is absorbing: the Default row has a single count or probability in the Default column.
- A cohort contains the issuers rated (not in default) at the start of its period, as in rating-agency static-pool studies: issuers already in default are not cohort members. Cohort sizes, transition counts and any total number of transitions or issuers cover the non-default starting ratings only; the Default row comes from the absorbing convention, not from counted issuers.

**How to implement:**
1. Check the inputs and print them: each file's separator, header and first column (the beginning-of-period rating), the destination columns, whether cells are counts or percentages, and the task's mapping.
2. For each cohort, sum the source rows and columns into the target scale with the mapping; drop the censored columns.
3. When the task supplies defaults counted elsewhere (defaults not visible in the transition table, for example issuers withdrawn before defaulting), add the difference between those defaults and the visible ones to the Default column of the matching row, as the task describes. These issuers were rated at the start of the period (the transition table had moved them to a withdrawn column), so they are cohort members: after the move they are part of their row's total and of the cohort size.
4. Cohort sizes: the non-default row totals of the corrected count matrices of step 3. Build the cohort-size table once from them and print it; every reported total of transitions or issuers is the sum of that same table (`sizes[rating_columns].to_numpy().sum()`), not a second count over the raw files or over all rows.

**Limitations and cautions:** Percent tables must be converted back to counts with the row's issuer count before pooling; pooling percentages weights small cohorts as much as large ones.

**Double check:** Each count is a non-negative integer and the sum of all row totals equals the total number of transitions reported anywhere else in the outputs; if two totals differ, they count different rows (for example with or without the Default row), so state which and derive both from the same counts.

atoms.title: Rating transition matrices: count matrices, cohort and pooled estimates, multi-year default probabilities, homogeneity tests and generator matrices / Topic 2: Cohort and pooled transition matrices
atoms.text:
## Topic 2: Cohort and pooled transition matrices

**Purpose:** Estimate one-period transition probabilities per cohort and pooled over cohorts.

**When to use:** The task asks for annual transition matrices or an average transition matrix.

**How to implement:**
1. Cohort matrix: $P^{(t)}_{ij} = C^{(t)}_{ij} / \sum_k C^{(t)}_{ik}$ for rows with a positive total.
2. Pooled (issuer-weighted) matrix: $\bar{P}_{ij} = \sum_t C^{(t)}_{ij} / \sum_t \sum_k C^{(t)}_{ik}$, the same as summing the count matrices first; it differs from the plain mean of the cohort matrices.
3. Set the Default row to the unit vector of the Default column.

**Limitations and cautions:** A row with no issuers in a cohort has no probabilities; leave it out of that cohort rather than writing zeros that would later be averaged.

**Double check:** Every row sums to 1 within rounding and every entry lies in $[0, 1]$; if not, a censored column was kept in the totals or a row total is zero.

atoms.title: Rating transition matrices: count matrices, cohort and pooled estimates, multi-year default probabilities, homogeneity tests and generator matrices / Topic 3: Multi-year cumulative default probabilities
atoms.text:
## Topic 3: Multi-year cumulative default probabilities

**Purpose:** Project default probabilities over several years from a one-year matrix under the Markov assumption.

**When to use:** The task asks for default probabilities accumulated over several periods.

**How to implement:**
1. Check the inputs: the one-year matrix (Topic 2) and the horizons.
2. $PD_i(h) = [\bar{P}^h]_{i,\mathrm{Default}}$, with `numpy.linalg.matrix_power(P, h)`.

**Limitations and cautions:** The projection assumes time-homogeneous Markov transitions; Topic 4 tests that assumption across cohorts.

**Double check:** $PD_i(h)$ does not decrease with $h$ for every rating and, for a monotone matrix, increases from better to worse ratings; if it decreases with $h$, the Default row is not absorbing.

atoms.title: Rating transition matrices: count matrices, cohort and pooled estimates, multi-year default probabilities, homogeneity tests and generator matrices / Topic 4: Chi-square homogeneity test of transitions across cohorts
atoms.text:
## Topic 4: Chi-square homogeneity test of transitions across cohorts

**Purpose:** Test whether the transition distribution out of one rating is the same in every cohort (time homogeneity of the Markov chain).

**When to use:** The task asks to test the Markov property, stationarity or homogeneity of transitions across years.

**Constraints:**
- One contingency table per starting rating, with one row per cohort and one column per destination rating, filled with counts (not probabilities).
- Apply the column and row filters the task states before testing (for example dropping destination columns whose total count is below a minimum), and always drop rows (cohorts) and columns whose total is zero: an all-zero row or column has zero expected counts, which the test cannot use.
- When fewer than two rows or two columns remain, the test has no information: report statistic 0, degrees of freedom 0 and p-value 1 (and no rejection), unless the task defines another value. Never write a negative or placeholder number for a statistic, degrees of freedom or p-value.

**How to implement:**
1. Check the inputs and print, per starting rating, the table's shape before and after the filters.
2. `scipy.stats.chi2_contingency(table)` returns the statistic, the p-value, the degrees of freedom $(r - 1)(c - 1)$ and the expected counts; it applies Yates' continuity correction only when the degrees of freedom equal 1 (`correction=False` turns it off), so use the setting the task names.
3. Reject at the task's significance level when the p-value is below it.

**Limitations and cautions:** Sparse cells make the chi-square approximation unreliable, which is why minimum-count filters exist; with the filters the test covers only the remaining destinations.

**Double check:** For every rating the statistic is non-negative, the degrees of freedom equal $(r - 1)(c - 1)$ of the filtered table and the p-value lies in $[0, 1]$; if not, a placeholder or an unfiltered zero row slipped in, so rebuild the table.

atoms.title: Rating transition matrices: count matrices, cohort and pooled estimates, multi-year default probabilities, homogeneity tests and generator matrices / Topic 5: Generator matrix by matrix logarithm
atoms.text:
## Topic 5: Generator matrix by matrix logarithm

**Purpose:** Estimate a continuous-time generator $Q$ with $\bar{P} \approx e^{Q}$.

**When to use:** The task asks for a continuous-time generator or transition intensities.

**Constraints:** A valid generator has non-negative off-diagonal entries, non-positive diagonal entries and rows summing to zero; the Default row is zero.

**How to implement:**
1. $Q = \log \bar{P}$ with `scipy.linalg.logm`, keeping the real part (discard an imaginary part of rounding size; a large one means the logarithm does not exist as a real generator).
2. Regularize as the task states; the common fix sets negative off-diagonal entries to 0 and then sets each diagonal entry to minus the sum of the row's off-diagonal entries.
3. Set the Default row to zero.

**Limitations and cautions:** The regularized $Q$ no longer reproduces $\bar{P}$ exactly; $e^{Q}$ (`scipy.linalg.expm`) differs from $\bar{P}$ by the size of the removed entries.

**Double check:** Row sums of $Q$ are 0 within rounding, off-diagonals are $\ge 0$ and $\|e^{Q} - \bar{P}\|$ is small; if not, the regularization step was skipped or applied before taking the real part.

atoms.title: Rating transition matrices: count matrices, cohort and pooled estimates, multi-year default probabilities, homogeneity tests and generator matrices / Topic 6: Comparing with a reference transition matrix
atoms.text:
## Topic 6: Comparing with a reference transition matrix

**Purpose:** Compare an estimated matrix with a published long-run matrix on the same scale.

**When to use:** The task gives a reference matrix (often in percent and with a not-rated column) and asks for deviations.

**How to implement:**
1. Drop the not-rated column, convert percentages to probabilities and renormalize each row to sum to 1, the same withdrawal treatment as the estimate.
2. Align rows and columns by rating label, not by position.
3. Signed deviation $\Delta_{ij} = \bar{P}_{ij} - P^{\mathrm{ref}}_{ij}$.

**Limitations and cautions:** A reference built over a different period or region differs for economic reasons, not only estimation error; large deviations in the default column of speculative grades are expected in stress years.

**Double check:** Both matrices are row-stochastic on the same labels before the subtraction; the deviations of each row sum to 0.

References: Jafry and Schuermann (2004), Measurement, estimation and comparison of credit migration matrices, Journal of Banking and Finance 28(11); Israel, Rosenthal and Wei (2001), Finding generators for Markov chains via empirical transition matrices, Mathematical Finance 11(2); Lando and Skodeberg (2002), Analyzing rating transitions and rating drift with continuous observations, Journal of Banking and Finance 26.

atoms.title: Instrumented PCA: conditional loadings, estimation and identification / overview
atoms.text:
# Instrumented PCA: conditional loadings, estimation and identification

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this note for a factor model in which observed characteristics determine exposures to unobserved common factors. Ordinary PCA estimates unrestricted static exposures; it does not impose the characteristic-loading relation below. Explicit definitions of timing, missing data, weighting, normalization and evaluation take precedence. Do not replace an unidentified convention with a convenient rescaling.

atoms.title: Instrumented PCA: conditional loadings, estimation and identification / 1. Model and notation
atoms.text:
## 1. Model and notation

Characteristics must be available before the return interval they describe. Let the eligible asset set at date $t$ contain only observations admitted by the specified missing-data policy. A missing return is not a zero return. If the task states a replacement rule for missing values, apply it once to the panel before any estimation or summary. Every later statistic and every per-asset regression then uses all assets of the replaced panel, not a masked or complete-case subset.

| Symbol | Meaning | Dimensions |
|---|---|---|
| $r_t$ | Vector of observed excess returns at date $t$ | $N_t$ by 1 |
| $Z_t$ | Predetermined characteristics; one row per eligible asset | $N_t$ by $L$ |
| $\Gamma$ | Common map from characteristics to factor exposures | $L$ by $K$ |
| $f_t$ | Contemporaneous latent factor returns | $K$ by 1 |
| $B_t$ | Asset exposures implied by the characteristics | $N_t$ by $K$ |
| $\varepsilon_t$ | Residual returns | $N_t$ by 1 |
| $F$ | Matrix whose row $t$ is $f_t'$ | $T$ by $K$ |

The exposure matrix changes with the characteristics even though its mapping is fixed:

$$
B_t=Z_t\Gamma
$$

Returns combine these exposures with common shocks and residual risk:

$$
r_t=B_t f_t+\varepsilon_t
$$

Changing a characteristic changes exposure; it is not an additive return forecast unless that extension is explicitly included. A constant column of characteristics permits common baseline exposures. It is not by itself a time-series pricing intercept.

atoms.title: Instrumented PCA: conditional loadings, estimation and identification / 2. Least-squares estimation
atoms.text:
## 2. Least-squares estimation

With equal weight on every eligible asset-date observation, the objective is the sum of squared pricing residuals:

$$
Q(\Gamma,F)=\sum_t\|r_t-Z_t\Gamma f_t\|_2^2
$$

Alternating least squares minimizes over one block with the other fixed. Each block is linear least squares, but the joint problem is bilinear. Decreasing residual loss does not prove a unique global optimum. Initialization, convergence criteria and the permitted number of iterations belong to the specified estimator. A prescribed initialization, for example factors drawn from a stated random seed, is part of that estimator: an SVD or PCA start converges to a different rotation and scale, and every rotation-dependent output (factor Sharpe ratios, loading norms, factor correlations and variance shares) changes with it. Use the stated generator and seed. Compute the convergence criterion on finite numbers only; a loss that contains NaN never meets a tolerance.

### Factor block: exposures given

Conditional on $\Gamma$, let $B_t=Z_t\Gamma$. If $B_t$ has full column rank, the normal equations give the cross-sectional factor estimate:

$$
f_t=(B_t'B_t)^{-1}B_t'r_t
$$

This is a regression of returns on exposures at that date. It needs sufficient independent exposures, not merely more assets than factors. Rank deficiency makes the factor vector nonunique; a least-norm solution is an additional convention, not newly identified economic information.

### Characteristic-map block: factors given

Let $z_{i,t}$ be the characteristic column vector for one observation and let $g$ stack the columns of $\Gamma$. The Kronecker product supplies a linear design vector:

$$
x_{i,t}=f_t\otimes z_{i,t}
$$

The scalar fitted return is unchanged by this vectorization:

$$
z_{i,t}'\Gamma f_t=x_{i,t}'g
$$

The normal equations for the characteristic map are:

$$
\left(\sum_{i,t}x_{i,t}x_{i,t}'\right)g
=\sum_{i,t}x_{i,t}r_{i,t}
$$

The sums use the same admitted observations and weights as the original objective. Reshaping $g$ must use the same column-stacking convention as the design. In numpy, with `Gamma` of shape (L, K), `np.kron(f, z) @ Gamma.ravel(order="F")` equals `z @ Gamma @ f`; with this design, the default row-major `ravel()` and `reshape(K, L)` without a transpose pair it with a different ordering and give a wrong map. Other Kronecker layouts can use other orders; what matters is that design, flattening and rebuilding use one convention. After solving for `g`, rebuild with `g.reshape(L, K, order="F")` and confirm on one observation that `z @ Gamma @ f` equals `np.kron(f, z) @ g`. Solving least squares by QR or SVD avoids explicitly forming an inverse; an ill-conditioned normal matrix does not become well identified by inversion.

A panel array of shape (T, N, L) built from a long table must keep stock and characteristic on their own axes. `DataFrame.pivot(values=[several columns])` orders the resulting columns characteristic first and stock second, so a direct `reshape(T, N, L)` of its values mixes stocks; build one pivot per characteristic, reindex every pivot to the same date order and the same stock order, stack them on the last axis, then compare one (date, stock, characteristic) cell with the long table.

For exact block solutions, an alternating step cannot increase $Q$. Compare fitted returns or the objective when diagnosing convergence: unconstrained factors and loadings can change scale without changing predictions. An arbitrary numerical tolerance is not an economic identification condition.

atoms.title: Instrumented PCA: conditional loadings, estimation and identification / 3. Rotation, scale and centered covariance
atoms.text:
## 3. Rotation, scale and centered covariance

Use this section before interpreting individual factors or scale-sensitive summaries. For any nonsingular matrix $H$, these transformations leave fitted returns unchanged:

$$
\Gamma^*=\Gamma H,\qquad f_t^*=H^{-1}f_t
$$

Thus least-squares fit alone does not determine factor scale or axes. For a scalar rescaling, factor standard deviations change inversely to loading magnitudes. A factor Sharpe ratio is unchanged by positive scaling but reverses under a sign flip.

For an orthogonal rotation $Q$, rows of $F$ and columns of Gamma rotate by the same matrix:

$$
F^*=FQ,\qquad\Gamma^*=\Gamma Q,\qquad Q'Q=I
$$

The uncentered factor second moment is:

$$
M_F=\frac{F'F}{T}
$$

If $M_F=Q\Lambda Q'$, the rotated second moment is diagonal:

$$
\frac{(FQ)'(FQ)}{T}=\Lambda
$$

In numpy, with eigenvectors `Q` from the factor second moment, rotate as `F_rot = F @ Q` and `Gamma_rot = Gamma @ Q` (not `Q.T`), then check that `Z @ Gamma_rot @ f_rot` reproduces the fitted returns. A norm or singular-value check cannot catch a wrong rotation, since both are unchanged by any orthogonal matrix. This rotation does not select a new scale. Orthogonal rotations preserve Gamma's Frobenius norm and singular values; they only relabel its axes. Repeated eigenvalues leave rotations within the repeated-eigenvalue subspace unresolved.

The centered population-form factor covariance subtracts the outer product of the factor mean:

$$
\Omega_F=\frac{F'F}{T}-\bar f\bar f',
\qquad\bar f=\frac1T\sum_t f_t
$$

Diagonal uncentered second moments therefore do not generally imply zero centered correlations. A rotation based on centered covariance answers a different question. State which object is being diagonalized, and do not remove mean factor premia merely to make the two objects coincide.

If orthonormal loading columns are required and $\Gamma$ has full column rank, a thin QR factorization supplies one possible normalization:

$$
\Gamma=UR,\qquad U'U=I
$$

Compensating factors preserve the same fitted returns:

$$
\Gamma^*=U,\qquad F^*=FR'
$$

This changes scale and is not interchangeable with an orthogonal eigenvector rotation when scale-sensitive quantities are prescribed. Any subsequent sign choice must flip both the factor and its matching loading column. A zero factor mean cannot determine that sign.

### A fully stated normalization versus an axis rotation

When the chosen convention explicitly requires both orthonormal loading columns and a diagonal uncentered factor second moment, the two operations can be combined. For full-rank $\Gamma=UR$, form $F_1=FR'$ and eigendecompose its uncentered moment as $F_1'F_1/T=Q\Lambda Q'$. Then:

$$
\Gamma_*=UQ,\qquad F_*=F_1Q,\qquad
\Gamma_*'\Gamma_*=I,\qquad F_*'F_*/T=\Lambda
$$

The product $F_*\Gamma_*'$ remains $F\Gamma'$. This is one explicit scale-and-axis normalization; a task requesting only an orthogonal rotation has not necessarily requested the preceding QR scale change. Eigenvalue ordering, repeated-eigenvalue subspaces and zero means can leave additional labeling choices. Centered correlations must still be calculated from centered covariance; diagonal uncentered moments alone cannot guarantee zero centered correlation when more than one factor has nonzero mean.

atoms.title: Instrumented PCA: conditional loadings, estimation and identification / 4. Fit and factor-return interpretation
atoms.text:
## 4. Fit and factor-return interpretation

Let $\hat r_{i,t}$ denote the fitted return. An uncentered total $R$-squared compares residual squares with squared raw excess returns over the same eligible observations:

$$
R^2_{\mathrm{total}}
=1-\frac{\sum_{i,t}(r_{i,t}-\hat r_{i,t})^2}{\sum_{i,t}r_{i,t}^2}
$$

For a centered cross-sectional $R$-squared, let $I_t$ be the eligible assets at date $t$ and let $\bar r_t$ be their mean return. the denominator removes that date's cross-sectional mean:

$$
R^2_{\mathrm{CS},t}
=1-\frac{\sum_{i\in I_t}(r_{i,t}-\hat r_{i,t})^2}
{\sum_{i\in I_t}(r_{i,t}-\bar r_t)^2}
$$

A time average of these ratios differs from pooling their numerators and denominators. An uncentered cross-sectional convention is also possible; follow the definition rather than infer it from the word $R$-squared. Zero denominator cases require a declared rule, not an arbitrary perfect-fit value.

With full-rank exposures, the least-squares factor estimate is also a linear combination of that date's returns. Its coefficient matrix is:

$$
A_t=(B_t'B_t)^{-1}B_t'
$$

These portfolios reproduce unit exposures to the modeled factors:

$$
A_tB_t=I
$$

They may use shorts and need not have unit net investment. In-sample latent factors are not automatically out-of-sample investable strategies: the characteristic map must also be known at the trading date.

For a stationary factor series under the usual uncorrelated-return annualization assumption, its annualized excess-return Sharpe ratio is:

$$
\mathrm{SR}_{k,\mathrm{annual}}
=\sqrt{A}\frac{\bar f_k}{s_k}
$$

Here $A$ is observations per year and $s_k$ uses the specified standard-deviation divisor. Serial correlation or zero standard deviation invalidates an automatic application of this expression.

atoms.title: Instrumented PCA: conditional loadings, estimation and identification / 5. Pricing-alpha diagnostics
Instrumented PCA: conditional loadings, estimation and identification / 6. Checks and limits
atoms.text:
## 6. Checks and limits

- Dimensions and missingness define the regression population; do not shift rows by position when dates differ.
- Conditional block updates must not worsen the same least-squares objective, within numerical error.
- General rotation/scale transformations preserve predictions only with a compensating loading/factor transformation.
- Distinguish centered covariance from uncentered moments and positive scale from sign orientation.
- A fitted factor model does not establish a causal interpretation of the characteristics, and a static-alpha test is not a test that all dynamic loadings are zero.

atoms.title: Instrumented PCA: conditional loadings, estimation and identification / 7. Sources and derivation scope
atoms.text:
## 7. Sources and derivation scope

Kelly, Pruitt and Su (2019), [Instrumented Principal Component Analysis, author working paper dated December 8, 2019](https://www.cireqmontreal.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/pruitt.pdf), Sections 1 and 3.2: the characteristic-loading model, least-squares estimation and alternating block regressions. This working paper is distinct from their 2019 JFE article, *Characteristics Are Covariances: A Unified Model of Risk and Return*, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2019.05.001).

The vectorization, transformation, covariance and diagnostic identities here are direct algebra under the stated definitions; they do not claim a uniquely prescribed normalization. The GRS expression is the conventional regression statistic of Gibbons, Ross and Shanken (1989), [A Test of the Efficiency of a Given Portfolio](https://www2.itc.kansai-u.ac.jp/~koji_ota/GRS_test/GibbonsRossShanken_1989_Econometrica.pdf), Sections 2 and 7, with maximum-likelihood-form covariance divisors as explicitly defined above; it is not a new exact-test result for estimated IPCA factors.

atoms.title: Performance metrics: drawdown, Sharpe ratio, Sortino and Calmar ratios, win rate / overview
atoms.text:
# Performance metrics: drawdown, Sharpe ratio, Sortino and Calmar ratios, win rate

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this note when a task reports performance statistics of a return series or an equity curve. Each metric below has more than one standard reading; the table under each says which wording picks which one and what to use when the task is silent.

atoms.title: Performance metrics: drawdown, Sharpe ratio, Sortino and Calmar ratios, win rate / Drawdown
atoms.text:
## Drawdown

Drawdown at time t compares the curve with its running peak: `dd_t = 1 - W_t / max_{s <= t} W_s` for a wealth or equity curve W.

| Choice | Options | Pick by |
|---|---|---|
| Curve | wealth $W_t = W_0 \prod_s (1 + r_s)$ from simple returns; `exp(cumulative log return)` from log returns; a cumulative-return curve `R_t` | the series the task names. With log returns, drawdown is `1 - exp(L_t - max L)`, not the difference of log levels. On a cumulative-return curve, `1 + R_t` is the wealth index; dividing by the peak of `R_t` itself is a different number and is used only when the task writes it |
| First point | the starting capital (or 1.0) as the first point, so a loss in the first period counts; or the period-end values only | starting capital when the task starts the curve from an initial capital or a value of 1 and says nothing else; period-end values when it defines drawdown on the equity curve from the first close |
| Sign | a positive magnitude (0.25 for a 25% fall); or a negative number `(W - peak) / peak` | "magnitude", "non-negative", "peak-to-trough decline" → positive; "as a negative number", "≤ 0", or the formula with `W - peak` → negative; silent → positive magnitude, and use it as a positive denominator in a Calmar ratio |
| Scale | decimal or percent points | the unit notes of the output; see the unit conventions entry |

atoms.title: Performance metrics: drawdown, Sharpe ratio, Sortino and Calmar ratios, win rate / Sharpe and Sortino ratios
atoms.text:
## Sharpe and Sortino ratios

| Choice | Options | Pick by |
|---|---|---|
| Numerator | mean excess return over a risk-free rate, or the mean return | deduct the risk-free rate when the task gives one and speaks of excess return; do not subtract when it says not to, when it says the risk-free rate is zero, or gives no rate |
| Annualization | $\sqrt{A} \cdot \mathrm{mean} / \mathrm{std}$ with A periods per year; or an unannualized ratio | "annualized" → A from the task, else 252 for daily trading data, 12 monthly, 52 weekly, 365 for calendar-day or 24/7 data; silent on annualization → report the per-period ratio only when the task's numbers are per period, and say which |
| Standard deviation | sample (`ddof=1`) or population (`ddof=0`) | the task's statement; silent → `ddof=1`, the sample estimator and the pandas default; numpy's `np.std` defaults to `ddof=0`, so pass it explicitly |
| Zero volatility | undefined | the task's rule (0, null or NaN); never a division by zero written as inf |
| Sortino denominator | downside deviation `sqrt(mean(min(r - target, 0)^2))` over all periods, or the standard deviation of the negative returns only | the formula the task writes; silent → the first (all periods, target 0 or the stated minimum acceptable return) |

Calmar ratio: annualized return divided by the maximum drawdown magnitude over the same period; the annualized return follows the task's rule (arithmetic $\mathrm{mean} \cdot A$ or geometric `(W_T / W_0)^(A / n) - 1`).

atoms.title: Performance metrics: drawdown, Sharpe ratio, Sortino and Calmar ratios, win rate / Win rate and hit rate
atoms.text:
## Win rate and hit rate

| Choice | Options | Pick by |
|---|---|---|
| Unit | closed trades, or periods (days, months) | "trades" → closed round trips; "days", "periods", "hit rate of the signal" → periods |
| Zero result | a loss, excluded, or a win | the task's inequality ("> 0" makes zero a non-win); silent → only results above zero count as wins, and every trade or period stays in the denominator |
| Open position at the end | excluded, or closed at the last price | the task's rule; silent → only closed trades |

For periodic simple returns $r_1, \dots, r_N$ and starting capital $W_0$:

1. Wealth path with the starting capital as the first point: $W_0$, then $W_t = W_0 \prod_{s \le t} (1 + r_s)$.
2. Drawdown as a positive magnitude: $\mathrm{DD}_t = 1 - W_t / \max_{s \le t} W_s$; the maximum drawdown is $\max_t \mathrm{DD}_t$, which lies in $[0, 1)$. The same value follows from cumulative log returns $L_t$: $1 - \exp(L_t - \max_{s \le t} L_s)$.
3. Annualized Sharpe ratio with $A$ periods per year: $\sqrt{A}\,\bar{r}/s_r$, with the sample standard deviation (divisor $N-1$).
4. Sortino ratio: $\sqrt{A}\,\bar{r}/d$, with the downside deviation $d = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum \min(r_t, 0)^2}$ unless the task defines another target or divisor.
5. Win rate: the share of periods with $r_t > 0$; a zero is not a win, and every period stays in the denominator.

Sources: Sharpe (1994), "The Sharpe Ratio", Journal of Portfolio Management 21(1); Sortino and Price (1994), "Performance Measurement in a Downside Risk Framework", Journal of Investing 3(3); Magdon-Ismail and Atiya (2004), "Maximum Drawdown", Risk 17(10).

atoms.title: Annualization and return conventions / overview
atoms.text:
# Annualization and return conventions

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this when a task turns prices into returns, aggregates returns over time, or reports annualized returns or volatilities. A number or formula the task states always wins; the rows below say what to use when it does not.

atoms.title: Annualization and return conventions / Decisions
atoms.text:
## Decisions

| Decision | Options | How the task text selects | When the text is silent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Periods per year A | a stated annualization factor; 252; 365 or 365.25; 52; 12 | A given factor or "periods per year" is used as is. "Trading days" or daily exchange data usually means 252; calendar-day accrual, assets that trade every day, or "calendar days" mean 365 (or 365.25 if written); weekly 52; monthly 12. | Count the observations per year in the data's date column and use the conventional value that matches its frequency, then state it. |
| Volatility scaling | sqrt(A) * sd of period returns; a method the task gives for dependent returns | sqrt(A) assumes uncorrelated period returns; the same rule gives sqrt(h) for an h-period horizon. | sqrt(A), stated as an i.i.d. approximation. |
| Annual return | arithmetic: A * mean(r); geometric: (1 + R_total) ** (A / n) - 1 | "Arithmetic", a formula of mean times A, or a Sharpe-ratio numerator usually means arithmetic; "compound", "CAGR", "geometric" or a formula with a power means geometric. The years elapsed can be n / A or the calendar span in days / 365 (or 365.25). | Report what the field name says (a "CAGR" field is geometric); otherwise arithmetic for ratios built from means, geometric for growth of wealth, and say which. |
| Return definition | log: ln(P[t] / P[t-1]); simple: P[t] / P[t-1] - 1 | "log", "ln", "continuously compounded" mean log; "percentage change", "pct_change", "simple", "arithmetic return" mean simple. | Simple returns for portfolios and wealth, log returns for models written in logs; state the choice. |
| Aggregating over time and across assets | log returns add over time; simple returns compound over time; portfolio returns weight simple returns | A portfolio's return is the weighted sum of simple returns; weighting log returns is only an approximation. | — |

Use one definition for every quantity derived from the same series: a Sharpe ratio, a volatility and a drawdown reported together come from the same returns and the same A.

atoms.title: Annualization and return conventions / Check
atoms.text:
## Check

1. Simple and log returns are linked exactly: $\ln(1 + r^{s}_t) = r^{\ell}_t$; compound simple returns, add log returns, and both give the same total return.
2. Periods per year $A$ come from the data: count the rows per calendar year (about 252 for weekday data, 12 monthly, 52 weekly, 365 calendar daily).
3. Arithmetic annualized return: $A \cdot \bar{r}$.
4. Geometric annualized return over $n$ periods: $\prod_t (1 + r_t)^{A/n} - 1$, which equals $\exp(A \cdot \overline{r^{\ell}}) - 1$.
5. Annualized volatility: $\sqrt{A} \cdot s_r$, with the sample standard deviation (divisor $n-1$).
6. The geometric return is below the arithmetic one whenever the volatility is positive; if it is not, the compounding or the period count is wrong.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / overview
atoms.text:
# Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this reference for positions driven by historical signals, cash-funded trades and portfolio performance measurement. It explains financial accounting and information availability, not a strategy's choice of indicator or trading threshold.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Map the conventions
atoms.text:
## Map the conventions

Identify the observation time, decision time, fill time and valuation time separately. A signal using a period's final price is not available earlier in that period. A rule that fills at a later opening price does not earn the intervening return on newly purchased shares. Explicit task conventions determine corporate-action adjustments, price units, fees, financing, rounding and final liquidation.

An adjusted-price series may incorporate splits or distributions; its adjustment definition matters. Applying distributions again to a total-return-adjusted valuation can double count them. Adjusted fractional holdings describe a synthetic accounting convention and need not equal exchange-traded share counts through a corporate action.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Cash and holdings at a trade
atoms.text:
## Cash and holdings at a trade

Let q be signed shares traded, positive for buying; p the execution price; h the shares before execution; B cash; and F the nonnegative transaction charge. The following identity assumes immediate settlement and no external cash movement at that instant.

**Cash and shares after execution**

$$
\begin{gathered}
B_{\mathrm{new}} = B-q\cdot p-F \\
h_{\mathrm{new}} = h+q
\end{gathered}
$$

**Value at the execution price**

$$
B_{\mathrm{new}}+h_{\mathrm{new}}\cdot p = B+h\cdot p-F
$$

Buying does not itself create a loss equal to the purchase notional: cash becomes an asset. Selling converts an asset to cash. Fees reduce equity. Between trades, financing accrues according to the stated lending/borrowing convention and holdings are marked to the chosen valuation price.

For a long purchase with flat charge f, proportional rate c and available cash B, assuming these are charged only when a positive trade occurs:

**Cash-feasible whole-share limit**

$$
q_{\mathrm{max}} = \max (0, \operatorname{floor}((B-f)/(p\cdot (1+c))))
$$

A risk budget divided by a stop distance is a sizing heuristic, not a loss guarantee: a gap can make the realized exit worse than the stop level. A trailing-stop decision depends on when its reference peak is observed; it does not imply execution at that peak or stop price.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Returns from marked equity
atoms.text:
## Returns from marked equity

For positive consecutive portfolio values $V_{\mathrm{prev}}$ and V, with no external flows between them:

**Single-period simple return**

$$
r = V/V_{\mathrm{prev}}-1
$$

When deposits or withdrawals occur, a raw value ratio mixes capital flows with performance. Time-weighted returns split the measurement at external flows and link the resulting subperiod returns. Purchases and sales within the portfolio are internal transfers, not external contributions.

**Geometrically linked wealth index**

$$
W_{t} = \prod _{j=1}^{t} (1+r_{j})
$$

A signal may deliberately sum historical returns or compound them; these are different ranking rules. Changing one to the other is not a harmless numerical improvement.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Annualization and risk measures
atoms.text:
## Annualization and risk measures

Let A be observations per year, n the number of measured periods, and $s_{r}$ the standard deviation under the prescribed divisor. Arithmetic annual return and geometric annual growth answer different questions.

**Arithmetic annual mean**

$$
\mu _{\mathrm{annual}} = A\cdot \operatorname{mean}(r)
$$

**Compound annual growth for positive terminal wealth**

$$
\mathrm{growth}_{\mathrm{annual}} = W_{n}^{A/n}-1
$$

**Conventional volatility scaling**

$$
\mathrm{vol}_{\mathrm{annual}} = \sqrt{A}\cdot s_{r}
$$

The last expression assumes an appropriate uncorrelated-return approximation; serial covariance changes multi-period variance. Sharpe's numerator ordinarily uses excess returns and arithmetic mean. A specified alternative such as growth divided by volatility must be labeled as that convention, not silently replaced. Zero volatility makes the usual ratio undefined.

**Drawdown with positive high-water mark $H_{t}$**

$$
\begin{gathered}
H_{t} = \max (W_{\mathrm{initial}},W_{1},\ldots ,W_{t}) \\
\mathrm{drawdown}_{t} = 1-W_{t}/H_{t}
\end{gathered}
$$

Maximum drawdown is the maximum of this positive loss fraction. Whether the initial capital point belongs to the observed curve must be explicit; omitting it can hide a loss in the first period. Position-price drawdown and portfolio-equity drawdown differ when cash, leverage or fees are present.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Long-short and repeated estimation
atoms.text:
## Long-short and repeated estimation

Net exposure is the sum of signed weights; gross exposure is the sum of their absolute values. A short book can be written two ways: signed weights, where each short weight is negative (with gross g split equally across n shorts, $-g/n$) and P&L is the sum of weight times return; or positive short sizes, where P&L is the long leg minus the short leg. Use one of them, not both, since applying a negative weight and then subtracting the short leg cancels the short side. Derive each sign from its long or short label, and check that the short leg's P&L has the opposite sign to its names' returns. A unit long leg minus a unit short leg has gross exposure two before any financing convention, so its reported return needs a stated capital denominator. Equity weights, return-spread indices and invested dollars are not interchangeable.

Forecasts, fitted transformations and rankings use information available by the decision time. When a position is the product of a signal and a volatility-based size, align the whole position with the return interval it earns: the holding applied to the return of day t is built only from data through day t-1, both its signal and its volatility size. Lagging only the signal while the size uses a volatility that already includes the same day's squared return is look-ahead; lagging a series that is already aligned shifts it twice. A rule that defines a position at every date has no flat state; a warm-up period without enough history is dropped or handled as the task states, not set to zero exposure silently. The evaluated return series starts at the stated first trading date; days before it belong to the warm-up and enter no performance statistic unless the task says so. When the task states an evaluation or trading start after a signal or risk warm-up → every statistic and regression (mean, volatility, Sharpe, drawdown, hit rate, factor regression) uses the returns from that start onward, flat or cash days inside the evaluation period included → check that the number of return observations equals the length of the stated evaluation period. A task that asks for full-history statistics keeps the full history.

Evaluation window: take the portfolio returns from the stated first trading or evaluation date on (its row count equals the number of dates on or after that date), and compute every statistic and regression, including the hit rate (the share of returns above zero), from that window only.
A single lag is enough when the weights are built from data through t-1 and applied to the return of t; building from t-1 data and then shifting again uses information two days old. Once a sample already contains its rolling warm-up, do not trim it again. Walk-forward evaluation separates historical estimation from subsequent realizations. Selecting a model using a later full sample is a retrospective comparison, not proof of live predictive performance.

When a strategy holds constant target weights from one rebalance date to the next → start the weight frame as NaN, set the rebalance rows, then forward-fill. Rows before the first rebalance have no target yet: the task decides whether the evaluation starts at the first rebalance, holds no position until then, or holds a stated initial portfolio, and the choice changes volatility, Sharpe ratio and drawdown over that stretch:

Weights table: a complete row on each rebalance date (every asset, 0 for those exited), carried forward to the following dates. Rows before the first rebalance get the stated initial holding, or are dropped, as the task says.

Check that every non-rebalance day carries the most recent target, an all-zero target included; a frame started with zeros stays zero between rebalances after `ffill`, so positions exist only on rebalance days. When the strategy holds share counts whose weights drift with prices, carry the shares instead and recompute the weights each day.

When a cross-sectional long-short book is rebalanced on the first trading day of every month from a daily signal → use the tested engine in the Python session rather than your own holdings loop: hand-written loops for this book keep slipping on the rebalance dates, the signal lag, exits and the first position. Write your own only where the task's rules differ from the contract in the comments below:

The provided helper `backtest_tools.monthly_long_short(returns, signal, first_trade_row, n_long, n_short, w_long, w_short, cost_bps)` runs this backtest; its result holds the daily returns from the first trade row on and the number of rebalances. Its inputs:

1. `returns`: daily simple returns, one column per asset, on the trading-day index, with missing values handled as the task says.
2. `signal`: the same index and columns; row $t$ uses data through row $t$. Do not shift it: the engine ranks on row $i-1$ for the book of row $i$.
3. `first_trade_row`: the stated trading start as a row position; the book opens there and rebalances at each later month start.
4. Each rebalance writes the whole book (exits at 0); costs are `cost_bps` per unit of turnover, on the first row the new book earns.
5. Pass `max_position=` only for a cap the task states; a stated per-name weight that breaks a stated cap is a conflict to report.

The number of rebalances is one plus the number of month starts after the first trade date.

When a long-short strategy rebalances monthly from a daily signal and trading starts on a stated row → the book opens on the trading start row (even mid-month) and is rebalanced on the first trading day of each later month; each rebalance ranks on the previous row's signal, known at that close. Here `signal` row t uses data up to row t with no shift of its own, and it shares the returns' date index (a signal built on an integer index and reindexed to dates is all NaN). Adapt the signal and sizes to the task:

Monthly long-short book written out:

1. Rebalance dates: the stated trading start, then the first trading day of each later month.
2. On each rebalance date, rank the previous row of the signal (known at the prior close), which must have at least $n_{\mathrm{long}} + n_{\mathrm{short}}$ valid and varying values; give the $n_{\mathrm{long}}$ largest the long weight and the $n_{\mathrm{short}}$ smallest minus the short weight, and every other asset 0.
3. Write that complete row on the rebalance date, carry it forward to the next rebalance, and hold nothing before the start.
4. Costs per day: the sum of absolute weight changes from the previous day times the cost rate.
5. Portfolio return per day: $\sum_i w_{t,i} r_{t,i}$ minus the cost; the rebalance row's weights earn from that row.
6. Evaluate from the start date on.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Accounting checks
atoms.text:
## Accounting checks

On every row from the first rebalance on, count the positive and the negative weights and sum their absolute values: the counts equal the stated long and short leg sizes, the sum equals the stated gross exposure and never exceeds a stated leverage cap. A larger count means assets that left a leg kept their old weight (write the complete target row, 0 for every exited asset, before carrying weights forward). Print the first rebalance date next to the trading start date; when trading starts before the first scheduled rebalance date, say which reading of the first rebalance was used.

At a trade, the change in equity at its fill price equals negative fees. With all positions closed and no flows or financing, terminal cash minus initial cash equals the sum of net completed-trade profits. If positions remain open, unrealized profit also belongs in total equity. The product of value-based returns reproduces the terminal-to-initial equity ratio on the same interval.

atoms.title: Backtest timing, cash accounting and return conventions / Sources
atoms.text:
## Sources

[CFA Institute, GIPS Standards for Asset Owners (2020)](https://www.cfainstitute.org/-/media/documents/code/gips/2020-gips-standards-asset-owners.pdf), calculation methodology, for external-flow treatment and linked returns. Cash conservation, annualization distinctions and gross/net exposure above are direct accounting or algebraic identities. This note does not assert GIPS compliance of a backtest.

atoms.title: Collateralized cross-currency cashflows and resetting notionals / overview
atoms.text:
# Collateralized cross-currency cashflows and resetting notionals

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this note for multi-currency coupon streams, FX-reset principal and spread risk. Contractual exchange directions, reset dates, fixings, settlement and collateral currency determine the cashflows. Explicit task conventions take precedence. The deterministic formulas below are not a general stochastic reset-convexity model.

atoms.title: Collateralized cross-currency cashflows and resetting notionals / Currency-consistent present value
atoms.text:
## Currency-consistent present value

Let domestic currency be collateral currency, $S$ instantaneous domestic units per foreign unit, $D_d(t,T)$ the domestic discount factor, and $F(t,T)$ the collateral-consistent FX forward. A known foreign cashflow $C_f$ paid at $T$ has domestic value:

$$
\mathrm{PV}_d(C_f,T)=D_d(t,T)F(t,T)C_f
$$

Define the foreign discount curve under domestic collateral by:

$$
D_{f\mid d}(t,T)=\frac{D_d(t,T)F(t,T)}S
$$

Then the same value is $S D_{f\mid d}(t,T)C_f$. A foreign domestic-collateral curve generally differs from that currency's own-collateral OIS curve. Using an observed FX forward and then applying an extra basis multiplier can count the same basis twice.

Implied cross-currency basis. With S in domestic units per foreign unit, the no-basis forward is $F_{\mathrm{CIP}}=S\,D_f/D_d$; the currency with the higher rate trades at a forward discount, and $S\,D_d/D_f$ is a direction error. Quoted as a continuous spread on the foreign leg, the basis is $b=-\ln(F_{\mathrm{mkt}}/F_{\mathrm{CIP}})/T$. A market forward above the no-basis forward gives a negative basis, and a widening basis means more negative. State the year fraction, and annualize before reporting in basis points.

For a random foreign cashflow, the domestic discounted expectation contains joint FX/cashflow dependence. Replacing both factors by separate forecasts is an additional deterministic approximation, not a universal no-arbitrage identity.

atoms.title: Collateralized cross-currency cashflows and resetting notionals / Projected and already-fixed coupons
atoms.text:
## Projected and already-fixed coupons

Let $P_f$ be a projection pseudo-discount curve and $\alpha_i$ the contractual year fraction for $[T_{i-1},T_i]$. An unfixed simple forward is:

$$
L_i(t)=\frac{P_f(t,T_{i-1})/P_f(t,T_i)-1}{\alpha_i}
$$

A foreign coupon with signed receiver/payer direction $s_f\in\{-1,1\}$, positive notional $N_i$ and spread $b$ is:

$$
C_{f,i}=s_fN_i\alpha_i(L_i+b)
$$

The coupon for $[T_{i-1},T_i]$ uses the notional in force during that interval. With a start-of-period reset, this is $N_{f,i-1}$, set at $T_{i-1}$; the reset at $T_i$ sets the next interval, unless the contract specifies otherwise. Once the fixing is known, its observed rate replaces the projected forward. A valuation roll can change which coupons are fixed. Projection and discount curves serve different purposes; the spread's currency leg and compounding are contractual.

atoms.title: Collateralized cross-currency cashflows and resetting notionals / Reset exchanges
atoms.text:
## Reset exchanges

Suppose a domestic reference notional is $N_d$ and a foreign notional resets using domestic-per-foreign FX $X_i$. The equal-value foreign notional is:

$$
N_{f,i}=\frac{N_d}{X_i}
$$

For the side that originally lends foreign principal, increasing that principal requires an additional payment. A genuine cash-settled reset at its contractual exchange date therefore has cashflow:

$$
C_{\mathrm{reset},i}=N_{f,i-1}-N_{f,i}
$$

Initial lending is $-N_{f,0}$ and final repayment is $+N_{f,m}$. Principal cashflows telescope to zero in foreign units when all exchanges are included; their discounted domestic values need not cancel. The borrower has opposite signs. A bookkeeping notional reset without a principal payment is a different contract. Already-settled principal exchanges are not future cashflows.

Using $X_i=F(t,T_i)$ for unknown future resets is a deterministic-forward approximation. In general, expected reciprocal FX differs from reciprocal expected FX, and random notionals can correlate with coupons.

atoms.title: Collateralized cross-currency cashflows and resetting notionals / All-in spread and risk
atoms.text:
## All-in spread and risk

If all other cashflows, notionals and curves are held fixed and the spread enters coupons linearly, trade value is affine in that spread. The signed spread annuity is: For the foreign-leg formula below, the spread is paid on that foreign leg; a domestic-leg spread omits the FX-forward conversion.

$$
A_b=\sum_i s_fN_i\alpha_iD_d(t,T_i)F(t,T_i)
$$

For $A_b\ne0$, the total par spread is:

$$
b_{\mathrm{par}}=-\frac{\mathrm{PV}(0)}{A_b}
$$

At a current spread $b_0$, the incremental spread change to par is $-\mathrm{PV}(b_0)/A_b$; it is not the all-in spread unless added to $b_0$. If notionals or curves depend on the trial spread, the affine identity no longer applies.

A zero-rate bump with other curves frozen differs from a market-quote bump with recalibration. Holding quoted forwards fixed while moving OIS curves changes implied basis; holding basis fixed generally changes forwards. State which objects are independent before interpreting rate, basis or FX sensitivity. A central derivative divides by the bump; a signed one-basis-point P&L multiplies a rate derivative by $10^{-4}$, with any DV01 sign convention stated separately.

atoms.title: Collateralized cross-currency cashflows and resetting notionals / References
atoms.text:
## References

[Fujii and Takahashi, A General Framework for the Benchmark Pricing in a Fully Collateralized Market](https://arxiv.org/html/1508.06339), collateral-dependent currency valuation. Cashflow signs, telescoping principal identity and affine spread formulas above follow directly from the stated deterministic contract, rather than specifying a universal reset-swap convention.

atoms.title: Corrado (1989) generalised rank test (method): the cross-event rank statistic for event studies / overview
atoms.text:
# Corrado (1989) generalised rank test (method): the cross-event rank statistic for event studies

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Purpose: a nonparametric test of abnormal returns on an event day or over an event window, built from ranks.

Before ranking: relative event days (-5 ... +5) are labels, not array positions. When the estimation residuals and the
event-window abnormal returns are joined into one array, map each relative day to its position explicitly; a negative
relative day used as a NumPy index reads from the end of the array.

When the estimation residuals and the event-window abnormal returns are joined into one array (estimation window first), relative event day $d$ sits at position $n_{\mathrm{est}} + k$, where $k$ is the index of $d$ within the event window. Check that the position of day 0 reads the event-day abnormal return.

How to compute

Ranks. For each event i, put its estimation-window residuals and its event-window abnormal returns into one array of T_i values and rank them jointly (1 = smallest, ties get the average rank). Turn each rank into a centred score:

$$
d_{it} = \frac{\mathrm{rank}_{it}}{T_i + 1} - 0.5
$$

Scaling. There are two forms; they give different numbers. Pick the one that matches how the task describes the normalisation:

| form | when the task describes | daily statistic Z_t |
|---|---|---|
| event-level | each event normalised by the dispersion of its own scores, or a statistic built event by event and then combined | s_i = sqrt(mean of d_it^2 over all T_i days of event i); Z_t = sqrt(N_t) * mean over events of (d_it / s_i) |
| pooled-day | the dispersion over time of the daily average score across events | D_t = mean over events of d_it; S = sqrt(mean of D_t^2 over all pooled days); Z_t = D_t / S |

If the wording settles neither, state which form was used.

Window statistic, both forms: Z_window = (sum of Z_t over the window days) / sqrt(number of window days).

Easy to get wrong

- Every dispersion (s_i or S) is taken over all pooled days of the event, estimation window plus event window, never over the event window alone.
- Rank within each event's own pooled array, never across events and never within the event window only.
- Keep the numerator and the denominator from the same form.
- Divisors are plain means (population form), not n - 1.

Check before writing the output: compute both forms from your own d matrix, print them, and confirm the value you write equals one of them.

Relative event days are labels, not positions. In each pooled array (estimation days first, then the event window)
relative day `day` sits at position `n_est + (day - first_day)`, where `first_day` is the first label of the event
window (for a window -m..+m it is -m). Indexing with `n_est + day` reads the wrong day whenever the window starts
before day 0.

For one relative day, given each event's score array $d_i$, estimation length $n_i$ and the first event-window label $\ell$:

1. Position of the day in event $i$: $n_i + (\mathrm{day} - \ell)$.
2. Event-level form: $s_i = \sqrt{\operatorname{mean}(d_i^2)}$ over all pooled days of event $i$, and $Z = \sqrt{N}\, \operatorname{mean}_i (d_{i,\mathrm{pos}} / s_i)$.
3. Pooled-day form (needs equal $T_i$): $D_t = \operatorname{mean}_i d_{it}$, $S = \sqrt{\operatorname{mean}_t D_t^2}$, and $Z = D_{\mathrm{pos}}/S$.
4. Print both forms and confirm that the written value equals one of them.

Sources: Corrado (1989), Journal of Financial Economics 23(2); Corrado and Zivney (1992), Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 27(3).

Reminder: Corrado dispersions (s_i or S) use all pooled days, estimation plus event window, never the event window alone.
Reminder: pick the event-level or pooled-day form from the task's wording, keep numerator and denominator from that form, and print both forms once to check.

atoms.title: Rating transitions, credit losses and portfolio aggregation / overview
atoms.text:
# Rating transitions, credit losses and portfolio aggregation

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this reference for Gaussian-factor rating migration, default-only portfolio losses, and loss aggregation across scenarios and obligors. It distinguishes these models from full migration-based bond revaluation; it does not estimate a transition matrix from censored rating histories.

atoms.title: Rating transitions, credit losses and portfolio aggregation / 1. Shared Foundations
atoms.text:
## 1. Shared Foundations

Map notation by economic meaning, units and horizon. Explicit task definitions take precedence; if definitions conflict, identify the ambiguity and state the interpretation. A label such as mean loss alone does not identify the averaging population.

Let i index obligors, s index independent scenarios, and k index terminal rating states. $\operatorname{E}_{i}$ is exposure in currency, $R_{i}$ is a recovery fraction, and $p_{ik}$ is the probability of state k conditional on obligor i's initial rating. All probabilities are decimals. Expectations below are under the specified risk distribution, which need not be a risk-neutral pricing measure.

atoms.title: Rating transitions, credit losses and portfolio aggregation / 2. State mapping and dependence
atoms.text:
## 2. State mapping and dependence

Each transition row is a categorical probability distribution, including every terminal state in the model.

$$
\begin{gathered}
p_{ik} \ge  0 \\
\sum _{k} p_{ik} = 1
\end{gathered}
$$

For a chosen state ordering, $b_{ik}$ is the cumulative-normal threshold. $\Phi$ denotes the standard normal distribution function; $b_{\mathrm{i0}}$ is minus infinity and $b_{\mathrm{iK}}$ is plus infinity, where K is the number of states.

$$
\begin{gathered}
b_{ik} = \Phi _{\mathrm{inverse}}(\sum _{j=1}^{k} p_{ij}) \\
\mathrm{state}_{i} = k \;\text{when}\; b_{i,k-1} < Z_{i} \le  b_{ik}
\end{gathered}
$$

This construction gives each interval probability $p_{ik}$ by subtraction of two cumulative probabilities. If states run best to worst, high Z is bad; if they run worst to best, low Z is bad. Both conventions are valid when thresholds and the state mapping agree. They give the same distribution but not the same simulated scenarios: with a fixed seed, the bonds that default in a given draw differ between the two orientations. In the CreditMetrics formulation the latent variable is a standardized asset return, so a low value is bad: default is the lowest interval and the best rating the highest, with thresholds cumulated from the default end of the transition row. Use that orientation when the latent variable is described as an asset return or ability-to-pay index, and keep it in every place that reads the thresholds. Equality at a threshold has zero probability under a continuous normal model. Zero-probability states have empty intervals.

For a common nonnegative loading $\beta _{i}$, a unit-normal systematic factor M and mutually independent unit-normal idiosyncratic factors $\epsilon _{i}$ give unit marginal variance.

$$
\begin{gathered}
Z_{i} = \beta _{i}\cdot M + \sqrt{1-\beta _{i}^{2}}\cdot \epsilon _{i} \\
0 \le  \beta _{i} \le  1 \\
\operatorname{Corr}(Z_{i},Z_{j}) = \beta _{i}\cdot \beta _{j}, \text{for distinct} i,j
\end{gathered}
$$

In a homogeneous model $\beta _{i} = \sqrt{\rho}, \rho$ is the pairwise latent correlation. With unequal loadings, $\beta _{i}$ squared is the systematic variance share, not every pair's correlation. Default-indicator correlation is a different quantity.

For upper-tail default probability $p_{iD}$ and $\beta _{i} < 1$, the conditional default probability is:

$$
\begin{gathered}
c_{i} = \Phi _{\mathrm{inverse}}(1-p_{iD}) \\
\operatorname{P}(\mathrm{default}_{i} \vert  M=m) = 1-\Phi ((c_{i}-\beta _{i}\cdot m)/\sqrt{1-\beta _{i}^{2}})
\end{gathered}
$$

For lower-tail default, the corresponding probability is:

$$
\begin{gathered}
c_{i} = \Phi _{\mathrm{inverse}}(p_{iD}) \\
\operatorname{P}(\mathrm{default}_{i} \vert  M=m) = \Phi ((c_{i}-\beta _{i}\cdot m)/\sqrt{1-\beta _{i}^{2}})
\end{gathered}
$$

At $\beta _{i} = 1$ the latent value equals M and the event is deterministic conditional on M; the formulas with a zero denominator are not applicable. Probabilities zero and one represent impossible and certain default without a finite threshold.

atoms.title: Rating transitions, credit losses and portfolio aggregation / 3. Which loss model applies?
atoms.text:
## 3. Which loss model applies?

When only default causes loss, $D_{is}$ is the default indicator and $\mathrm{LGD}_{i}$ is the lost fraction of exposure. For deterministic exposure and recovery:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{LGD}_{i} = 1-R_{i} \\
L_{is} = \operatorname{E}_{i}\cdot \mathrm{LGD}_{i}\cdot D_{is} \\
L_{s} = \sum _{i} L_{is} \\
\operatorname{E}[L] = \sum _{i} \operatorname{E}_{i}\cdot \mathrm{LGD}_{i}\cdot p_{iD}
\end{gathered}
$$

Correlation changes the distribution but not this expected-loss identity. Random recovery or exposure correlated with default requires the expectation of their product instead.

When nondefault migration changes market value, a default-only loss is insufficient. Let H be the risk horizon, $C_{ij}$ future contractual cash flows paid at dates $t_{ij} > H$, and $\operatorname{P}_{k}$(H,$t_{ij}$) the rating-conditioned valuation discount factors at H. Nondefault horizon value is:

$$
V_{i}(H,k) = \sum _{j:t_{ij}>H} C_{ij}\cdot \operatorname{P}_{k}(H,t_{ij})
$$

Cash flows received on or before H belong to horizon wealth separately, with any specified reinvestment. Default recovery must follow the contract's recovery base and payment timing. Horizon loss is specified reference wealth minus actual wealth, both measured at $H$. Reference wealth may, for example, be the horizon value conditional on the initial rating remaining unchanged; state the requested reference explicitly; a present-value loss discounts consistently. Do not subtract today's price directly from an undiscounted future value. Transition probabilities and rating-dependent valuation inputs have distinct roles. These are the default/nondefault valuation branches of CreditMetrics [1].

atoms.title: Rating transitions, credit losses and portfolio aggregation / 4. Scenarios, groups and averaging
Rating transitions, credit losses and portfolio aggregation / 5. Quantiles and tails with default-loss atoms
atoms.text:
## 5. Quantiles and tails with default-loss atoms

For loss L and confidence $\alpha$ in (0,1), the lower quantile convention is:

$$
q_{\alpha} = \inf  \{x : \operatorname{P}(L \le  x) \ge  \alpha \}
$$

Interpolated empirical quantiles are a different finite-sample convention. A task may define a strict or inclusive conditional tail mean. These definitions are generally different at a loss atom:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{tail}_{\mathrm{strict}} = \operatorname{E}[L \vert  L > q_{\alpha}] \\
\mathrm{tail}_{\mathrm{inclusive}} = \operatorname{E}[L \vert  L \ge  q_{\alpha}]
\end{gathered}
$$

An empty strict tail has no conditional mean. Integrated-quantile expected shortfall fills exactly probability $1-\alpha$, taking only the required mass at the quantile [2].

$$
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha} = (\operatorname{E}[L\cdot \operatorname{indicator}(L>q_{\alpha})] \\
+ q_{\alpha}\cdot (\operatorname{P}(L\le q_{\alpha})-\alpha ))/(1-\alpha )
\end{gathered}
$$

An equivalent expression, for a finite first moment, is [2]:

$$
\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha} = \min _{z} \{z + \operatorname{E}[\max (L-z,0)]/(1-\alpha )\}
$$

For equally weighted scenarios, retain the largest losses until the tail mass is filled, allowing a fractional boundary scenario. Averaging a rounded number of scenarios is an approximation unless the tail size is an integer. Whichever tail definition is required, additive group attribution uses the same portfolio-tail scenarios and boundary weights for every group; separate group tails do not in general add to portfolio ES.

atoms.title: Rating transitions, credit losses and portfolio aggregation / 6. Checks and Scope
atoms.text:
## 6. Checks and Scope

Marginal transition frequencies should recover the input probabilities within sampling error, regardless of dependence. Group loss totals sum exactly scenario by scenario. Expected default-only loss has the analytic check in Section 3. Sampling precision for a probability is governed by independent scenarios; dependent names within a scenario are not independent replications.

Nonnegative exposures and LGD in [0,1] imply loss lies between zero and total exposure. With known deterministic LGDs the upper bound tightens to the sum of exposure times LGD. VaR need not exceed expected loss: a rare severe loss can produce a zero quantile and positive mean. ES, strict tail means and inclusive tail means must not be silently interchanged.

This entry does not cover transition-history estimation, recovery calibration, regulatory capital rules, valuation of callable credit instruments, or arbitrarily dependent stochastic recoveries. Full rating migration revaluation needs contractual cash flows and horizon valuation curves, not merely a default probability.

For cumulative-probability thresholds, set the first and last endpoints explicitly to $-\infty$ and $+\infty$. Do not compute the final endpoint by applying the inverse CDF to a rounded row total.

atoms.title: Rating transitions, credit losses and portfolio aggregation / References
atoms.text:
## References

[1] Gupton, Finger and Bhatia (1997), CreditMetrics Technical Document, Sections 2.3 and 3.1–3.2: rating-dependent revaluation and latent-threshold dependence. [Original document](https://www.phy.pmf.unizg.hr/~bp/CMTD1.pdf).

[2] Rockafellar and Uryasev (2002), Conditional Value-at-Risk for General Loss Distributions: discrete distributions and mass at the quantile. [Author manuscript](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~rtr/papers/rtr187-CVaR2.pdf).

atoms.title: Estimator variants: ddof, skewness and kurtosis, recursion seeds, rounding to whole units, Student-t scale / overview
atoms.text:
# Estimator variants: ddof, skewness and kurtosis, recursion seeds, rounding to whole units, Student-t scale

The task description inside <task_instructions> takes priority over this card: where it gives a different formula, input, setting or convention, follow the task description.

Use this when a task computes standard deviations or z-scores, runs an exponential average or a variance recursion, sizes positions in whole units, or uses a Student-t distribution. A choice the task states always wins.

atoms.title: Estimator variants: ddof, skewness and kurtosis, recursion seeds, rounding to whole units, Student-t scale / Decisions
atoms.text:
## Decisions

| Decision | Options | How the task text selects | When the text is silent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Divisor of a standard deviation | ddof=1 (sample, unbiased variance) or ddof=0 (population, maximum likelihood) | "sample", "unbiased", "ddof=1", or an inference statistic (t-statistic, standard error) mean ddof=1; "population", "ddof=0", or a normal maximum-likelihood fit mean ddof=0. | Depends on the quantity: a reported volatility or standard deviation of returns, a Sharpe ratio and an inference statistic use ddof=1 (sample); z-normalizing columns before a PCA (a correlation-matrix PCA) uses ddof=0, as sklearn StandardScaler and scipy.stats.zscore do; a moment inside a HAC (Newey-West) test statistic uses divisor $T$, consistent with that estimator's covariance. For other quantities defaults differ by library: pandas Series.std / DataFrame.std / cov use ddof=1, numpy std / var and scipy.stats.zscore use ddof=0, sklearn StandardScaler uses ddof=0; pick one deliberately and state it. Always pass ddof explicitly and use the same value for every series the task treats alike. |
| Skewness and kurtosis | biased sample moments ($g_1 = m_3/m_2^{3/2}$, excess $g_2 = m_4/m_2^2 - 3$) or bias-corrected ($G_1$, $G_2$); excess or raw kurtosis | A named function means its own defaults: `scipy.stats.skew(x)` is $g_1$ (`bias=True`), `scipy.stats.kurtosis(x)` is excess $g_2$ (`fisher=True`, `bias=True`); "unbiased" or "adjusted" means $G_1$, $G_2$ (`bias=False`, also what pandas `Series.skew()` and `Series.kurt()` return); "Pearson" or "raw" kurtosis means `fisher=False` (3 added). | Defaults differ by library: scipy gives the biased $g_1$, $g_2$; pandas gives the bias-corrected $G_1$, $G_2$. Call the function the task names, or pass `bias` explicitly, and use the same choice for every series. |
| Start of an exponential average (EMA) | first observation, `ewm(span, adjust=False)`; the simple mean of the first span values, starting at position span - 1; the weighted average with `adjust=True` | "seeded with the simple moving average" or "SMA seed" means the second; "recursive" or a formula with the previous value means the first; "pandas ewm" with defaults means the third. | The first-observation recursion, stated, with the warm-up values kept or dropped as the text says. |
| Start of a variance recursion (EWMA, GARCH) | sample variance of the whole series or of a first block; first squared return; backcast; zero | The text names it; a fitted GARCH from a library uses that library's backcast. | Sample variance of the estimation series, stated; the effect fades with the decay factor. |
| Start of a running quantity | a stated date's value (a signal day, an entry day), initial capital, or the first observation | The text says where a running peak, running total or high-water mark starts. | The first observation of the series the quantity is defined on. |
| Whole units | floor, round, or keep fractional | Buying with a cash budget uses floor (never exceed the budget); a count of names floor(q * n) differs from round(q * n); "round" means round. | Floor for shares or contracts bought with cash, then recompute the cash left; fractional only when the text allows fractional holdings. |
| Student-t scale | scipy `t(df, loc, scale)` has standard deviation scale * sqrt(df / (df - 2)); a standardized (unit-variance) t uses scale = sd * sqrt((df - 2) / df) | When the text gives a volatility for t innovations, decide whether it is the scale or the standard deviation; "standardized t" means unit variance. | Treat a stated volatility as the standard deviation and convert to scale, stated. |

atoms.title: Estimator variants: ddof, skewness and kurtosis, recursion seeds, rounding to whole units, Student-t scale / Check
atoms.text:
## Check

1. Standard deviation: pandas `Series.std()` uses divisor $n-1$; NumPy `std` uses divisor $n$ unless `ddof=1` is given.
2. `scipy.stats.zscore` uses the population standard deviation (divisor $n$): $(x - \bar{x}) / s_{n}$.
3. Skewness: `scipy.stats.skew(x)` equals $g_1$; pandas `Series.skew()` equals $G_1 = g_1\sqrt{n(n-1)}/(n-2)$, which equals `scipy.stats.skew(x, bias=False)`; with a few hundred observations the two differ in the third decimal. Kurtosis likewise: `scipy.stats.kurtosis(x)` is excess $g_2$, pandas `Series.kurt()` is the bias-corrected excess $G_2$.
4. Exponential moving average with span $k$ has $\alpha = 2/(k+1)$. The recursive form `ewm(span=k, adjust=False)` starts at the first observation; the SMA-seeded form leaves the first $k-1$ values undefined, seeds with the mean of the first $k$ values, and continues $E_t = \alpha p_t + (1 - \alpha) E_{t-1}$. They differ early in the series.
5. Whole shares with a fixed fee: $\lfloor (\text{cash} - \text{fee}) / \text{price} \rfloor$, so that shares times price plus fee does not exceed the cash and one more share would.
6. Student t with $\nu$ degrees of freedom and a target standard deviation $\sigma$: the scale is $\sigma \sqrt{(\nu - 2)/\nu}$, because the variance of a t variable with scale $s$ is $s^2 \nu / (\nu - 2)$.
